=== NOTES 2:4 | Preamble – Text, Keywords, 42ND Amendment and Its Status
## SUB 0 | 42nd Amendment, 1976 – Socialist, Secular, Integrity
[4:0:0] # What the 42nd Amendment did to the Preamble
[4:0:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [4:0:1.0] Words added | Socialist, Secular, Integrity (three words)
  [4:0:1.1] Description of India | "Sovereign Democratic Republic" → "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic"
  [4:0:1.2] Fraternity clause | "unity of the Nation" → "unity and integrity of the Nation"
  [4:0:1.3] Year / context | 1976, during the Emergency (1975-77), Indira Gandhi government
  [4:0:1.4] Based on | Swaran Singh Committee
  [4:0:1.5] Nickname | "Mini Constitution" – it changed the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule and 53 Articles
[4:0:2] - **Only amendment of the Preamble so far:** the **42nd (1976)**; asked about 25 times (APPSC G2 2008, 2011, 2025 Mains; AEE 2008; Endowment 2008; JL 2003; Polytechnic 2019; Degree Lecturers 2020; Constable 2016; SSC, NDA 2018, UPPSC, MPPSC 2023).
[4:0:3] - **⚠ Trap:** not the 1st, 2nd, 17th, 24th, 25th, 38th, 40th, 41st, 43rd, 44th, 45th, 46th, 52nd, 73rd or 86th Amendment ("1976 Second Amendment" is wrong).
[4:0:4] - **'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted between 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic'.**
[4:0:5] - **Integrity** was **not** in the Preamble in **1975**; it came in **1976** (SSC 2019; UPPSC 2006). The word **"unity"** was in the **original** text – only "and integrity" was added (a question saying "'Unity of the Nation' was added by the 42nd" means this change).
[4:0:6] - **NOT added by the 42nd:** **Fraternity**, **Sovereign**, Democratic, Republic (all original); **Gram Swarajya**, Dignity of person, Privacy, Liberal are not 42nd words.
[4:0:7] - **Assertion-reason:** "India is a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic" (A) is true and its reason – the 42nd Act **substituted** these words for "Sovereign Democratic Republic" (R) – correctly explains it.
[4:0:8] # Other changes of the 42nd Amendment (for "not associated" items)
[4:0:9] - Added **Fundamental Duties** (Part IVA) and new DPSPs; **curtailed** judicial review in some matters but did **not abolish** it entirely.
[4:0:10] - **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down its Art. 368 clauses **(4) and (5)** (unlimited amending power, exclusion of judicial review) and the clause giving **DPSPs full priority over all Fundamental Rights** – restoring the balance of Parts III and IV.
[4:0:11] > Status today: in **Dr Balram Singh v. Union of India (25 Nov 2024)** the Supreme Court **upheld 'Socialist' and 'Secular'** and dismissed the challenges to their insertion (as of 2026; the words were again debated politically in Jul 2025).
[4:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.11 (42nd Amendment), p.230, p.232; Rocket Polity #14 p.36-37; app notes 2:4 sub 7; sci.gov.in (Balram Singh, 25 Nov 2024)
## SUB 1 | Preamble Text – Order of Words, Original 1949 Text, Words Not in It
[4:1:0] # The text (as amended in 1976)
[4:1:1] - **WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA**, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a **SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC** and to secure to all its citizens: **JUSTICE**, social, economic and political; **LIBERTY** of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; **EQUALITY** of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all **FRATERNITY** assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
[4:1:2] - **Order:** **Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic** (code C, A, D, B for Socialist A, Democratic B, Sovereign C, Secular D); objectives in order **Justice → Liberty → Equality → Fraternity**.
[4:1:3] - **India is declared secular by the Preamble** (Fundamental Rights, DPSP and 9th Schedule do not "describe" India as secular).
[4:1:4] - **Equality of** → **status** (and of opportunity); not "of nationality", "religion" or "community".
[4:1:5] # Original 1949 text vs now
[4:1:6] TABLE head: Item | 26 Nov 1949 / 26 Jan 1950 | Now (after 1976)
  [4:1:6.0] Description of India | "Sovereign Democratic Republic" | "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic"
  [4:1:6.1] Fraternity clause | "unity of the Nation" | "unity and integrity of the Nation"
  [4:1:6.2] Words absent in 1949 | Socialist, Secular, Integrity | added
[4:1:7] - **Exact status on 26 January 1950:** a **Sovereign Democratic Republic** (UPSC 2021).
[4:1:8] - **Not in the 1949 Preamble:** Socialism / Socialist, Secular, Integrity; "Reliable" and "Non-religious" were never in it; **Republic** was in the original (UPPSC 2009; Uttarakhand 2024 → 2, 3, 4).
[4:1:9] # Words NOT in the Preamble at all
[4:1:10] - **Federal / federation** (APPSC Deputy Surveyors 2012; UPPSC 2021) – "Quasi-federal" is not in it either.
[4:1:11] - **Freedom** (it uses **Liberty**), **Right** (as a word), **Public Welfare** / **Welfare State**, **Adult franchise**, **Fundamental Duties**, "**People's**".
[4:1:12] - **Religious Justice**, **Natural** or **Cultural** justice (justice is only **social, economic, political**).
[4:1:13] - **Political Liberty** and **Economic Liberty** as categories; liberty "of action" (liberty is only of **thought, expression, belief, faith, worship**) (UPSC 2017; APPSC G2).
[4:1:14] - Words that ARE in it: Fraternity, Equality, Justice, **Unity**, Integrity, Thought, Opportunity, **Dignity**, Republic, Sovereign.
[4:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.229-230 (text, 42nd words); Rocket Polity #14 p.36-37; app notes 2:4 sub 1
## SUB 2 | We, the People – Source of Authority, Date and Adoption
[4:2:0] - **Source of the Constitution / of political power:** the **people of India** – the Preamble opens "**We, the People of India**", showing **people's sovereignty**; the Constitution derives its authority from the people (APPSC G1 2002, G2, AEE 2012, CDPO 2013; HWO 2017).
[4:2:1] - **⚠ Trap:** not the Constitution, Parliament, "Parliament and State Legislatures", the President or the Supreme Court.
[4:2:2] - The Preamble **indicates the source** from which the Constitution comes (APPSC G2 2011).
[4:2:3] - **"We, the People of India"** is used in the **Preamble**, not in the FRs, DPSPs or Citizenship part.
[4:2:4] - **Enacting clause:** "We, the people of India … **in our Constituent Assembly** … do hereby **adopt, enact and give to ourselves** this Constitution" – the Constitution is declared adopted and enacted by the **people of India**, acting through the **Constituent Assembly** (when only the CA is offered, it is the answer for "adopted by").
[4:2:5] # The date
[4:2:6] - **Date in the Preamble:** **26 November 1949** = **adoption** of the Constitution (drafting completed; signed by the President of the CA) – not 26 January 1950 (commencement), 24 January 1950 or 13 December 1946.
[4:2:7] - **Commencement:** **26 January 1950** (some provisions – citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament – took effect on 26 Nov 1949).
[4:2:8] - **Constitution Day:** **26 November**, observed **since 2015** (Constitution Day 2019 = 26 Nov) (APPSC G2 Mains 2017; JL 2020).
[4:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.136-137, p.229-230; Rocket Polity #14 p.36-37; app notes 2:4 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | Is the Preamble Part of the Constitution? – Cases and Legal Status
[4:3:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Held on the Preamble
  [4:3:0.0] Berubari Union (President's reference) | 1960 | Not a part of the Constitution (the first such ruling); a "key to the minds of the makers"; aid to interpretation where an Article is ambiguous
  [4:3:0.1] Golaknath | 1967 | About amending Fundamental Rights; not the Preamble case (distractor)
  [4:3:0.2] Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Is a part of the Constitution (overruled Berubari); amendable under Art. 368 but the basic structure cannot be destroyed; 13 judges
  [4:3:0.3] S.R. Bommai | 1994 | Relied on the Preamble – secularism a basic feature; Preamble treated as integral part
  [4:3:0.4] LIC of India | 1995 | Reaffirmed the Preamble is an integral part
  [4:3:0.5] Minerva Mills | 1980 | Struck down 42nd Amendment Art. 368 clauses – not a Preamble-status case
[4:3:1] - **"Preamble is a part" =** **Kesavananda Bharati** (APPSC TWO 2012, G2 2008, ZSWO 2025); with no Kesavananda option, **Bommai** (UPPSC 2012); A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi, Mohini Jain, Sajjan Singh are distractors.
[4:3:2] - **"Not a part" =** **Berubari, 1960** (not 1968; Kesavananda was 1973, not 1970).
[4:3:3] # Legal nature
[4:3:4] - **Non-justiciable** – **not enforceable** in a court of law (UPPSC 2019).
[4:3:5] - **Neither a source of power** to the legislature **nor a prohibition** on its powers; confers no power and creates no right by itself.
[4:3:6] - **Part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts** (UPSC 2020).
[4:3:7] - **Cannot override** the specific provisions of the Constitution; where a provision is clear, the Preamble yields.
[4:3:8] - **Aid to interpretation:** may be invoked to determine the **ambit of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles** (APPSC G1).
[4:3:9] - **Amendable** under Art. 368 (done once, 1976) – so "it cannot be amended" is false; "not a part of the Constitution" is false.
[4:3:10] - **Enacted after** the rest of the Constitution, so that it conformed to the text – "enacted before the entire Constitution" is false (APPSC G1 2023 → I and III incorrect).
[4:3:11] - Reflects the **philosophy, ideals and objectives** of the Constitution – the **mind of the makers** (UPSC 2017) and the **objective of the Constitution** (UPPSC 2013) are reflected in the Preamble, not in FRs, DPSP or FDs.
[4:3:12] > Statement sets: "Objectives Resolution became the Preamble ✓; non-justiciable ✓; can't be amended ✗; can't override specific provisions ✓" → **I, II and IV** (UPPSC 2009, Panchayat Secretary). "Not a part ✗; amended only under Art. 368 ✓; three words added in 1976 ✓" → **B and C**.
[4:3:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.159 (cases), p.229 (status); Rocket Polity #14 p.37; app notes 2:4 sub 4-5
[4:3:14] - **S.R. Bommai (1994):** a State government acting against **secularism** can be dismissed under Art. 356.
[4:3:15] - **Waman Rao (1981):** basic-structure review applies to amendments made **after 24 April 1973** (the Kesavananda judgment date).
[4:3:16] - **Secularism** was part of the basic structure **even before** the word 'Secular' was inserted in 1976 (Kesavananda 1973; Bommai 1994).
## SUB 4 | Keywords and Objectives – Meaning
[4:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [4:4:0.0] Sovereign | Supreme authority; free internally and externally; not subject to any external authority
  [4:4:0.1] Socialist | Democratic socialism – a mixed economy (public and private sectors); a blend of Marxism and Gandhism, leaning towards Gandhian socialism
  [4:4:0.2] Secular | Equal respect for all religions; no State religion; before 1976 the word appeared only in Art. 25(2)(a); the term is not defined in any Article
  [4:4:0.3] Democratic | Government by the people; representative parliamentary democracy; covers political, social and economic democracy; universal adult franchise and rule of law are its marks
  [4:4:0.4] Republic | Elected head of State (the President, indirectly elected for 5 years); no hereditary element; public offices open to all
[4:4:1] - **Republic ≠ PM:** India is a republic because its **head of State (President) is elected** – not because ministers are responsible to Parliament or hold office at the President's pleasure.
[4:4:2] - **Philosophy of the Constitution:** welfare state, socialist state, political equality – but **not a Communist State** (UPPSC 2015).
[4:4:3] - India is a **democratic polity, a sovereign State, a democratic society and a welfare state** – all four (UPPSC 2012); the **welfare-state** idea is found in the **Preamble and the DPSP** (UPPSC 1997).
[4:4:4] - **Not valid (APPSC G1 2024):** "'democratic' is a mix of British Fabian Socialism and American Populism"; "Republic = elected Prime Minister"; "Liberty is neither absolute nor qualified"; "Fraternity originally denoted only dignity of the individual" → **none valid**.
[4:4:5] # Objectives
[4:4:6] TABLE head: Objective | Of / kinds
  [4:4:6.0] Justice | Social, economic and political – three kinds
  [4:4:6.1] Liberty | Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship – five
  [4:4:6.2] Equality | Status and opportunity – civic, political, economic dimensions
  [4:4:6.3] Fraternity | Sense of brotherhood; assures dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation; promoted by single citizenship
[4:4:7] - **Goals secured to all:** justice (social, economic, political), liberty of thought and expression, equality of opportunity and **dignity of the individual** – **all** of them (UPPSC 1998).
[4:4:8] - **Liberty** = **absence of restraints plus opportunity to develop one's personality**; UPSC 2019 "most appropriate definition" = **opportunity to develop oneself fully** (positive liberty); liberty is not licence to do whatever one likes.
[4:4:9] - **Law and liberty (UPSC 2018):** "**If there are no laws, there is no liberty**" – law is the condition of liberty.
[4:4:10] - **Political theory links:** popular/political **sovereignty** – **Rousseau** (general will); **distributive justice** – **Aristotle**.
[4:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.166 (secular state), p.230-232 (keywords, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity); Rocket Polity #14 p.36; app notes 2:4 sub 2-3; UPSC CSE 2018, 2019 official keys
## SUB 5 | Making and Sources of the Preamble's Ideals
[4:5:0] - **Basis:** the **Objectives Resolution** of **Jawaharlal Nehru** – moved **13 December 1946**, adopted **22 January 1947**; its modified version became the Preamble (Nehru "proposed the Preamble"; not Ambedkar, B.N. Rau or Gandhi) (APPSC ASWO; Uttarakhand 2006; APPSC JA).
[4:5:1] - The Constitution of India was **not** the first to begin with a Preamble (the **US** Constitution did); the Preamble has been amended **once**, not twice.
[4:5:2] TABLE head: Element | Source
  [4:5:2.0] Idea of a Preamble; "We, the people" | USA
  [4:5:2.1] Language of the Preamble | Australia
  [4:5:2.2] Liberty, Equality, Fraternity (the "trinity"); Republic | French Revolution (1789) / French Constitution
  [4:5:2.3] Justice – social, economic and political | Russian Revolution (1917), USSR
  [4:5:2.4] Fraternity (possible) | Art. 1 of the UDHR (1948)
[4:5:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Liberty-equality-fraternity is **not** from the Russian, American or Glorious Revolution or the UN Charter; justice is **not** from the French Revolution.
[4:5:4] - **Third reading** of the Constitution: **17-26 November 1949**; Preamble enacted last.
[4:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.140, p.152 (Q.14), p.155 (sources table), p.229, p.231; Rocket Polity #14 p.36; app notes 2:4 sub 0
## SUB 6 | Descriptions of the Preamble – Who Said What
[4:6:0] TABLE head: Description | Person
  [4:6:0.0] "Identity card of the Constitution" | N.A. Palkhivala
  [4:6:0.1] "Political horoscope" / "horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic" | K.M. Munshi
  [4:6:0.2] "Key-note" to the Constitution | Ernest Barker
  [4:6:0.3] "Key to the minds of the makers" | Supreme Court, Berubari (1960)
  [4:6:0.4] "Soul" of the Constitution | Thakurdas Bhargava (the Preamble is called the soul of the Constitution)
  [4:6:0.5] "Heart and soul" | Ambedkar – Article 32, not the Preamble
[4:6:1] - **"Key of the Constitution"** – the standard attributions are **Ernest Barker** ("key-note") and the **Supreme Court** (Berubari, Sajjan Singh: "key to open the mind of the makers"); no reliable source gives it to Gandhi, Motilal Nehru, Ambedkar or Indira Gandhi.
[4:6:2] - **Critic of inserting 'Secular' (1976):** constitutional scholar **D.D. Basu** held the insertion unnecessary and productive of vagueness – "productive of more mischief than benefit" (owner to confirm against Basu's *Introduction to the Constitution of India*).
[4:6:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity #14 p.37; PMF Polity Part 1 p.42 (Palkhivala); app notes 2:4 sub 8; blog.lukmaanias.com (Preamble, 2025: Basu on 'secular')

  x: Liberty means absence of restraints on individual activity plus opportunities to develop personality, not freedom from every restraint.

=== NOTES 2:5 | Parts, Schedules and Articles of the Constitution
## SUB 0 | Eighth Schedule – Languages
[5:0:0] # The 22 scheduled languages
[5:0:1] - **Eighth Schedule = languages recognised by the Constitution** (Arts. **344(1) and 351**) – the "regional languages" / "official languages" schedule; **not** the Fourth, Sixth, Seventh or Ninth.
[5:0:2] - **Number:** originally **14**, now **22** (not 18, 21 or 24).
[5:0:3] - **The 22:** Assamese, Bengali, **Bodo**, **Dogri**, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, **Kashmiri**, **Konkani**, **Maithili**, Malayalam, **Manipuri**, Marathi, **Nepali**, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, **Santhali**, **Sindhi**, Tamil, Telugu, **Urdu**.
[5:0:4] - **NOT in the Eighth Schedule:** **English**, **Rajasthani**, **Bhojpuri**, **Gondi**, Bhutia (Bhoti), Tulu, Chhattisgarhi, Gor Boli (Lambadi) – all asked as the odd one out.
[5:0:5] - Hindi, Sanskrit, Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati, Kashmiri were among the **original 14**.
[5:0:6] # Languages added by amendment
[5:0:7] TABLE head: Amendment | Year | Languages added
  [5:0:7.0] 21st | 1967 | Sindhi
  [5:0:7.1] 71st | 1992 | Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali
  [5:0:7.2] 92nd | 2003 | Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali
[5:0:8] - **71st ≠ Maithili:** Maithili came with the **92nd** (UPSC 2024: 71st = Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali only).
[5:0:9] - **Konkani** entered in **1992** (not 2003). 96th Amendment (2011) renamed Oriya as **Odia** (no new language).
[5:0:10] - In **1990** Sindhi was the only language added by amendment; since 1992 Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali also are.
[5:0:11] # Official Language Commission (Art. 344)
[5:0:12] - First **Official Language Commission** set up **7 June 1955** under Art. 344 – chairman **B.G. Kher**; report 1956, reviewed by a parliamentary committee under **G.B. Pant**; **Official Languages Act 1963**.
[5:0:13] - Official language provisions = **Part XVII, Arts. 343–351**.
[5:0:14] # Demands for inclusion (current linkage)
[5:0:15] - No fixed criteria for inclusion (**Pahwa Committee 1996**, **Sitakant Mohapatra Committee 2003**); demands are raised in Parliament – e.g. **Chhattisgarhi** in the Rajya Sabha (CGPSC 2019, 2020) → the **8th Schedule**.
[5:0:16] - **Jun 2026**: fresh demands to include **Bhojpuri** (Konkani, Maithili, Santali are already in).
[5:0:17] - **Jul 2026**: Ministry of Tribal Affairs told Parliament of continuing demands to include **Gor Boli (Lambadi)**, the **Banjara** language of AP and Telangana (PIB).
[5:0:18] - **Sep 2026**: Karnataka made **Tulu** an additional official language in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi – Tulu is **not** in the Eighth Schedule.
[5:0:19] > Odd-one-out pattern: English (3 times), Rajasthani, Gondi, Bhojpuri, Bhutani – none is scheduled; Urdu, Sindhi, Nepali, Dogri, Kashmiri, Sanskrit are.
[5:0:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.157; Indian_Polity Part 1 ch.2 (8th Schedule list); PMF Lens Jul 2026 1.23; Praveen CA360 Sep 2026 (Tulu); Official Languages Commission – Lok Sabha debates 5 May 1955 and Report 1956
## SUB 1 | The Twelve Schedules – Contents
[5:1:0] # Schedule → contents → Articles
[5:1:1] TABLE head: Schedule | Contents | Articles
  [5:1:1.0] First | Names of the States and Union Territories and their territories | 1 and 4
  [5:1:1.1] Second | Emoluments, allowances, privileges – President, Governors, Speakers/Chairmen, Judges, CAG | 59, 65, 75, 97, 125, 148, 158, 164, 186, 221
  [5:1:1.2] Third | Forms of oaths and affirmations | 75, 84, 99, 124, 148, 164, 173, 188, 219
  [5:1:1.3] Fourth | Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) to States and UTs | 4 and 80
  [5:1:1.4] Fifth | Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes | 244
  [5:1:1.5] Sixth | Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram | 244 and 275
  [5:1:1.6] Seventh | Division of powers – Union, State and Concurrent Lists | 246
  [5:1:1.7] Eighth | Languages – 22 | 344 and 351
  [5:1:1.8] Ninth | Acts protected from judicial review (land reforms etc.) | 31B
  [5:1:1.9] Tenth | Anti-defection – disqualification on the ground of defection | 102 and 191
  [5:1:1.10] Eleventh | Powers of Panchayats – 29 matters | 243G
  [5:1:1.11] Twelfth | Powers of Municipalities – 18 matters | 243W
[5:1:2] - **Match (APSLPRB SI 2017):** 7th = distribution of powers, 10th = anti-defection, 11th = Panchayats, 12th = Municipalities.
[5:1:3] - **Wrong pairs asked:** "Ninth – allocation of seats in the Council of States" (that is the **Fourth**); "Eleventh – Municipalities" (that is the **Twelfth**; the Eleventh = Panchayats).
[5:1:4] - **New State created → First Schedule changes** (names and territories; the Fourth changes too when Rajya Sabha seats are re-allotted).
[5:1:5] - **PESA districts / Scheduled Areas** are identified under the **Fifth Schedule** (PESA 1996 extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas); the Sixth covers the four north-eastern States.
[5:1:6] # Schedules added by amendment
[5:1:7] TABLE head: Schedule | Added by
  [5:1:7.0] 9th | 1st Amendment, 1951 – first added
  [5:1:7.1] 10th | 52nd Amendment, 1985
  [5:1:7.2] 11th | 73rd Amendment, 1992 (with Part IX)
  [5:1:7.3] 12th | 74th Amendment, 1992 (with Part IXA) – last added
[5:1:8] # Third Schedule – oaths
[5:1:9] - Covers: Union and State **ministers**; candidates for and members of **Parliament** and **State legislatures**; Judges of the **Supreme Court** and **High Courts**; the **CAG**.
[5:1:10] - "Bear true faith and allegiance … uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India … **perform the duties of my office without fear or favour** … **uphold the Constitution and the laws**" = Form IV – **Judges of the Supreme Court (incl. the Chief Justice of India) and the CAG**. The President's oath says "preserve, protect and defend"; an MP's "faithfully discharge the duty".
[5:1:11] - **Outside the Third Schedule:** President – **Art. 60**; Vice-President – **Art. 69**; Governor – **Art. 159**.
[5:1:12] # Seventh Schedule – three Lists
[5:1:13] TABLE head: List | Originally | Now
  [5:1:13.0] Union | 97 | 100
  [5:1:13.1] State | 66 | 61
  [5:1:13.2] Concurrent | 47 | 52
[5:1:14] - Changes came mainly through the **42nd Amendment (1976)** (items moved from the State to the Concurrent List). Strictly counted after the **101st Amendment (GST)** the Union List has 98 and the State List 59 entries; the standard exam figures are 100 and 61.
[5:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.156-157, p.266-267; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.16-17, p.30 (Fifth Schedule); Constitution of India, Third Schedule Form IV (legislative.gov.in)
## SUB 2 | Ninth Schedule – Land Reforms and Judicial Review
[5:2:0] # Basics
[5:2:1] - Added by the **First Amendment Act, 1951** – the **first Schedule added** – during the prime ministership of **Jawaharlal Nehru** (not the 8th, 9th or 42nd Amendment).
[5:2:2] - Linked with **Article 31B**: Acts placed in it cannot be challenged for violating Fundamental Rights.
[5:2:3] - Purpose: to protect **state land-reform and zamindari-abolition laws** from judicial scrutiny – so **land reform laws are in the 9th Schedule** (not the 7th, 8th or 10th).
[5:2:4] - Acts: **13** originally → about **284** now (NextGen counts 282).
[5:2:5] - **I.R. Coelho (2007):** laws added **after 24 April 1973** (the Kesavananda date) are **open to judicial review** on the basic-structure test.
[5:2:6] # Tamil Nadu 69% reservation
[5:2:7] - The **Tamil Nadu Reservation Act, 1993/94** (69% reservation for SCs, STs and OBCs – above the 50% Indra Sawhney limit) was placed in the **IX Schedule** by the **76th Amendment Act, 1994** to shield it from judicial review.
[5:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.157, p.217, p.261; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.17; Indian_Polity Part 1 ch.5 p.90 (76th Amendment)
## SUB 3 | Parts of the Constitution
[5:3:0] # The 25 Parts
[5:3:1] TABLE head: Part | Subject | Articles
  [5:3:1.0] I | Union and its Territory | 1–4
  [5:3:1.1] II | Citizenship | 5–11
  [5:3:1.2] III | Fundamental Rights | 12–35
  [5:3:1.3] IV | Directive Principles | 36–51
  [5:3:1.4] IV-A | Fundamental Duties (42nd, 1976) | 51-A
  [5:3:1.5] V | The Union – Executive, Parliament, Judiciary, CAG | 52–151
  [5:3:1.6] VI | The States | 152–237
  [5:3:1.7] VII | States in Part B of the First Schedule – repealed (7th Amendment, 1956) | —
  [5:3:1.8] VIII | Union Territories | 239–242
  [5:3:1.9] IX | Panchayats (73rd, 1992) | 243–243-O
  [5:3:1.10] IX-A | Municipalities (74th, 1992) | 243-P–243-ZG
  [5:3:1.11] IX-B | Co-operative Societies (97th, 2011) | 243-ZH–243-ZT
  [5:3:1.12] X | Scheduled and Tribal Areas | 244–244-A
  [5:3:1.13] XI | Relations between the Union and the States | 245–263
  [5:3:1.14] XII | Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits | 264–300-A
  [5:3:1.15] XIII | Trade, Commerce and Intercourse | 301–307
  [5:3:1.16] XIV | Services under the Union and the States (incl. Public Service Commissions, Arts. 315–323) | 308–323
  [5:3:1.17] XIV-A | Tribunals (42nd, 1976) | 323-A–323-B
  [5:3:1.18] XV | Elections | 324–329-A
  [5:3:1.19] XVI | Special provisions relating to certain classes (SC/ST/Anglo-Indian seats, commissions) | 330–342
  [5:3:1.20] XVII | Official Language | 343–351
  [5:3:1.21] XVIII | Emergency | 352–360
  [5:3:1.22] XIX | Miscellaneous | 361–367
  [5:3:1.23] XX | Amendment | 368 only
  [5:3:1.24] XXI | Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Art. 370, 371–371J) | 369–392
  [5:3:1.25] XXII | Short title, commencement, Hindi text, repeals | 393–395
[5:3:2] - **Wrong pair asked:** "Part XX – Municipalities" (Part XX = Amendment; Municipalities = **Part IX-A**).
[5:3:3] - **73rd Amendment, 1992 → new Part IX** (Panchayats) + Eleventh Schedule; **74th → Part IX-A (Municipalities)** + Twelfth Schedule – not district boards or townships. Parts X and XI were in the original Constitution.
[5:3:4] - **Part IX-B:** in 2021 (*Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah*) the SC struck it down **for State co-operative societies**; it survives for **multi-State co-operatives** – the Part is still counted.
[5:3:5] - Part XIV-A came by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** – which also added Part IV-A – not the 44th.
[5:3:6] # Deleted Parts and Articles
[5:3:7] TABLE head: Provision | What happened
  [5:3:7.0] Part VII (Part B States) | Repealed by the 7th Amendment, 1956 (not the 44th) – now the only vacant Part number (the old Part IX was reused in 1992)
  [5:3:7.1] Art. 2A (Sikkim as associate State) | Inserted by the 35th, omitted by the 36th Amendment
  [5:3:7.2] Art. 329A | Omitted by the 44th Amendment
  [5:3:7.3] Art. 242 (Part VIII) | Repealed
  [5:3:7.4] Right to Property (Arts. 31, 19(1)(f)) | Deleted by the 44th; now Art. 300A – a legal right
[5:3:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.18-19 (Rocket Sheet #6); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.158; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57-58 (Part IX-B); SC, Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (20 Jul 2021)
## SUB 4 | Tenth Schedule – Anti-defection
[5:4:0] - **Anti-defection law = Tenth Schedule** (Arts. **102(2) and 191(2)**) – not the 2nd, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th or 9th.
[5:4:1] - Added by the **52nd Amendment Act, 1985** (Rajiv Gandhi government) – not the 42nd, 50th, 51st, 53rd, 85th or 95th.
[5:4:2] - **91st Amendment (2003)** removed the **'split'** (one-third) exception; **merger** (two-thirds) still protected; the presiding officer decides disqualification (subject to judicial review – *Kihoto Hollohan*, 1992).
[5:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.59, p.157; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.17
## SUB 5 | Key Articles – Number Game
[5:5:0] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [5:5:0.0] 1 | "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"
  [5:5:0.1] 32 | Right to constitutional remedies
  [5:5:0.2] 110 | Definition of a Money Bill
  [5:5:0.3] 123 | Ordinance power of the President
  [5:5:0.4] 143 | Advisory jurisdiction of the SC
  [5:5:0.5] 280 | Finance Commission
  [5:5:0.6] 300A | Right to property – legal right
  [5:5:0.7] 312 | All-India Services
  [5:5:0.8] 315–323 | Public Service Commissions (320 = functions)
  [5:5:0.9] 324 | Election Commission
  [5:5:0.10] 326 | Adult suffrage (elections on the basis of adult suffrage)
  [5:5:0.11] 330–334 | Reservation of seats – SCs, STs (and the Anglo-Indian nomination of Arts. 331/333, lapsed in Jan 2020 – 104th Amendment)
  [5:5:0.12] 338 / 338A / 338B | NCSC / NCST / NCBC
  [5:5:0.13] 340 | Commission for Backward Classes
  [5:5:0.14] 343–351 | Official Language
  [5:5:0.15] 356 | President's Rule
  [5:5:0.16] 368 | Amendment of the Constitution
  [5:5:0.17] 370 | Temporary provisions for J&K – made inoperative in 2019
[5:5:1] - **Match (UPPSC 2023):** 324 – Election Commission, 315 – PSC, 280 – Finance Commission, 338 – NCSC.
[5:5:2] - **Reorganisation of States, 1956 = 7th Amendment Act** (abolished Part A/B/C/D States, created States and UTs; repealed Part VII).
[5:5:3] - **Right to Property** omitted as a Fundamental Right by the **44th Amendment (1978)** – not the 40th, 42nd or 46th.
[5:5:4] # Article 1 – Union of States
[5:5:5] - India is a **"Union"** – not the result of an agreement among States; **States cannot secede**.
[5:5:6] - "**An indestructible Union of destructible States**".
[5:5:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.10-11 (article list), p.38-40 (44th); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.158
## SUB 6 | Special Provisions – Articles 371 to 371J
[5:6:0] TABLE head: Article | State | Special provision
  [5:6:0.0] 371 | Maharashtra and Gujarat | Development boards – Vidarbha, Marathwada, Saurashtra, Kutch
  [5:6:0.1] 371A | Nagaland | Naga customs, customary law, land – Parliament's laws apply only if the Assembly agrees
  [5:6:0.2] 371B | Assam | Assembly committee of members from tribal areas
  [5:6:0.3] 371C | Manipur | Assembly committee of members from the Hill areas
  [5:6:0.4] 371D | Andhra Pradesh (and Telangana) | Equitable opportunities in public employment and education for regions
  [5:6:0.5] 371E | Andhra Pradesh | Central University by parliamentary law
  [5:6:0.6] 371F | Sikkim | Incorporation, assembly size, governance
  [5:6:0.7] 371G | Mizoram | Mizo practices, customary law, land

  [5:6:0.9] 371I | Goa | Assembly at least 30 members (usual minimum 60)
  [5:6:0.10] 371J | Karnataka | Hyderabad–Karnataka region (six backward districts) – development board, reservation; 98th Amendment, 2012
[5:6:1] - All are in **Part XXI**; **Art. 371** is "the" special-provisions Article (not 369, 370 or 372). Art. 370 (J&K) is not in the 371 series.
[5:6:2] - **Arts. 371D and 371E** came by the **32nd Amendment, 1973** (Six-Point Formula after the Jai Andhra and Telangana agitations); the 32nd also dropped the old AP clause from Art. 371.
[5:6:3] - **North-East trap:** 371A Nagaland, **371B Assam**, 371C Manipur.
[5:6:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 2 p.8-9 (Rocket Sheet #48); PMF Polity Part 3 (Arts. 371–371J)
## SUB 7 | Counts – Original vs Present (as of 2026)
[5:7:0] TABLE head: Item | Original (26 Nov 1949) | Now (2026)
  [5:7:0.0] Articles | 395 (with the Preamble) | about 470 – numbering still ends at 395; new ones lettered (243ZH–243ZT, 330A, 334A …)
  [5:7:0.1] Parts | 22 | 25
  [5:7:0.2] Schedules | 8 | 12
[5:7:1] - **Parts:** 22 + 4 added (**IV-A, IX-A, IX-B, XIV-A**) − Part VII repealed = **25** (Part IX of 1950 was repealed in 1956 and a new Part IX inserted in 1992). Some books still print 24 Parts or "447 Articles" – outdated.
[5:7:2] - **Schedules:** 8 + 4 added (**9th–12th**) = **12** (not 9, 10, 11 or 14).
[5:7:3] - Latest enacted amendment as of 2026: **106th (2023)** – women's reservation (Arts. 239AA, 330A, 332A, 334A); no amendment has added a Part or Schedule since 2011.
[5:7:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.118, p.142, p.160; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.18; Indian_Polity Part 1 ch.2 (470 Articles, 25 Parts); PIB via SuperKalam 26 Jul 2026 (amendments to the 106th)

=== NOTES 2:6 | Union and Its Territory – Articles 1-4, New States and Cession
## SUB 0 | Union Territories – Count, Administration and Legislatures
[6:0:0] # How many States and UTs
[6:0:1] - **Now (2026): 28 States and 8 Union Territories** (APPSC 2021 key; Indian_Polity Part 1 p.48).
[6:0:2] - **29 States + 7 UTs** was true only from 2014 (Telangana) to **5 August 2019**; **28 + 7** was the count from 1987 to 2014 (APPSC Draftsman 2012 key) and again from 31 Oct 2019 to 25 Jan 2020; **28 + 8** from **26 January 2020** (merger of DNH and Daman & Diu).
[6:0:3] - **8 UTs:** **Andaman and Nicobar, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Delhi (NCT), Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Puducherry**.
[6:0:4] - **Goa is a State** (since 1987), not a UT; **Delhi is a UT** (First Schedule) with special status as the **National Capital Territory** by the **69th Amendment, 1991**.
[6:0:5] - **Smallest UT** by area: **Lakshadweep** (about 32 sq km); largest: **Ladakh**.
[6:0:6] - UTs replaced the **Part C and Part D States** under the **7th Amendment, 1956**.
[6:0:7] # Puducherry – spread over three States
[6:0:8] - **Puducherry** UT = **Puducherry and Karaikal (in Tamil Nadu)**, **Mahe (in Kerala)** and **Yanam (in Andhra Pradesh)** → spread over **3 States**; **Yanam** is the part of a UT located in AP.
[6:0:9] - **Coastal UTs (other than island UTs):** **Puducherry** and **Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu** → **two** (Lakshadweep and A&N are islands).
[6:0:10] - **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** was under **Portuguese** rule (not French) until **1954**; **Diu** is an island in the **Gulf of Khambhat**; **Daman and Diu** were separated from Goa in 1987 (Goa statehood, 56th Amendment).
[6:0:11] # Administration
[6:0:12] - **Art. 239:** the **President administers every UT through an Administrator** (LG / Chief Commissioner / Administrator).
[6:0:13] - **Art. 239(2):** the **Governor of an adjoining State** may be the administrator – the **Governor of Punjab is the Administrator of Chandigarh**; he then acts **independently of his State Council of Ministers**.
[6:0:14] - **Lakshadweep** has its own **Administrator**, not the Governor of Kerala (UPSC 2009: only the Chandigarh statement is correct).
[6:0:15] - **Art. 240:** the **President makes regulations** for **A&N Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh**, and for **Puducherry** only while its legislature is suspended or dissolved (the old "Goa, Daman and Diu" entry was omitted in 1987).
[6:0:16] # Legislatures and High Courts
[6:0:17] TABLE head: UT | Legislature | High Court
  [6:0:17.0] Delhi | Art. 239AA (69th, 1991) | Own High Court (the only UT with one of its own)
  [6:0:17.1] Puducherry | Art. 239A (14th, 1962) | Madras HC
  [6:0:17.2] Jammu and Kashmir | J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 (Art. 239A applied) | Common HC of J&K and Ladakh
  [6:0:17.3] Ladakh | None | Common HC of J&K and Ladakh
  [6:0:17.4] Chandigarh | None | Punjab and Haryana HC
  [6:0:17.5] Lakshadweep | None | Kerala HC
  [6:0:17.6] A&N Islands | None | Calcutta HC
  [6:0:17.7] DNH and Daman & Diu | None | Bombay HC (also covers Goa)
[6:0:18] - **"State" in Art. 54 (election of the President)** includes **NCT of Delhi and UT of Puducherry** (Explanation added by the **70th Amendment, 1992**); the 2019 Act applied Art. 239A to J&K but did not amend Art. 54.
[6:0:19] > Bombay HC covers Maharashtra, Goa, DNH and Daman & Diu – **Lakshadweep** is the odd one out (APSLPRB SI 2019).

## SUB 1 | New States – Amendments and Chronology
[6:1:0] # State → year → instrument
[6:1:1] TABLE head: Year | State | Act / Amendment
  [6:1:1.0] 1953 | Andhra State | Andhra State Act – first linguistic State (1 Oct 1953)
  [6:1:1.1] 1956 | Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Mysore… | States Reorganisation Act (1 Nov 1956)
  [6:1:1.2] 1960 | Maharashtra and Gujarat | Bombay Reorganisation Act (1 May 1960)
  [6:1:1.3] 1963 | Nagaland (1 Dec 1963) | State of Nagaland Act, 1962 + 13th Amendment (1962), Art. 371A
  [6:1:1.4] 1966 | Haryana (from Punjab) | Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966
  [6:1:1.5] 1971 | Himachal Pradesh (UT → State) | State of Himachal Pradesh Act, 1970
  [6:1:1.6] 1972 | Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya | North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971; Meghalaya first an autonomous State within Assam (22nd Amendment, 1969)
  [6:1:1.7] 1975 | Sikkim – 22nd State | 35th (1974) associate State; 36th (1975) full State
  [6:1:1.8] 1987 | Mizoram (20 Feb 1987) – 23rd | State of Mizoram Act, 1986 + 53rd Amendment
  [6:1:1.9] 1987 | Arunachal Pradesh (20 Feb 1987) – 24th | 55th Amendment
  [6:1:1.10] 1987 | Goa (30 May 1987) – 25th State | Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act + 56th Amendment
  [6:1:1.11] 2000 | Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (Jharkhand 15 Nov 2000) | Reorganisation Acts, 2000
  [6:1:1.12] 2014 | Telangana (2 June 2014) – 29th State, capital Hyderabad | AP Reorganisation Act, 2014
[6:1:2] - **Chronology drills:** Maharashtra 1960 → Haryana 1966 → HP 1971 → Mizoram 1987 (**B, D, A, C**, APPSC G1 2008); Nagaland 1963 → Haryana 1966 → Sikkim 1975 → Arunachal 1987 (UPSC 2007); Nagaland → Haryana → Meghalaya 1972 → Sikkim (UPPSC 2010); AP 1953/56 → Haryana → HP → Sikkim (UPPSC 2014).
[6:1:3] - **Formed last** among AP (1956), Gujarat (1960), Karnataka (Mysore 1956) and **Punjab** (present form **1966**) → **Punjab** (CDS 2006).
[6:1:4] - **Renamings:** **Madras → Tamil Nadu** (1969), **Mysore → Karnataka** (1973) – "Mysore renamed Tamil Nadu" is the false statement.
[6:1:5] # UT entries by amendment
[6:1:6] - **Goa, Daman and Diu** made a UT → **12th Amendment, 1962**; **Pondicherry** → **14th Amendment, 1962**.
[6:1:7] # Sikkim
[6:1:8] - **35th Amendment (1974):** Sikkim an **"associate State"** – the **first and only** associate State (inserted **Art. 2A** and the **Tenth Schedule**); came into force 1 March 1975.
[6:1:9] - **36th Amendment (1975):** after a **referendum** and **abolition of the monarchy**, Sikkim became a **full State – the 22nd** (omitted Art. 2A and the Tenth Schedule); Assembly of **not less than 32 members**. Today Sikkim is simply **part of the Indian territory** (a State in the First Schedule).
[6:1:10] - **Government of Sikkim Act, 1974** set up its first elected government.
[6:1:11] # North-East facts
[6:1:12] - **Arunachal Pradesh:** capital **Itanagar**, named after **Ita Fort** ('fort of bricks'); two National Parks – **Namdapha, Mouling**.
[6:1:13] - **Tripura:** **Part C State** (1950) → **UT** (1956) → **full State** (1972).
[6:1:14] - **Nagaland:** created by the **State of Nagaland Act, 1962**, with the **13th Amendment** inserting **Art. 371A** – UPSC 2025 accepted "came into existence on the basis of a Constitutional Amendment Act" (all three pairs correct).
[6:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.236-237; Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) p.48-52 (evolution of States); Constitution 35th, 36th, 53rd, 55th, 56th Amendments; pmfias.com/state-description-matching-pyq-2025 and civilsdaily.com (UPSC 2025 answer "All three"); app notes 2:6 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Articles 1–4 – Union, Territory and the First Schedule
[6:2:0] # What each Article says
[6:2:1] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [6:2:1.0] 1 | "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"; States and territories in the First Schedule; Art. 1(3) territory of India
  [6:2:1.1] 2 | Admission or establishment of new States (not part of the Union of India)
  [6:2:1.2] 3 | Formation of new States; alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
  [6:2:1.3] 4 | Laws under Arts. 2 and 3 amend the First and Fourth Schedules; Art. 4(2): not deemed an amendment under Art. 368
[6:2:2] - Part I = **Articles 1–4**; the Constitution calls the Centre the **"Union"** (Union Government, Union List), not "Centre".
[6:2:3] - **"Union" not "Federation" (Ambedkar):** the Indian federation is **not the result of an agreement among States**, and **no State has the right to secede** – "an **indestructible Union of destructible States**".
[6:2:4] # Union of India vs Territory of India
[6:2:5] TABLE head: Union of India | Territory of India (Art. 1(3))
  [6:2:5.0] States only – members of the federal system sharing powers with the Union | States + Union Territories + territories that may be acquired
[6:2:6] - So **UTs are covered by "Territory of India" and not by "Union of India"** (APPSC G1: **Only IV**); both expressions are in the Constitution, and the **First Schedule** lists **States and UTs**.
[6:2:7] - Grama Sachivalayam 2020: the **Union of India** includes **States only (A only)**.
[6:2:8] - **Acquiring territory:** India as a sovereign State acquires foreign territory **"as understood in public international law"** – cession, conquest, occupation (**N. Masthan Sahib v. Chief Commissioner, Pondicherry**); e.g. **Pondicherry, Goa, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Sikkim**. Such territory need not join an existing State (it may be a UT).
[6:2:9] # First Schedule
[6:2:10] - **First Schedule = names of the States and UTs and their territorial extent** → it **must be amended to create a new State** (UPSC 2001; APPSC G2 Mains 2019; APPSC HO 2021). Fourth Schedule = Rajya Sabha seats (also amended).
[6:2:11] # Article 3 – power and procedure
[6:2:12] - **Power vests in Parliament** (not the President, the Council of Ministers or an SRC): form a new State by **separating** territory, **uniting** States or parts, uniting territory to a part of a State; **increase or diminish** area; alter **boundaries or name**.
[6:2:13] - **Admission of new States is NOT under Art. 3** – it is **Art. 2**; creating a new State out of existing States is **Art. 3** (CGPSC 2014).
[6:2:14] - **Procedure:** Bill only on the **President's recommendation**; President **refers it to the State legislature concerned** for views within a time limit; **Parliament is not bound** by the views; **no fresh reference** needed for each amendment to the Bill; for a **UT, no reference** at all.
[6:2:15] - **Consent of the State is not required** to alter its boundaries – Parliament acts "without their consent".
[6:2:16] - Passed by a **simple majority** in the ordinary legislative process (**Art. 4(2)**).
[6:2:17] - **Renaming Kerala → 'Keralam'**: Union Cabinet approval began the **Article 3** procedure.
[6:2:18] - Parliament **cannot cede** territory under Art. 3 – cession needs an **Art. 368** amendment (see Cession).
[6:2:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.233-235, p.237 (Articles 1-4 table); Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) p.47-50 (Union vs Territory, Masthan Sahib, Art. 2, Art. 3); app notes 2:6 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | Reorganisation Commissions, Andhra State and the SRA 1956
[6:3:0] # Commissions
[6:3:1] TABLE head: Body | Year | Members | Recommended
  [6:3:1.0] Dhar Commission | June 1948 | S.K. Dhar (chairman), Panna Lall, Jagat Narain Lal | Administrative convenience, not language
  [6:3:1.1] JVP Committee (Congress) | December 1948 | Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya | Rejected language as the basis
  [6:3:1.2] Fazl Ali Commission (SRC) | 22 December 1953 | Fazl Ali (chairman), K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru | Broadly accepted language, rejected "one language–one State"; reported 30 Sept 1955
[6:3:2] - **Dhar Commission** was appointed by **Rajendra Prasad** (President of the Constituent Assembly); it held linguistic States a threat to national unity.
[6:3:3] - **Pattabhi Sitaramayya** was in the **JVP Committee**, **not in the SRC**.
[6:3:4] - **SRC appointment:** announced **22 December 1953** (MHA resolution dated 29 Dec 1953); suggested **Telangana** stay separate till about **1961**.
[6:3:5] - **SRC's four factors:** unity and security of India; linguistic and cultural homogeneity; financial, economic and administrative considerations; welfare of the people.
[6:3:6] - **SRC recommended:** abolish the **Part A/B/C** classification; abolish the **Rajpramukh** institution and special agreements with princely States; abolish the Centre's general control under **Art. 371** (a question that prints "Article 171" makes that item false → "Only C" is not a recommendation).
[6:3:7] # Andhra State, 1953
[6:3:8] - **Potti Sriramulu** died (**15 December 1952**) after a **56-day fast** → **Andhra State** formed **1 October 1953** from the **Telugu-speaking districts of Madras State** – the **first linguistic State**; capital **Kurnool**.
[6:3:9] - Exams also ask "Andhra Pradesh created as a language-based State in **1953**" – they mean Andhra State.
[6:3:10] # States Reorganisation Act, 1956
[6:3:11] - In force **1 November 1956**: **14 States + 6 UTs**; **Andhra State + Telangana region of Hyderabad = Andhra Pradesh** (capital **Hyderabad**); Kerala formed.
[6:3:12] - Large-scale reorganisation **on a linguistic basis = 1956**; the related amendment = **7th Amendment, 1956** (Part A/B/C/D classification ended).
[6:3:13] - Set up **five Zonal Councils** (the Indian territory divided into **five zones**).
[6:3:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.236-237; Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) p.50-52; app notes 2:6 sub 2-3; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_Reorganisation_Commission (citing MHA Resolution 29 Dec 1953)

## SUB 6 | Cession of Territory
[6:6:0] TABLE head: Instance | Year | Outcome
  [6:6:0.0] Berubari reference | 1960 | Cession of Berubari (West Bengal) to Pakistan (Nehru–Noon 1958): Art. 3 does not cover cession → Art. 368 amendment → 9th Amendment, 1960
  [6:6:0.1] SC position | 1969 | Boundary settlement ≠ cession – done by executive action, no amendment
  [6:6:0.2] India–Bangladesh LBA | 1974 (2011 protocol) | 111 Indian enclaves to Bangladesh, 51 Bangladeshi enclaves to India; 100th Amendment, 2015; amended First Schedule entries of Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Tripura
  [6:6:0.3] Katchatheevu | 1974–76 | To Sri Lanka by agreements, no constitutional amendment

=== NOTES 2:7 | Citizenship – Articles 5-11, Citizenship Act 1955, Oci and Caa 2019
## SUB 0 | Part II – Articles 5 to 11
[7:0:0] # Constitutional framework
[7:0:1] - Citizenship = **Part II, Articles 5–11** (Part I = Arts. 1–4 Union and territory; Part III = Arts. 12–35 Fundamental Rights).
[7:0:2] - Part II only **identifies who became citizens at the commencement (26 January 1950)**; acquisition and loss afterwards are left to **Parliament (Art. 11)** → **Citizenship Act, 1955**.
[7:0:3] - **Arts. 5–8** are the Articles that define the categories of citizens at commencement (APPSC G2 Mains 2017 key "Articles 5 to 8"); Arts. 9–11 are general provisions.
[7:0:4] TABLE head: Article | Deals with
  [7:0:4.0] 5 | Citizenship at the commencement – domiciled in India + (a) born in India, or (b) either parent born in India, or (c) ordinarily resident 5 years before 1950
  [7:0:4.1] 6 | Migrants from Pakistan to India – cut-off 19 July 1948 (after it, registration after 6 months' residence)
  [7:0:4.2] 7 | Migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 who returned under a resettlement permit
  [7:0:4.3] 8 | Persons of Indian origin residing outside India – register at an Indian diplomatic or consular office
  [7:0:4.4] 9 | Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship → not a citizen
  [7:0:4.5] 10 | Continuance of the rights of citizenship, subject to Parliament's law
  [7:0:4.6] 11 | Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
[7:0:5] - **Wrong statement trap:** "Articles **4 to 10** deal with migrants to Pakistan and persons of Indian origin abroad" – false (that is **Arts. 7 and 8**; Part II is 5–11).
[7:0:6] - Art. 6 = migrants **FROM** Pakistan; Art. 7 = migrants **TO** Pakistan.
[7:0:7] # What citizenship gives
[7:0:8] - Citizen-only rights: **Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30**; the **right to vote** for the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; the **right to become a member** of Parliament and State legislatures – "citizenship means **full civil and political rights**" (CDS 2014: all three).
[7:0:9] - Citizen-only offices: **President, Vice-President, SC/HC judges, Governor, Attorney General, Advocate General**.
[7:0:10] - **President:** in India both a citizen **by birth and a naturalised** citizen are eligible; in the **USA only a natural-born** citizen.
[7:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.238-240, p.244 (Articles 5-11 table); Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship; app notes 2:7 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Acquisition – Five Modes
[7:1:0] # Modes and Sections of the Citizenship Act, 1955
[7:1:1] TABLE head: Mode | Section | Key condition
  [7:1:1.0] Birth | 3 | jus soli (modified) – see periods below
  [7:1:1.1] Descent | 4 | Born outside India, either parent an Indian citizen at birth; birth registered at an Indian consulate – jus sanguinis
  [7:1:1.2] Registration | 5 | PIO ordinarily resident 7 years; spouses of citizens; minor children of citizens
  [7:1:1.3] Naturalisation | 6 | 12 years (11 of the preceding 14 + the last 12 months); oath of allegiance; waivable for distinguished service to science, art, literature, world peace
  [7:1:1.4] Incorporation of territory | 7 | Centre notifies who become citizens when a territory joins – Goa, Pondicherry, Sikkim
[7:1:2] - **Five modes:** **Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalisation, Incorporation of territory** (Act passed **1955**).
[7:1:3] - **Not modes:** **property or land ownership**, **depositing money in Indian banks**, **ethnic identity**; **marriage** is not a separate mode (only a registration category). **Domicile** was a condition only under Art. 5.
[7:1:4] # Citizenship by birth – three periods
[7:1:5] TABLE head: Born in India | Rule
  [7:1:5.0] 26 Jan 1950 – 30 Jun 1987 | Citizen regardless of parents' nationality (1986 Amendment)
  [7:1:5.1] 1 Jul 1987 – 2 Dec 2004 | At least one parent an Indian citizen
  [7:1:5.2] From 3 Dec 2004 | Both parents citizens, or one Indian and the other not an illegal migrant
[7:1:6] - So today a person born in India is a citizen **only if at least one parent is Indian**, subject to other conditions (APPSC ASWO key).
[7:1:7] - **Excluded** from birth: children of **foreign diplomats** and **enemy aliens**.
[7:1:8] # Residence periods – then and now
[7:1:9] - Before the 2003 Act (in force 3 Dec 2004) naturalisation needed **1 year + 4 of the preceding 7 years = 5 years** (APPSC G1 2003 key: 5 years); **now 12 years**; registration of PIO now **7 years**; CAA communities **5 years**.
[7:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.240-242 (modes, pre-2004 naturalisation conditions); Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship (Sections 3-7, 2003 Amendment); Citizenship Act 1955 (indiacode.nic.in) Third Schedule; app notes 2:7 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Single Citizenship – No Dual Citizenship
[7:2:0] - India: **single citizenship** and a **single domicile** for the Union and the States – allegiance only to the Union; **no separate State citizenship** (UPSC 2021: "one citizenship and one domicile" is the only correct statement).
[7:2:1] - **Source:** **Britain**; **Canada** also has single citizenship.
[7:2:2] - **USA** and **Switzerland**: **dual** – national + State/cantonal (UPSC 2005: "India and USA both have single citizenship" is false).
[7:2:3] - India does **not allow dual citizenship** with another country (Art. 9, Sec. 9): a citizen who **acquires another country's citizenship loses Indian citizenship** – APPSC A–R: both true, R explains A (key).
[7:2:4] TABLE head: Country | Citizenship
  [7:2:4.0] India, Britain, Canada | Single
  [7:2:4.1] USA, Switzerland | Dual (national + state)
[7:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.243 (single citizenship, USA, Switzerland, Canada); Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship; app notes 2:7 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Citizenship (Amendment) Acts and the CAA, 2019
[7:3:0] # Amendments to the 1955 Act
[7:3:1] TABLE head: Year | Change
  [7:3:1.0] 1986 | Birth from 1 July 1987 needs one parent an Indian citizen
  [7:3:1.1] 2003 | Birth rule from 3 Dec 2004 (other parent not an illegal migrant); Overseas Citizenship for PIOs of 16 specified countries (Sec. 7A); Sec. 14A (National Register)
  [7:3:1.2] 2005 | OCI widened to PIOs of all countries except Pakistan and Bangladesh
  [7:3:1.3] 2015 | PIO card merged with OCI → "OCI Cardholder"
  [7:3:1.4] 2019 (CAA) | Route for 6 communities from 3 countries; naturalisation residence cut to 5 years
[7:3:2] - **No amendment in 2008** (APPSC key); the 1986 Act took effect on 1 July 1987 – there is no "1987 Act".
[7:3:3] - Basis moved from **jus soli to jus sanguinis**.
[7:3:4] # CAA, 2019
[7:3:5] TABLE head: Stage | Date
  [7:3:5.0] Lok Sabha | 9 December 2019
  [7:3:5.1] Rajya Sabha (Parliament passed) | 11 December 2019
  [7:3:5.2] President's assent | 12 December 2019
  [7:3:5.3] Rules effective | 11 March 2024
[7:3:6] - **Purpose:** citizenship for **persecuted minorities** – **Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian** (**six**; Muslims not covered) from **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan** (not Sri Lanka) – A–R: both true, R explains A.
[7:3:7] - Cut-off: entered India **on or before 31 December 2014**; citizenship counts **from the date of entry**.
[7:3:8] - **Exempt:** **Sixth Schedule** tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura and **Inner Line Permit** areas.
[7:3:9] - **2026:** Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026 – affidavit on any Pakistani, Afghan or Bangladeshi passport, **surrender within 15 days** of approval; **19 Aug 2026 MHA order** – applications in 8 States/UTs processed by **District Collectors**; challenge under **Art. 14** pending before a Bench under **CJI Surya Kant**.
[7:3:10] ~~ Sources: Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship (2003 Amendment, OCI, CAA); nishithdesai.com dual-citizenship-for-persons-of-indian-origin-5843 and eparlib.nic.in (16 specified countries); app notes 2:7 sub 5-6
## SUB 4 | Who Regulates Citizenship – Parliament (Art. 11)
[7:4:0] TABLE head: Authority | Role
  [7:4:0.0] Parliament (Art. 11) | Alone legislates on and prescribes conditions for acquisition and termination → Citizenship Act, 1955
  [7:4:0.1] Central Government (Home Ministry) | Administers the Act; determines questions of acquisition of foreign citizenship (Sec. 9(2)); frames Citizenship Rules (2009, amended 2026) under Sec. 18; deprives under Sec. 10
  [7:4:0.2] Election Commission | Checks citizenship only for electoral rolls (Art. 324, Art. 326 adult suffrage)
[7:4:1] - **No power** to make citizenship law: **State Legislatures**, the **President**, the **Election Commission**, the Union Cabinet, the Supreme Court, the Law Commission.
[7:4:2] - "**Exclusive power of determining the issue of citizenship**" (CGPSC 2013) → **Central Government** (Sec. 9(2)); "**competent to prescribe conditions**" → **Parliament**.
[7:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.239-240 (Art. 11, Citizenship Act); Citizenship Act 1955 Secs. 9(2), 18 (indiacode.nic.in); app notes 2:7 sub 1
## SUB 5 | NRI, PIO and OCI
[7:5:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [7:5:0.0] NRI | Indian citizen ordinarily residing outside India; holds an Indian passport
  [7:5:0.1] PIO | Foreign citizen who, or any of whose ancestors, was an Indian national; card merged into OCI (2015)
  [7:5:0.2] OCI | Person registered as an OCI Cardholder under Sec. 7A of the Citizenship Act, 1955
  [7:5:0.3] Commonwealth citizen | Citizen of a member country of the Commonwealth of Nations
  [7:5:0.4] Single citizenship | One citizenship for all of India
[7:5:1] - **OCI eligible:** foreign citizens of Indian origin, their **children/minor children of Indian citizens**, **foreign-origin spouses** of Indian citizens or OCIs.
[7:5:2] - **OCI barred:** if the person, a **parent or grandparent** was a citizen of **Pakistan or Bangladesh** – so an Indian who migrated to Pakistan after Partition is not eligible.
[7:5:3] - **OCI gets:** **lifelong (multiple-entry) visa**; OCI card alone enough to enter India (since 2016). **Not:** voting, contesting elections, constitutional offices; OCIs are **not citizens**.
[7:5:4] - **2015 Amendment** did **not** give NRIs any new voting right; **2026 Rules:** e-OCI cards.
[7:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.243 (OCI and PIO merger); Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship (OCI rights); app notes 2:7 sub 7
## SUB 6 | Loss of Citizenship – Three Modes
[7:6:0] TABLE head: Mode | Section | How
  [7:6:0.0] Renunciation | 8 | Voluntary, by declaration; minor children lose it too but may resume within 1 year of majority
  [7:6:0.1] Termination | 9 | Automatic on voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship
  [7:6:0.2] Deprivation | 10 | Compulsory, by the Central Government; only citizens by naturalisation, registration or Art. 5(c)
[7:6:1] - **Deprivation grounds:** fraud; **disloyalty** to the Constitution; helping an enemy in war; **2 years' imprisonment within 5 years** of naturalisation/registration; **7 years' continuous residence abroad**.
[7:6:2] - **A naturalised citizen can be deprived** (Sec. 10) – "never deprived" is false.
[7:6:3] - **No effect** on citizenship: **marrying a foreigner**, **criticising the government**, bank deposits, property → loss only by **renouncing** or **acquiring foreign citizenship** (UPPSC: **1 and 2 only**); all three modes → "All of the above" (CGPSC 2013).
[7:6:4] TABLE head: Section | Subject
  [7:6:4.0] 7A | Registration of OCI cardholders
  [7:6:4.1] 14A | National Register of Indian Citizens and national identity card
  [7:6:4.2] 18 | Power to make Rules
[7:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (full text) p.242-243; Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship; app notes 2:7 sub 4
## SUB 7 | NRC, NPR and Proof of Citizenship
[7:7:0] - **NRC (Assam):** identifies **genuine citizens in Assam**; eligibility = names in the **NRC of 1951** or electoral rolls up to **24 March 1971** (cut-off of the **Assam Accord, 1985**); **draft NRC published for Assam** (2018). The **2019 CAA was not an NRC amendment** – the Accord was given effect by **Sec. 6A** (1985).
[7:7:1] - **NRC** (citizens only) is a **subset of the NPR** (all usual residents); Sec. **14A** of the Citizenship Act.
[7:7:2] - **Not proof of citizenship:** **Aadhaar** (identity only, **Sec. 9, Aadhaar Act**), voter ID, ration card, passport.
[7:7:3] ~~ Sources: Indian_Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) ch. Citizenship; nrcassam.nic.in (eligibility, 24 March 1971); app notes 2:7 sub 8

=== NOTES 2:8 | Fundamental Rights – Article 12, Article 13 and Doctrines
## SUB 0 | Part III at a Glance – Six Groups, Number, Location
[8:0:0] # Where and how many
[8:0:1] - **Location:** **Part III, Articles 12–35** of the Constitution; called the **"Magna Carta of India"** (not Part I, II or IV; not Arts. 14–32 only).
[8:0:2] - **Number:** originally **seven**, now **six** Fundamental Rights (groups) – the **Right to Property (Art. 31)** was deleted by the **44th Amendment, 1978** (Janata Party government) and is now a **legal/constitutional right under Art. 300A (Part XII)**.
[8:0:3] - **Borrowed from:** the **Bill of Rights of the USA**; the **Motilal Nehru Report (1928)** had demanded a bill of rights.
[8:0:4] - **Why "fundamental":** they are **guaranteed and specifically protected by the Constitution**, the fundamental law of the land – not rights granted by any ordinary law, nor merely natural-law rights.
[8:0:5] # The six groups
[8:0:6] TABLE head: Group | Articles | Contents
  [8:0:6.0] Right to Equality | 14–18 | 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination (religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth); 16 public employment; 17 untouchability abolished; 18 titles abolished
  [8:0:6.1] Right to Freedom | 19–22 | 19 six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); 20 conviction; 21 life and personal liberty; 21A education; 22 arrest and detention
  [8:0:6.2] Right against Exploitation | 23–24 | 23 traffic in human beings, forced labour; 24 child labour in factories
  [8:0:6.3] Right to Freedom of Religion | 25–28 | conscience, religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction
  [8:0:6.4] Cultural and Educational Rights | 29–30 | minorities' culture; minorities' institutions
  [8:0:6.5] Right to Constitutional Remedies | 32 alone | writs; Art. 226 (High Courts) is outside Part III
[8:0:7] - **Classification traps:** **Art. 15** (prohibition of discrimination) and **Art. 17** (untouchability) fall under the **Right to Equality** – not Freedom of Religion, Exploitation or Cultural rights (UPSC 1995, 2020; SSC 2018).
[8:0:8] - **Wrong pair:** "Right to protection of life – **Art. 20**" is wrong; life and liberty is **Art. 21** (Art. 20 = protection in respect of conviction). Art. 15 discrimination, Art. 19 association and Art. 32 remedies are correct pairs.
[8:0:9] - **Description:** "a pledge to our people and a pact with the civilised world" – **S. Radhakrishnan**.
[8:0:10] > Asked as: "How many FRs?" (six – APPSC Drug Inspectors, Polytechnic Lecturers; SSC CGL 2017), "Which Part?" (III – APPSC G2 2008; SSC 2008, 2017), "Which Articles?" (12–35; Equality 14–18; Freedom 19–22), CDS 2003 "originally seven, now six – both correct".
[8:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.169-171; Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.38-40; app notes 2:8 sub 0
## SUB 1 | FR or Not? – Look-alike Rights
[8:1:0] # Not Fundamental Rights
[8:1:1] TABLE head: Right | Where it really is
  [8:1:1.0] Right to work / employment | DPSP Art. 41 (not an FR)
  [8:1:1.1] Equal pay for equal work | DPSP Art. 39(d)
  [8:1:1.2] Right to property | Art. 300A, legal right since the 44th Amendment (1978)
  [8:1:1.3] Right to vote and to be elected | Constitutional right (Art. 326) – UPSC 2017 official key; given effect by statute (RPA 1950 s.19, RPA 1951 s.62); NextGen calls it a statutory right
  [8:1:1.4] Right to information | Not listed in Part III; the Supreme Court reads it into Art. 19(1)(a) (RTI Act 2005 is a statute)
  [8:1:1.5] Right to protest, right to govern, right to citizenship, right of equal shelter | Not FRs (shelter is read into Art. 21 by courts, but no "right of equal shelter" is granted)
[8:1:2] # Look-alikes that ARE Fundamental Rights
[8:1:3] - **Education (6–14 years):** **Art. 21A**, inserted by the **86th Amendment, 2002**; the **RTE Act** was enacted in **2009**; both came into force on **1 April 2010**.
[8:1:4] - **Right to settle in any part of India** – Art. 19(1)(e); **gender equality** – Arts. 14, 15; **form associations**, **practise any profession** – Art. 19.
[8:1:5] - **Right to Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion** – all FR groups (the "odd one out" is always the DPSP or statutory right).
[8:1:6] > NDA 2015: of education, work, associations and profession, only the **right to work** is not an FR. Voting age was lowered to **18** by the **61st Amendment (1988)**.
[8:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.170-172, p.174 (vote: statutory right, RPA s.62); upsc.gov.in answer key CSP 2017 (constitutional right); app notes 2:8 sub 7
## SUB 2 | Citizens Only vs All Persons; Aliens
[8:2:0] # Who gets which right
[8:2:1] TABLE head: Citizens only | All persons (citizens + foreigners)
  [8:2:1.0] Art. 15 – no discrimination | Art. 14 – equality before law, equal protection of laws
  [8:2:1.1] Art. 16 – public employment | Art. 20 – protection in respect of conviction
  [8:2:1.2] Art. 19 – six freedoms (speech, movement, trade and profession…) | Art. 21 / 21A – life and liberty, education
  [8:2:1.3] Art. 29 – minorities' language and culture | Art. 22 – arrest safeguards (not enemy aliens)
  [8:2:1.4] Art. 30 – minorities' institutions | Arts. 23–24 – exploitation; Arts. 25–28 – religion; Art. 32 – remedies
[8:2:2] - **Five citizens-only Articles: 15, 16, 19, 29, 30** (Raj. PCS 2024; APPSC G1 2023: denied to aliens = Arts. **29–30, 19, 16** – **not 23–24**).
[8:2:3] - A **British citizen** (any foreigner) in India cannot claim **freedom of trade and profession** or **freedom of speech and expression**, free movement or residence (all Art. 19) – but gets equality before law, life and liberty, religious freedom (UPSC 1999).
[8:2:4] - **Non-citizens** get the **right to life and liberty** and **constitutional remedies** – not freedom of expression or of association (Art. 19).
[8:2:5] - **Aliens** are not given the citizens-only FRs – they are the category to whom FRs are "not given" (bankrupt or sick persons and political sufferers keep all their FRs).
[8:2:6] - Also citizens only: **contesting elections** (not an FR at all).
[8:2:7] - **Aliens:** the Constitution **does distinguish friendly and enemy aliens** – **enemy aliens** lose even the arrest-and-detention safeguards of **Art. 22(1)-(2)**, by **Art. 22(3)**.
[8:2:8] - **Companies** (legal persons) can claim the all-persons rights, but **not Art. 19**.
[8:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.172-173 (citizens-only Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30; all persons 14, 20, 21, 23, 25-28); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.38-39; app notes 2:8 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Features and Nature of Fundamental Rights
[8:3:0] # Features
[8:3:1] - **Justiciable:** a person can move the **Supreme Court directly (Art. 32)** and **High Courts (Art. 226)**; FRs are **above ordinary laws** (Art. 13).
[8:3:2] - **Not absolute but qualified:** the State can impose **reasonable restrictions** by law; the **courts judge reasonableness**; **Art. 19** lists **11 grounds** of restriction in all.
[8:3:3] - **Claimed against the State:** most FRs are available against **arbitrary State action** and **limit the power of the State – even Parliament**; some (15(2), 17, 23, 24) also bind private persons.
[8:3:4] - **Not sacrosanct:** Parliament can curtail them **only by a constitutional amendment** (not an ordinary law), without destroying the **basic structure**; they can be **suspended only as the Constitution prescribes** (Arts. 358-359).
[8:3:5] - **Negative and positive:** many are **negatively worded** (14, 15(1), 16(2), 18(1), 20, 22(1), 28(1)); **21A, 29, 30** confer privileges; **15, 17, 18, 20, 24** are absolute limits on legislative power.
[8:3:6] - **Both natural and legal**; they protect **individuals and minority groups** from arbitrary State action (both statements correct).
[8:3:7] - **Britain** has **no written FRs**; it relies on conventions and the rule of law.
[8:3:8] # Statement traps
[8:3:9] - **Wrong:** "FRs are **unamendable**", "**absolute**", "partly justiciable and absolute", "not limited by the Constitution", "all FRs are suspended in an emergency".
[8:3:10] - **Right:** "not absolute", "some only for citizens", "drawn from the American Constitution", "justiciable", "six in number", "granted by the Constitution".
[8:3:11] - **CDS 2004:** FRs are fundamental because they are protected and enforced by the Constitution, can be suspended only as it prescribes, and are enforceable against the State (I, II, III) – **not** because they cannot be amended.
[8:3:12] - **A–R (UPPSC 2015):** the Constitution is the longest (A true) and the FR chapter follows the American model (R true), but R does not explain A.
[8:3:13] - **Right to die:** **Gian Kaur (1996)** – no right to die (suicide) under Art. 21; **Common Cause (2018)** – right to **die with dignity** (passive euthanasia, living will) is part of Art. 21.
[8:3:14] - **India is not a fully federal constitution** – it is federal with a unitary bias ("quasi-federal").
[8:3:15] - **Golden Triangle:** **Arts. 14, 19 and 21** (Maneka Gandhi 1978; Minerva Mills 1980) – not 14-20-21, 14-15-16, 19-20-21 or 14-21-32.
[8:3:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.169-173 (features), p.200 (Golden Triangle 14, 19, 21); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.38-40, Part 1 p.59 (Maneka Gandhi: golden triangle); sci.gov.in (Common Cause v. UoI, 9 Mar 2018); app notes 2:8 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Limits on FRs – Restrictions, Armed Forces (Arts. 33-35), Emergency (358-359)
[8:4:0] # Who can restrict
[8:4:1] - **Reasonable restrictions** are imposed by **law** made by **Parliament** (and State legislatures within their field) – not by the President, Prime Minister or Supreme Court; the courts only **judge** their reasonableness.
[8:4:2] # Articles 33–35
[8:4:3] TABLE head: Article | Provision
  [8:4:3.0] 33 | Parliament alone may restrict or abrogate FRs of the armed forces, forces charged with maintenance of public order (police), intelligence/counter-intelligence staff, and persons in telecommunication systems set up for those forces – including non-combatants (barbers, cooks, carpenters). Examples: Army Act 1950, Air Force Act 1950, Navy Act 1957
  [8:4:3.1] 34 | Restrictions while martial law is in force; Parliament may pass an indemnity Act; "martial law" is not defined in the Constitution
  [8:4:3.2] 35 | Only Parliament (not States) legislates on 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and punishments for Part III offences – for uniformity
[8:4:4] - **CDS 2015 trap:** staff of **communication systems set up in the country in general** are **not** covered by Art. 33 – they enjoy FRs at par with other citizens; the armed forces, public-order forces and **their** communication staff are the restricted categories.
[8:4:5] # Emergency
[8:4:6] - **Art. 358:** when a National Emergency is declared on **war or external aggression**, **Art. 19 (Right to Freedom) is suspended automatically** (not on armed rebellion).
[8:4:7] - **Art. 359:** the **President** may by order suspend the right to move courts for **specified FRs** – **never Arts. 20 and 21** (**44th Amendment, 1978**).
[8:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.172 (Art. 19 suspension), p.223-225 (Arts. 33-35, 358-359); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.40; app notes 2:8 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Article 13 – Laws Void, Meaning of "Law", Amendments
[8:5:0] # Clauses
[8:5:1] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [8:5:1.0] 13(1) | Pre-constitution laws inconsistent with FRs are void to the extent of inconsistency
  [8:5:1.1] 13(2) | The State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges FRs; such post-constitution laws are void to that extent
  [8:5:1.2] 13(3)(a) | "Law" includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law
  [8:5:1.3] 13(4) | Art. 13 does not apply to Art. 368 amendments – added by the 24th Amendment, 1971
[8:5:2] - **Basis of judicial review** (with Arts. 32 and 226); it gives **constitutional provisions (FRs) precedence over laws** of Parliament and State legislatures.
[8:5:3] - 13(1) refers to laws in force before the **commencement of the Constitution** (26 Jan 1950), not "before Independence".
[8:5:4] - **UPSC 2026:** "law" in Art. 13 includes **custom or usage** – so the view that custom is included is correct and the view excluding it is wrong (only Y correct).
[8:5:5] # Are amendments "law"?
[8:5:6] TABLE head: Case / Amendment | Year | Position
  [8:5:6.0] Shankari Prasad | 1951 | Amendment is not "law" under Art. 13; Parliament can amend FRs (first such case)
  [8:5:6.1] Golaknath | 1967 | FRs have a transcendental position – Parliament cannot abridge FRs; prospective overruling
  [8:5:6.2] 24th Amendment | 1971 | Added Art. 13(4) in reply
  [8:5:6.3] Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | FRs amendable, but the basic structure cannot be destroyed
[8:5:7] - **Ninth Schedule:** added by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Arts. 31A and 31B**; **I.R. Coelho (2007)** – laws placed in it after 24 Apr 1973 are open to basic-structure review.
[8:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.179-182 (Art. 13 clauses, 13(4), Golaknath); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.38; app notes 2:8 sub 4, sub 9
## SUB 6 | Doctrines under Article 13
[8:6:0] TABLE head: Doctrine | Meaning | Case
  [8:6:0.0] Severability | Law is void only to the extent of inconsistency; the consistent, severable part remains valid | A.K. Gopalan (1950); R.M.D.C. (1957); Motor General Traders v. State of AP (1984)
  [8:6:0.1] Eclipse | A pre-constitution law inconsistent with an FR is not wiped out – it is dormant (overshadowed) and revives when the conflict is removed | Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP (1955); State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974) – extended to post-constitution laws for non-citizens
  [8:6:0.2] Waiver | A person cannot waive an FR | Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959)
  [8:6:0.3] Prospective overruling | A ruling operates only for the future | Golaknath (1967)
  [8:6:0.4] Progressive interpretation | Constitution as a living document | Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21; SaveLIFE Foundation v. UoI (2026) – right to trauma care under Art. 21
  [8:6:0.5] Absolute liability | Hazardous industry liable without exceptions | M.C. Mehta (1987) – Oleum gas leak
  [8:6:0.6] Territorial nexus | State law can operate outside the State if there is sufficient connection | State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957)
  [8:6:0.7] Pith and substance | Encroachment on another List – look at the true nature of the law | Federal doctrine (with aspect, colourable legislation, incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy)
[8:6:1] - **Eclipse vs severability:** eclipse = law **sleeps and revives**; severability = **bad part cut off, rest lives**. Eminent domain and pleasure are unrelated doctrines.
[8:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.180-182 (doctrines; Motor General Traders 1984; Ambica Mills 1974); app notes 2:8 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Article 12 – Meaning of "the State"
[8:7:0] # Definition
[8:7:1] - **Government and Parliament of India**; **Government and Legislature of each State**; **all local authorities** (municipalities, panchayats, district boards); **other authorities** within India or under the control of the Government of India (LIC, ONGC, electricity boards).
[8:7:2] - **Ambiguity – courts:** whether the **judiciary** is "other authority" is the grey area; in its judicial function it is **not** "State" (**Naresh Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, 1967**).
[8:7:3] - **Private bodies:** a writ does not ordinarily lie merely because a private body performs a public activity, unless the State is involved.
[8:7:4] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [8:7:4.0] Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal | 1967 | Statutory bodies are "other authorities"
  [8:7:4.1] R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority | 1979 | Laid down tests for an instrumentality or agency of the State
  [8:7:4.2] Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib | 1981 | Society running a Regional Engineering College = State; test is creation and control, not legal form
  [8:7:4.3] Pradeep Kumar Biswas | 2002 | State if financially, functionally and administratively dominated by government
[8:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.174-175, p.178-179 (Naresh 1967; other authorities); app notes 2:8 sub 3
## SUB 8 | Violation Scenarios
[8:8:0] TABLE head: Scenario | Article violated
  [8:8:0.0] Not paying minimum wages | Art. 23 – forced labour (PUDR / Asiad workers, 1982)
  [8:8:0.1] Child below 14 in a factory or mine | Art. 24
  [8:8:0.2] Admission denied in a State-aided institution on religion, race, caste, language | Art. 29(2)
  [8:8:0.3] Dalits kept from a public well | Art. 15(2)
  [8:8:0.4] Dalits kept from a public shop | Art. 17
  [8:8:0.5] Banning an association | Art. 19(4) – valid only on permitted grounds
  [8:8:0.6] Arts. 19/21 violated by a private individual | Ordinary legal remedy, not a writ
[8:8:1] - **Not violations (reasonable restrictions):** **banning secessionist activities** (sovereignty and integrity, 16th Amendment 1963), **no loudspeakers in a religious procession** (public order, health – Church of God, 2000); a **book ban** is valid if it falls within Art. 19(2) grounds.
[8:8:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.173 (private violation: legal remedy); PUDR v. UoI (1982) 3 SCC 235; app notes 2:8 sub 8

  x: The Constitution originally contained seven groups of Fundamental Rights. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment, leaving six groups at present.

  x: The 44th Amendment removed property from Part III; it is now a constitutional/legal right under Article 300A in Part XII.

  *Part III, Articles 12 to 35 | Part IV, Articles 36 to 51 | Part III, Articles 14 to 32 only | Part IVA, Article 51A
  x: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35 (Art. 12 defines State, Art. 13 voids inconsistent laws, Arts. 33-35 cover limits and legislation). Part IV (Arts. 36-51) holds the Directive Principles and Part IVA (Art. 51A) the Fundamental Duties; Arts. 14-32 is only the span of the six groups, not the whole Part.

  During a National Emergency, the President's order under Article 359 cannot suspend the enforcement of which of the following Articles, as provided by the 44th Amendment, 1978?
  Articles 14 and 19 | *Articles 20 and 21 | Articles 21 and 32 | Articles 19 and 22
  x: Since the 44th Amendment (1978), enforcement of Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Art. 359. Arts. 14, 19, 22 and the right to move courts under Art. 32 for other rights can be affected by such an order, so the other pairs are wrong.
[n79471b49dc2] sub4
  Which Article provides for restriction of Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force?
  Article 33 | *Article 34 | Article 35 | Article 359
  x: Article 34 concerns restrictions during martial law and indemnity by Parliament; Article 33 deals with the armed forces.
[f96720666a013] sub4
  Under Article 35, who has the power to legislate on Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34?
  State Legislatures | *Parliament only | Both Parliament and State Legislatures | The President
  x: Article 35 gives this power to Parliament alone, for uniformity.
[f9a03be850189] sub4

1. It allows restrictions on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force.

3. The Constitution defines 'martial law'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  *1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | 1 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; 'martial law' is not defined in the Constitution.
[naee50e62ea5] sub5
  Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
  *Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage | Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368 | Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court | Only an Act passed by Parliament
  x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
[n7ad0cee72cf] sub5
  How are constitutional amendments made under Article 368 treated under Article 13(4)?
  Treated as ordinary laws under Article 13 | Void if they abridge any Fundamental Right | Valid only for State subjects | *Not treated as 'law' under Article 13
  x: Article 13(4), inserted by the 24th Amendment, says Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368.
[n41b73c525d4] sub5
  Article 13(1) makes void, to the extent of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights, laws in force before which event?
  Independence | *The commencement of the Constitution | The First Amendment | The 24th Amendment
  x: Article 13(1) covers laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution, not 'before Independence'.
[n5491751c43a] sub5

  Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | *Golaknath (1967) | Shankari Prasad (1951) | Maneka Gandhi (1978)
  x: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a transcendental position and held Parliament could not abridge them; the 24th Amendment (1971) responded by adding Art. 13(4). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) came after and laid down the basic structure; Shankari Prasad had upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21.
[f4a00c9de3b95] sub5
