  Golaknath | *Shankari Prasad | Kesavananda Bharati | I.R. Coelho
  x: Shankari Prasad (1951) held an amendment is not 'law'; Golaknath (1967) took the opposite view.
[faeb1f6990ef6] sub5

  1st Amendment, 1951 | 44th Amendment, 1978 | *24th Amendment, 1971 | 86th Amendment, 2002
  x: The 24th Amendment (1971) added Article 13(4) in reply to Golaknath.

[nc9657ec54a8] sub6
  Which of the following pairs of doctrine and meaning is wrongly matched?

  x: Eclipse means an inconsistent law stays dormant and may revive; voiding only the inconsistent portion is severability.
[nf3ca3525db4] sub6

  x: Under eclipse the law is dormant, not dead, and revives when the conflict is removed.

  x: Ambica Mills (1974) applied eclipse to post-constitution laws for non-citizens; Bhikaji Narain (1955) applied it to a pre-constitution law.

=== NOTES 2:9 | Right to Equality – Articles 14-18; Reasonable Classification, Reservation Jurisprudence
## SUB 0 | Articles 14–18 – Which Article Says What
[9:0:0] # The five Articles of the Right to Equality
[9:0:1] - The Right to Equality = **five Articles, 14 to 18** (Part III) – not 13–17, 15–19 or 16–20. Article 13 is not one of them; **Art. 19 belongs to the Right to Freedom** (the odd one out in a 14/15/16/19 list).
[9:0:2] TABLE head: Article | Content | Available to
  [9:0:2.0] 14 | "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India" | All persons (citizens and foreigners)
  [9:0:2.1] 15 | Prohibition of discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth | Citizens only
  [9:0:2.2] 16 | Equality of opportunity in public employment | Citizens only
  [9:0:2.3] 17 | "Untouchability" abolished; its practice in any form forbidden; enforcing any disability from it is an offence punishable by law | All (also binds private persons)
  [9:0:2.4] 18 | Titles abolished, except military and academic distinctions | —
[9:0:3] - **Match (UPSC 2004):** 14 = equality before law / equal protection; 15 = no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; 16 = equal opportunity in public employment; 17 = untouchability abolished.
[9:0:4] - Art. 14 operates **within the territory of India** (not "deep space" or "high seas").
[9:0:5] - "All are equal before law" / "equal protection of the laws" = **Article 14** (not 12, 13, 15, 21 or 22).
[9:0:6] - Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth – not Arts. 19, 23 or 25.
[9:0:7] - Art. 14 = all persons; **Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29** = citizens only. Equal protection of the law is open to all persons.
[9:0:8] - Related: **Art. 23** prohibits **human trafficking** and forced labour (Right against Exploitation); **Art. 30** – minorities' right to establish educational institutions; Art. 29 – cultural and educational rights of any section.
[9:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.169, p.184-185, p.188-197; PMF Polity Notes p.61-62
## SUB 1 | Articles 15 and 16 – Clauses and Special Provisions
[9:1:0] # Article 15 – clauses
[9:1:1] TABLE head: Clause | Content | Added by
  [9:1:1.0] 15(1) | State shall not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth (descent is not among them) | Original
  [9:1:1.1] 15(2) | Access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of entertainment; use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads – binds private persons as well as the State | Original
  [9:1:1.2] 15(3) | Special provisions for women and children | Original
  [9:1:1.3] 15(4) | Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs/OBCs), SCs and STs – "nothing in this Article or in clause (2) of Article 29 shall prevent the State …" | 1st Amendment, 1951 (after Champakam Dorairajan)
  [9:1:1.4] 15(5) | Reservation for SEBC/SC/ST in admission to educational institutions, including private aided or unaided; excludes Art. 30 minority institutions | 93rd Amendment, 2005
  [9:1:1.5] 15(6) | EWS – up to 10% in education | 103rd Amendment, 2019
[9:1:2] - The wording is "socially and **educationally** backward classes" – **not "socially and economically"**; a statement using "economically" is the wrong one.
[9:1:3] - Article 15 special provisions cover women, children, SEBCs, SCs, STs, EWS; **aged persons are NOT covered**.
[9:1:4] - Art. 15 is **limited to citizens** – "Art. 15 is not limited to citizens" is the wrong statement.
[9:1:5] # Article 16 – clauses
[9:1:6] TABLE head: Clause | Content | Added by
  [9:1:6.0] 16(1) | Equality of opportunity for all citizens in employment or appointment to any office under the State | Original
  [9:1:6.1] 16(2) | No citizen ineligible or discriminated on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence | Original
  [9:1:6.2] 16(3) | Parliament only may prescribe a residence requirement for certain jobs | Original
  [9:1:6.3] 16(4) | Reservation in appointments for backward classes not adequately represented in State services | Original
  [9:1:6.4] 16(4A) | SC/ST reservation in promotion – then with consequential seniority (nullified the "catch-up" rule) | 77th (1995); 85th (2001)
  [9:1:6.5] 16(4B) | Backlog (carried-forward) vacancies a separate group, outside the 50% ceiling | 81st (2000)
  [9:1:6.6] 16(5) | Office in a religious or denominational institution may be kept for persons of that religion/denomination | Original
  [9:1:6.7] 16(6) | EWS – up to 10% in public employment | 103rd (2019)
[9:1:7] - **Equal opportunity in public employment** = **16(1) and 16(2)**, for **all citizens** (not only citizens born in India, not all persons).
[9:1:8] - **Reservation in employment** = **16(4)**; **OBC reservation** = **Arts. 15(4) and 16(4)**.
[9:1:9] - **Reservation in promotions:** first provided by the **77th Amendment, 1995** (Art. 16(4A)); the **85th (2001)** extended it with consequential seniority. 16(4A) is **enabling** – it lets, not obliges, the State to reserve.
[9:1:10] - **103rd Amendment, 2019** (passed as the **124th Amendment Bill**) – Arts. **15(6) and 16(6)**, EWS up to **10%**; the 102nd = NCBC, not EWS.
[9:1:11] - **105th Amendment (2021)** restored the States' power to identify SEBCs (reversed the Maratha-case reading of the **102nd**).
[9:1:12] # Related reservation Articles
[9:1:13] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [9:1:13.0] 340 | President appoints a commission on the conditions of SEBCs
  [9:1:13.1] 338B | NCBC – constitutional body (102nd Amendment)
  [9:1:13.2] 342A | President specifies SEBCs for the Central List; States keep their own lists (102nd, 105th)
  [9:1:13.3] 335 | SC/ST claims to be considered consistently with efficiency of administration
[9:1:14] - **Protective discrimination:** special provisions for SCs/STs (e.g. the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989**) rest on the **doctrine of protective discrimination** – not severability, preferred position or harmonious construction.
[9:1:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.188-195; PMF Polity Notes p.61-62; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.38-39; Constitution of India, Arts. 15-16 (legislative.gov.in)
## SUB 2 | Article 14 – Equality Before Law, Equal Protection, Reasonable Classification
[9:2:0] # Two faces of Article 14
[9:2:1] TABLE head: Equality before law | Equal protection of the laws
  [9:2:1.0] British origin (Dicey) | American origin (US 14th Amendment)
  [9:2:1.1] Negative concept: absence of special privileges; no one above law | Positive concept: like treated alike in equal circumstances
  [9:2:1.2] All equally subject to ordinary law and ordinary courts | Permits reasonable classification
[9:2:2] - Art. 14 contains **both** concepts – "Art. 14 has only equality before law, not equal protection" is false.
[9:2:3] - An implication of equality is the **absence of privileges** (not of restraints, competition or ideology).
[9:2:4] - "Equals must be treated equally, unequals differently": the State **can treat unequals differently** to create a level playing field, and **among equals the law should be equal and equally administered** (A and R both true, R explains A).
[9:2:5] # Reasonable classification and arbitrariness
[9:2:6] - Art. 14 **forbids class legislation**, **not reasonable classification** (not rural/urban legislation).
[9:2:7] - **Twin test**: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus** with the law's object.
[9:2:8] - **E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)**: "Equality and arbitrariness are **sworn enemies**" / equality is **antithetic to arbitrariness**.
[9:2:9] - **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: any arbitrary State action breaks Art. 14. A law giving the executive **unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power** violates **Article 14** (UPSC 2021; not Arts. 28, 32, 44).
[9:2:10] - Article 14 puts a **limitation on legislative power** (UPPCS 1999 key: Art. 14).
[9:2:11] - **11 Apr 2026**: SC held the State cannot treat **pensioners** differently from serving employees on **dearness allowance** without valid classification (Kerala/KSRTC).
[9:2:12] - **Feb 2026**: SC questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the **UGC equity regulations** (**Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India**).
[9:2:13] # Exceptions – equality is not absolute
[9:2:14] TABLE head: Provision | Immunity / special status
  [9:2:14.0] Art. 361 | President and Governors not answerable to courts; no criminal case during term; civil case only after two months' notice
  [9:2:14.1] Art. 361A (44th, 1978) | No liability for a true, non-malicious report of proceedings of Parliament/State legislatures
  [9:2:14.2] Arts. 105 / 194 | MPs / MLAs: immunity for anything said or vote given in the House
  [9:2:14.3] International law | Foreign sovereigns, ambassadors, diplomats and UN agencies immune from civil and criminal proceedings
[9:2:15] - APPSC G1: **Arts. 194 and 361A** show equality in India is **not absolute**; in India equality is guaranteed by the **Constitution** (Dicey's "rights from courts" idea does not fit India).
[9:2:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.184-188; PMF Polity Notes p.61; E.P. Royappa (1974) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) as cited there
## SUB 3 | Rule of Law – Dicey
[9:3:0] - **A.V. Dicey** (British jurist), *Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution* (**1885**). India borrowed the Rule of Law from **Britain** (with parliamentary government, single citizenship, cabinet system) – **not from the GoI Act 1935** (that gave the federal scheme, Governor, emergency powers).
[9:3:1] - **Three elements**: (1) **absence of arbitrary power** (**limitation of powers**) – regular law supreme, no punishment except for a distinct breach of law; (2) **equality before law**; (3) **primacy of individual rights** (**liberty and civil rights**) – rights from judicial decisions.
[9:3:2] - **Not an element**: "**people's responsibility to the Government**" → features asked = **1, 2 and 4** (UPSC 2018). "The State has inherent unlimited police powers" – false.
[9:3:3] - Rule of Law means every citizen is **equal before law**, gets **equal protection**, suffers **no discrimination** and enjoys **no special privileges**.
[9:3:4] - Dicey opposed the French **droit administratif** (officials subject only to special administrative tribunals).
[9:3:5] - **India accepts (1) and (2) but reverses (3)**: in India the **Constitution is the source of rights**.
[9:3:6] - Rule of Law in India rests on **Article 14**; it is a **basic feature** – **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
[9:3:7] - Rule of Law operates in a **democracy** (not dictatorship, monarchy, autocracy); APPSC calls it the force that **moves the machine of democracy**.
[9:3:8] TABLE head: Rule of Law | Rule by Law
  [9:3:8.0] Government subordinate to law | Ruler above law; law as a weapon of state control
  [9:3:8.1] Laws just, fair, non-arbitrary | Governs citizens only
[9:3:9] - **Rule of Law Index** – released by the **World Justice Project** (not Amnesty, ICJ or OHCHR); measuring since 2008.
[9:3:10] > The Rule of Law is British, not American: the Indian Constitution resembles the **US** in **Fundamental Rights** (Bill of Rights), judicial review and equal protection.
[9:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.155 (borrowed features), p.184-187; PMF Polity Notes p.61; World Justice Project (worldjusticeproject.org)
## SUB 4 | Article 17 – Untouchability
[9:4:0] - **Article 17** abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form (not Arts. 14, 15, 16, 18, 19 or 21). Adopted amid cries of "**Mahatma Gandhi ki Jai**".
[9:4:1] - "Untouchability" is **not defined** in the Constitution or the Act. Art. 17 also operates **against private individuals**.
[9:4:2] - Untouchability as a social practice = **boycotting**, **insult and oppression**, **exploitation** (not equality or integration).
[9:4:3] - **Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955** → renamed **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** by the **1976** amendment (the title keeps 1955). A person convicted under it is disqualified for election to Parliament/State legislature.
[9:4:4] - **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989** – further law against caste atrocities.
[9:4:5] - **False evidence (Sec. 3(2)(i), PoA Act):** a non-SC/ST person who fabricates false evidence so that an SC/ST member is convicted of a **capital offence** gets **imprisonment for life and fine**; if the innocent SC/ST member is **executed**, the punishment is **death**.
[9:4:6] - MPPSC 2015: the Article through which SCs/STs are given fundamental socio-economic and cultural protection = **Article 17**.
[9:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.195-196; PMF Polity Notes p.62
## SUB 5 | Article 18 – Titles and Awards
[9:5:0] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [9:5:0.0] 18(1) | State confers no title except military or academic distinctions
  [9:5:0.1] 18(2) | A citizen shall not accept a foreign title at all – no consent route
  [9:5:0.2] 18(3) | A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust needs the President's consent to accept a foreign title
  [9:5:0.3] 18(4) | No office-holder may accept a present, emolument or office from a foreign State without the President's consent
[9:5:1] - So the Constitution bans **both** the State conferring titles **and** citizens accepting foreign titles.
[9:5:2] - **Abolishes titles = Article 18** (not 17, 24 or 25).
[9:5:3] - **Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Shri** are given under **Article 18** (military/academic-type distinctions, not titles).
[9:5:4] - **Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (Dec 1995)**: **Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles**, but must **not be used as prefixes or suffixes**; equality admits distinction of merit, not hereditary titles.
[9:5:5] - Art. 18 helps **social equality** by ending artificial distinctions.
[9:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.196-197; PMF Polity Notes p.62
## SUB 6 | Types of Equality
[9:6:0] TABLE head: Type | Articles
  [9:6:0.0] Social | 15, 17, 18 – Arts. 17 and 18 provide social equality
  [9:6:0.1] Economic | DPSP 39(b), 39(c), 39(d)
  [9:6:0.2] Political | 325, 326 – no exclusion from rolls, adult suffrage
[9:6:1] - **Economic equality is NOT part of the FR to equality.** Included: equality before law (14), social equality (15), equal opportunity (16).
[9:6:2] - "**Political freedom without economic equality is an illusion**" – attributed in Indian textbooks to **G.D.H. Cole** (the idea goes back to Bakunin's "a pretence, a fraud, a lie").
[9:6:3] - Preamble promises "**equality of status and of opportunity**".
[9:6:4] - **Ambedkar**: liberty, equality, fraternity = an **inseparable trinity**.
[9:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.185, p.188; Constitution, Preamble and Arts. 39, 325-326
## SUB 7 | Reservation Jurisprudence
[9:7:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [9:7:0.0] Champakam Dorairajan | 1951 | Madras Communal G.O. struck down under Art. 29(2) → 1st Amendment, Art. 15(4)
  [9:7:0.1] M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore | 1962 | Caste not the sole test; reservation reasonable, generally below 50%
  [9:7:0.2] Janki Prasad Parimoo v. J&K | 1973 | Caste alone not the sole determinant of backwardness under 15(4)
  [9:7:0.3] Indra Sawhney (Mandal) | 16 Nov 1992 | 9 judges, 6:3; upheld 27% OBC; creamy layer excluded; 50% ceiling; no reservation in promotions; ordered a permanent body (NCBC)
  [9:7:0.4] Samatha v. State of AP | 1997 | No tribal land leases in Schedule V areas to non-tribals/private parties
  [9:7:0.5] M. Nagaraj | 2006 | Upheld 77th, 81st, 85th with conditions: quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation, efficiency (Art. 335)
  [9:7:0.6] Ashoka Kumar Thakur | 2008 | Upheld the 93rd Amendment; 27% OBC in central institutions
  [9:7:0.7] Niyamgiri (Orissa Mining Corp.) | 2013 | Gram Sabha's role under the Forest Rights Act, 2006; Dongria Kondh
  [9:7:0.8] Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta | 2018 | No proof of backwardness for SC/ST promotions; creamy layer extended to SC/ST promotions
  [9:7:0.9] Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil (Maratha) | 2021 | Maratha quota struck for crossing 50%
  [9:7:0.10] Janhit Abhiyan | 2022 | Upheld 103rd, 10% EWS, 3:2
  [9:7:0.11] State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh | 1 Aug 2024 | 7 judges, 6:1; overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004); sub-classification of SCs/STs allowed
[9:7:1] - Order: **Champakam → Balaji → Indra Sawhney → Nagaraj**.
[9:7:2] - Creamy layer and the 50% cap **originate in Indra Sawhney (1992)**; OBC creamy layer **₹8 lakh a year (2017)**.
[9:7:3] - Exceptions to 50%: **carried-forward vacancies (81st)**; extraordinary situations; **EWS 10%** (Janhit Abhiyan). No State legislature has free power to cross the ceiling.
[9:7:4] - **Apr 2026**: Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy layer with the **central income limits**.
[9:7:5] - **Aug 2026**: Centre **opposes** an income-based creamy layer for **SCs and STs**.
[9:7:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.193-194; PMF Polity Notes p.61-62; old app notes (case table) checked against Indra Sawhney (1992), Janhit Abhiyan (2022), Davinder Singh (2024)

=== NOTES 2:10 | Right to Freedom – Article 19 (six Freedoms) and Reasonable Restrictions
## SUB 0 | Article 19 – the Six Freedoms
[10:0:0] - **Article 19** guarantees **six freedoms** to citizens (not Arts. 14, 18, 20, 21 or 22) – **seven originally** (asked as "seven freedoms" in older papers); the 7th, property, was deleted.
[10:0:1] - **Right to Freedom** group = **Articles 19–22** (four Articles); Arts. 14–16 belong to the Equality group.
[10:0:2] TABLE head: Clause | Freedom | Restricted by
  [10:0:2.0] 19(1)(a) | Speech and expression | 19(2)
  [10:0:2.1] 19(1)(b) | Assemble peaceably and without arms | 19(3)
  [10:0:2.2] 19(1)(c) | Form associations or unions or co-operative societies (co-ops added by 97th, 2011) | 19(4)
  [10:0:2.3] 19(1)(d) | Move freely throughout the territory of India | 19(5)
  [10:0:2.4] 19(1)(e) | Reside and settle in any part of India | 19(5)
  [10:0:2.5] 19(1)(f) | Acquire, hold and dispose of property – deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978 | —
  [10:0:2.6] 19(1)(g) | Practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business | 19(6)
[10:0:3] - **Match:** 19(1)(a) = speech and expression; (b) = assemble peaceably without arms; (c) = associations or unions; (d) = move freely throughout India.
[10:0:4] - **Not in Article 19(1):** **equal opportunity** (Art. 16), **property** (deleted 1978), **moving out of the country** (travel abroad = **Art. 21**, Maneka Gandhi 1978), **freedom of conscience** (Art. 25).
[10:0:5] - **Property** was removed as a Fundamental Right by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (now Art. 300A, a legal right).
[10:0:6] - **97th Amendment (2011)**: the new right to **form co-operative societies** in 19(1)(c); also **Article 43B** and **Part IXB**.
[10:0:7] - In force from **26 January 1950** – Art. 19 of the original Constitution provided freedom of expression.
[10:0:8] - Related Articles: **Art. 20** – protection in respect of conviction for offences; **Art. 21** – protection of life and personal liberty; **21A** (86th, 2002) – education; **Art. 22** – arrest and detention, preventive detention without an **Advisory Board**: max **three months**.
[10:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.197, p.200-207; PMF Polity Notes p.62-63; Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978
## SUB 1 | Freedom of Speech and Expression – Press and Implied Rights
[10:1:0] - Freedom of speech is **the most essential ingredient of democracy** among the freedoms.
[10:1:1] - **Freedom of the press is not named in the Constitution**; it is **implied in / secured under 19(1)(a)** (not specially provided, not from a law of Parliament, executive power, Art. 361A or the Rule of Law). Trade, residence and association **are** expressly listed.
[10:1:2] - Speech is protected **irrespective of the medium of communication** – press, TV, internet.
[10:1:3] - The **right to know, receive and impart information** is part of 19(1)(a); RTI itself is not named in the Constitution.
[10:1:4] TABLE head: Implied right | Case
  [10:1:4.0] Press and circulation | Romesh Thappar (1950); Sakal Papers (1961); Indian Express (1985)
  [10:1:4.1] Hoisting the National Flag (also on private buildings) – 19(1)(a) | Naveen Jindal (2004) – industrialist Naveen Jindal's PIL in the Delhi HC; the Flag Code is only executive instructions
  [10:1:4.2] Right to silence (not singing the National Anthem) | Bijoe Emmanuel v. Kerala (1986) – speech and conscience (Art. 25)
  [10:1:4.3] Right to information / to know | State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975); voters' right to know candidates
  [10:1:4.4] Commercial speech | Tata Press (1995)
  [10:1:4.5] Speech and trade over the internet | Anuradha Bhasin (2020) – 19(1)(a), 19(1)(g)
  [10:1:4.6] Telecast; no government monopoly on airwaves | Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)
  [10:1:4.7] Against phone tapping | PUCL (1997) – safeguards
[10:1:5] - **National Anthem:** compelling it violates speech/expression and conscience, and **no law obliges anyone to sing it** (the 1971 Act punishes only preventing its singing) → all three statements correct (UPSC 1996).
[10:1:6] - **Internet access** is linked to **Article 19** (SSC 2020 key; Anuradha Bhasin) – "Right to access internet: Art. 21" is the mismatched pair; privacy and shelter are Art. 21 rights.
[10:1:7] - **Films may be pre-censored**, unlike the press, because they **reach larger audiences**.
[10:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.197, p.200, p.206; PMF Polity Notes p.62-63; Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986); Union of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004)
## SUB 2 | Reasonable Restrictions – 19(2) to 19(6)
[10:2:0] - In a democracy the right to freedom = **freedom with reasonable restrictions** – not unlimited, not as fixed by the Government or civil society.
[10:2:1] TABLE head: Clause | Freedom | Grounds
  [10:2:1.0] 19(2) | Speech | Eight: sovereignty and integrity, security of State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence
  [10:2:1.1] 19(3) | Assembly | Sovereignty and integrity; public order (not morality, not security of State)
  [10:2:1.2] 19(4) | Association | Sovereignty and integrity; public order; morality
  [10:2:1.3] 19(5) | Movement, residence | General public interest; protection of Scheduled Tribes
  [10:2:1.4] 19(6) | Profession, trade | General public interest; professional/technical qualifications; State trade or monopoly
[10:2:2] - **Not a 19(2) ground**: **sedition**, **views opposing the Government**, **unbecoming criticism**, "general public interest", economic grounds. The grounds are **exhaustive** (**Kaushal Kishor, 2023**).
[10:2:3] - **Defamation**: **slander = spoken** (oral), libel = written; civil (tort) and criminal liability.
[10:2:4] # Grounds added by amendments
[10:2:5] TABLE head: Amendment | Added
  [10:2:5.0] 1st (1951) | Public order, friendly relations, incitement; rewrote 19(6) – qualifications and State monopoly
  [10:2:5.1] 16th (1963) | Sovereignty and integrity of India in 19(2), (3), (4)
[10:2:6] # Test of reasonableness
[10:2:7] - **State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)**: nature of the right, purpose, extent and urgency of the evil, proportionality.
[10:2:8] - **Courts** decide reasonableness; a restriction must **not eclipse the right**; it must safeguard the **interest of the general public** and weigh **prevailing social values and needs**.
[10:2:9] - **Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962)** – the landmark judgment on **sedition**: s.124A IPC valid only for incitement to violence or public disorder.
[10:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.198-200, p.201 (sedition not a ground); PMF Polity Notes p.63; Kedar Nath Singh (1962) in Indian Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt)
## SUB 3 | Availability – Citizens Only; Detenus; Golden Triangle
[10:3:0] - Art. 19 is for **citizens only** – not foreigners, not a company as a legal person (citizen shareholders may sue). Freedom of speech is guaranteed **only to citizens**; life and liberty, equality before law and freedom of religion extend to foreigners too.
[10:3:1] - A **British citizen** in India cannot claim **freedom of trade and profession** (19(1)(g)).
[10:3:2] - Available against **State action**; but **Kaushal Kishor (2023)**: Arts. 19 and 21 enforceable against **non-State actors** too.
[10:3:3] - A person whose movement is taken away by **imprisonment or detention** does **not** lose his **freedom of expression** – he may write and publish books (State of Maharashtra v. Prabhakar Pandurang Sanzgiri, 1966).
[10:3:4] - **Golden triangle**: Arts. **14, 19, 21** – **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**.
[10:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.200; PMF Polity Notes p.62; Indian Polity Part 1 (detenu rights)
## SUB 4 | Assembly, Association, Movement and Profession
[10:4:0] - Assembly must be **peaceful and unarmed**; excludes violent or **armed** gatherings. A **gherao** of officials is **not** part of 19(1)(b); 19(3) allows public-order limits.
[10:4:1] - Right to protest is read from 19(1)(a), (b) and 21. **22 May 2026**: SC – peaceful protest is everybody's right but **must not disturb other citizens** or occupy public space.
[10:4:2] TABLE head: Action | Status | Case
  [10:4:2.0] Demonstration | Protected; strike not | Kameshwar Prasad (1962)
  [10:4:2.1] Strike | Not an FR – only a legal right | All India Bank Employees' Assn (1962)
  [10:4:2.2] Strike by govt employees | No right | T.K. Rangarajan (2003)
  [10:4:2.3] Bandh | Illegal – curbs others' freedoms | CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar
[10:4:3] - **FCRA**: Centre defends curbs under **19(4)** (25 Jun 2026); **INSAF (2020)** – only associations in **active politics** may be barred from foreign funds.
[10:4:4] - **19(5)**: entry and settlement of outsiders may be limited to protect **Scheduled Tribes** (Inner Line areas).
[10:4:5] - **19(6)**: State may prescribe **professional or technical qualifications** and run a trade **to the exclusion of citizens** (State monopoly) – inserted by the **1st Amendment**. **No right to a dangerous or immoral trade** (e.g. trafficking).
[10:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.199-200; PMF Polity Notes p.63
## SUB 5 | Speech and Press Cases
[10:5:0] TABLE head: Case | Ruling
  [10:5:0.0] Romesh Thappar v. Madras (1950) | Ban on journal Cross Roads struck; "public order" then not a ground → 1st Amendment
  [10:5:0.1] Kedar Nath Singh (1962) | Sedition valid only for incitement to violence
  [10:5:0.2] Bennett Coleman (1972) | Newsprint policy fixing pages violated press freedom
  [10:5:0.3] Aveek Sarkar (2014) | "Community standards" test for obscenity
  [10:5:0.4] Shreya Singhal (2015) | Sec. 66A IT Act struck – vague, overbroad
  [10:5:0.5] Anuradha Bhasin (2020) | Internet shutdowns must be proportionate, temporary, published
[10:5:1] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes p.63; old app notes (case table)
## SUB 6 | Article 19 During Emergency – 358 vs 359
[10:6:0] TABLE head: Article 358 | Article 359
  [10:6:0.0] Art. 19 suspended automatically – all six freedoms | Needs a Presidential order
  [10:6:0.1] Only for emergency on war or external aggression (44th Amendment), not armed rebellion | Suspends only enforcement of the rights named
  [10:6:0.2] Covers only Art. 19 | Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended (44th)
[10:6:1] - "Article ___ is suspended when emergency is imposed" → **Article 19** (not 21, 27 or 41).
[10:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.225 (suspension of FRs); Constitution Arts. 358-359
## SUB 7 | New Criminal Laws (from 1 July 2024)
[10:7:0] - **BNS, 2023** replaced the IPC; **BNSS, 2023** replaced the CrPC (statutory **Zero FIR**, video recording of search and seizure).
[10:7:1] TABLE head: Subject | Old | New
  [10:7:1.0] Sedition | s.124A IPC (in abeyance 2022) | s.152 BNS – endangering sovereignty, unity, integrity
  [10:7:1.1] Criminal defamation | IPC 499-500 | s.356 BNS
  [10:7:1.2] Hate speech | — | s.196 BNS
  [10:7:1.3] Unlawful assembly (five or more) | IPC s.141 | s.189 BNS
  [10:7:1.4] Prohibitory orders | CrPC s.144 | s.163 BNSS
[10:7:2] ~~ Sources: old app notes (BNS/BNSS table); PIB on the new criminal laws (1 Jul 2024)

[nindian-polity-16-16] sub0
  Which Article provides protection in respect of conviction for offences?
  19 | *20 | 21 | 22
  x: Article 20 gives protection in respect of conviction; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, 22 protects against arrest and detention, and 19 lists the six freedoms.

=== NOTES 2:11 | Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 – Protection in Conviction, Life and Liberty, Education, Preventive Detention
## SUB 0 | Article 21A – Right to Education, 86th Amendment and RTE Act
[11:0:0] # Article 21A
[11:0:1] - **Text:** the State shall provide **free and compulsory education** to all children of the age of **6 to 14 years** "in such manner as the State may, **by law**, determine". Only **elementary** education is an FR – not higher or professional education.
[11:0:2] - **Inserted by:** the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002** (introduced as the **93rd Amendment Bill**, 2001) – not the 42nd, 44th, 74th, 91st or the RTE Act itself (an Act cannot add an Article). The **93rd Amendment Act, 2005** is a different law (OBC reservation in educational institutions, Art. 15(5)).
[11:0:3] - **In force:** Art. 21A and the **RTE Act** both came into force on **1 April 2010** – so the year the right to education "came into force as an FR" is **2010**, though the amendment is of **2002**.
[11:0:4] - **Nature:** a **Fundamental Right** (not statutory, natural or a DPSP right); an **extension of the right to life (Art. 21)**; essential to the right to development as a human right. Aim: **"Education for All"**.
[11:0:5] - **Earlier position:** free and compulsory education was a **Part IV (DPSP)** provision – the original **Art. 45** asked the State to provide it for all children **until they complete 14 years** (within ten years).
[11:0:6] TABLE head: 86th Amendment changed | New content
  [11:0:6.0] Art. 21A (FR) | Free, compulsory education 6–14 years
  [11:0:6.1] Art. 45 (DPSP) | Early childhood care and education for children below 6
  [11:0:6.2] Art. 51A(k) (Fundamental Duty) | Parent/guardian to provide opportunities for education to child 6–14 – the 11th duty
[11:0:7] - **Not** a change of the 86th Amendment: deleting the **Right to Property** – that was the **44th (1978)**.
[11:0:8] # Cases before 21A
[11:0:9] TABLE head: Case | Year | Ruling
  [11:0:9.0] Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka | 1992 | Right to education flows from Art. 21
  [11:0:9.1] Unnikrishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh | 1993 | Read education into Art. 21: free education up to 14 years is a right; beyond that it depends on the State's economic capacity
[11:0:10] - **Sequence:** Mohini Jain (1992) → Unnikrishnan (1993) → 86th Amendment (2002) → RTE Act (2009) → in force (2010).
[11:0:11] # RTE Act, 2009 (Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act)
[11:0:12] - **Passed by Parliament:** Rajya Sabha 20 July 2009, Lok Sabha **4 August 2009** (assent 26 Aug 2009); **in force 1 April 2010**.
[11:0:13] - **Sec. 3:** every child of **6–14** has a right to free and compulsory education in a **neighbourhood school** till elementary education is complete.
[11:0:14] - **25%** of entry-level seats (class I or pre-school) in **unaided private schools** for children of weaker and disadvantaged groups of the neighbourhood; schools reimbursed; **not minority schools**.
[11:0:15] - **Duties:** appropriate Government and local authority to establish schools in the neighbourhood within **3 years**; **every parent/guardian** to admit the child; **funding is a concurrent responsibility of Centre and States** – the Centre does **not** bear sole responsibility.
[11:0:16] - Amendments: 2012, 2017, **2019** (no-detention policy relaxed – regular exams in classes 5 and 8), 2022.
[11:0:17] > Asked as: which Article/Amendment (86th – about 10 PYQs), the age (6–14), in force date/year (1 April 2010), FR or DPSP, 93rd Bill, Unnikrishnan (AP case), 25% quota, "not a feature of RTE" (sole central funding).
[11:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.206-207; Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.38-40; RTE Act 2009 (education.gov.in); app notes 2:11 sub 6
## SUB 1 | Article 20 – Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences
[11:1:0] - **Available to:** every person – **citizens, foreigners and legal persons** (companies). It cannot be suspended in an emergency (see last sub-section).
[11:1:1] TABLE head: Clause | Protection | Scope / NOT covered
  [11:1:1.0] 20(1) | No ex post facto criminal law – no conviction except for violating a "law in force" when the act was done, and no penalty greater than that law allowed | Only criminal laws – civil or tax laws can be retrospective; bars conviction/heavier penalty, not the trial; not applicable to preventive detention
  [11:1:1.1] 20(2) | No double jeopardy – no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once | Only before a court or judicial tribunal; not departmental or administrative proceedings
  [11:1:1.2] 20(3) | No self-incrimination – no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself | Covers testimonial compulsion (oral and documentary); not physical evidence – fingerprints, specimen signatures, blood, DNA (Kathi Kalu Oghad, 1961); voice sample for investigation is allowed (Ritesh Sinha, 2019)
[11:1:2] - **Ex post facto law** = a **retrospective** law (not prospective, not a Bill). Hence **Parliament cannot** make a **criminal law with retrospective effect** that convicts or enhances punishment.
[11:1:3] - **Double jeopardy:** maxim *nemo debet bis vexari*; Art. 20(2) rests on **autrefois convict** (previously convicted) – both prosecution **and** punishment are needed, so *autrefois acquit* is not covered. CrPC Sec. 300 → **Sec. 337 BNSS**.
[11:1:4] - **Nature:** 20(1) is **substantive** law of criminal liability and penalty; 20(2) and 20(3) are **procedural**. "Art. 20 does not protect against testimonial compulsion" is **false**.
[11:1:5] - **Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010):** involuntary **narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping** violate **Art. 20(3)** and **Art. 21** (personal liberty, privacy).
[11:1:6] - **Not in Art. 20:** **prohibition against torture** (that is **Art. 21**); preventive detention safeguards (Art. 22).
[11:1:7] > Asked as: "which Article – double jeopardy / self-incrimination" (about 10 PYQs), the clause (20(2), 20(3)), maxims (autrefois convict, ex post facto = retrospective), "NOT part of Art. 20" (torture), voice sample, Selvi.
[11:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.201-204; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) (Art. 20); Laxmikanth ch. Fundamental Rights (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt); Ritesh Sinha v. State of UP (2019) sci.gov.in; app notes 2:11 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Rights Read into Article 21 and the Right to Privacy
[11:2:0] # Article 21 at its widest
[11:2:1] - **Right to life** and **personal liberty** ("freedom"); available to **citizens and non-citizens**. Many unenumerated rights are read in by the Supreme Court – e.g. **food**, health, **shelter**, **livelihood**, dignity; **no right to permanent housing** is enumerated anywhere.
[11:2:2] TABLE head: Right | Case
  [11:2:2.0] Travel abroad; fair procedure | Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967); Maneka Gandhi (1978)
  [11:2:2.1] Privacy | Govind v. State of MP (1975); Malak Singh (1980); K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)
  [11:2:2.2] Privacy – phone tapping | PUCL v. Union of India (1997) – tapping infringes Art. 21
  [11:2:2.3] Livelihood | Olga Tellis (1985)
  [11:2:2.4] Shelter | Shantistar Builders v. N.K. Totame (1990); Chameli Singh (1995)
  [11:2:2.5] Emergency medical aid | Parmanand Katara (1989); Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) – emergency medical care
  [11:2:2.6] Clean environment and air | Subhash Kumar (1991)
  [11:2:2.7] Marry a person of choice | Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006); Shafin Jahan (Hadiya, 2018)
  [11:2:2.8] Human dignity | Francis Coralie Mullin (1981)
  [11:2:2.9] Free legal aid | M.H. Hoskot (1978); Hussainara Khatoon
  [11:2:2.10] Speedy trial | Hussainara Khatoon (1979)
  [11:2:2.11] Protection of women in police custody | Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983); handcuffing curbed in Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)
  [11:2:2.12] Compensation for violation | Nilabati Behera (1993)
  [11:2:2.13] Workplace sexual harassment | Vishaka (1997)
[11:2:3] - **Also under Art. 21:** rights of **transgender persons** (NALSA, 2014), of **craniopagus (conjoined) twins**, of a mentally retarded woman to bear a child (Suchita Srivastava, 2009) – all three (CDS 2017); protection against **torture** and **solitary confinement**.
[11:2:4] - **Marriage:** Art. 21 protects the choice of partner (**UPSC 2019: Art. 21**), but **Supriyo Chakraborty (2023)**: there is **no unqualified fundamental right to marry** as such. **Travel abroad** is an FR (Maneka). So APPSC G2 Mains 2025 key: **both statements right**.
[11:2:5] # Right to Privacy
[11:2:6] - **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 24 Aug 2017:** a **nine-judge** bench, unanimous (**9:0**) – privacy is a Fundamental Right, an intrinsic part of **Article 21 and the freedoms of Part III** (UPSC 2018, 2024: **Art. 21**).
[11:2:7] - **Overruled** M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent they denied privacy as an FR.
[11:2:8] - Test for limiting privacy: **legality** (a law), **legitimate aim**, **proportionality**.
[11:2:9] > Asked as: "right to privacy/marry/travel abroad/food is in which Article" (21), wrong case pair (**Govind = privacy, not property**), what is NOT an enumerated right.
[11:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.205-206; Laxmikanth ch. Fundamental Rights (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) (Art. 21 case list); sci.gov.in Puttaswamy (2017), Supriyo Chakraborty (2023); app notes 2:11 sub 3-4
## SUB 3 | Article 22 – Arrest and Preventive Detention
[11:3:0] # Punitive arrest – 22(1), 22(2)
[11:3:1] - Arrested person must be **told the grounds** of arrest; may **consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice**; must be **produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours** (**Art. 22(2)**, excluding journey time) – not 12, 48 hours or one week.
[11:3:2] - **22(3) exclusions:** **enemy aliens** and persons held under a **preventive detention** law – not ordinary foreigners or OCIs. So detention beyond 24 hours without a magistrate is allowed only in **preventive detention**.
[11:3:3] - **Also outside:** arrest on a **court order** (person in jail under judicial order), **civil arrest**, deportation of an alien.
[11:3:4] - **Not guaranteed:** **bail as of right**, trial by jury. CrPC Secs. 50, 57 → BNSS Secs. 47, 58. **Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025):** grounds must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.
[11:3:5] # Preventive detention – 22(4) to 22(7)
[11:3:6] - **Preventive** = detention **without trial**, on suspicion of future harmful acts; **punitive** = after trial and conviction. Justified for **public order**, not routine **law and order**.
[11:3:7] - **22(4):** no detention beyond **3 months** unless an **Advisory Board** (**High Court judges** or persons qualified to be) reports sufficient cause. **44th Amendment (1978)** cut it to **2 months**, but that clause was **never notified** – 3 months still applies.
[11:3:8] - **22(5):** grounds communicated + **earliest opportunity of representation**. **22(7):** **Parliament** fixes the maximum period and Advisory Board procedure.
[11:3:9] TABLE head: Who legislates | Subjects
  [11:3:9.0] Parliament alone | Defence, foreign affairs, security of India
  [11:3:9.1] Parliament and States | Public order, security of a State, essential supplies
[11:3:10] # Preventive detention laws
[11:3:11] TABLE head: Law | Year | Note
  [11:3:11.0] Preventive Detention Act | 1950 | First such law; lapsed 1969
  [11:3:11.1] UAPA | 1967 | Anti-terror; SC (Jan 2026): delay alone not a "trump card" for bail
  [11:3:11.2] MISA | 1971 | Used in the Emergency; repealed 1978
  [11:3:11.3] COFEPOSA | 1974 | Smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators
  [11:3:11.4] NSA | 1980 | Detention up to 12 months without charges
[11:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.208-209; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) (Art. 22, Advisory Board, 44th Amendment); app notes 2:11 sub 7-8
## SUB 4 | Article 21 – Procedure Established by Law, Due Process, Natural Justice
[11:4:0] - **Text:** "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to **procedure established by law**" – phrase from the **Japanese** Constitution; "**due process of law**" is American. Art. 21 does not use the words "due process".
[11:4:1] TABLE head: A.K. Gopalan (1950) | Maneka Gandhi (1978)
  [11:4:1.0] Any procedure enacted by the legislature suffices | Procedure must be just, fair and reasonable
  [11:4:1.1] Arts. 19, 21, 22 separate | Arts. 14, 19, 21 linked – the golden triangle
  [11:4:1.2] Protects only against the executive | Also against arbitrary legislation – in effect American due process read into Art. 21
[11:4:2] - **Due process of law**, in essence = the **principle of natural justice** (UPSC 2023); the doctrine is now read into **Article 21**.
[11:4:3] - **Natural justice:** **audi alteram partem** = "hear the other side" – the **right to be heard**; *nemo judex in causa sua* = no one a judge in his own cause.
[11:4:4] - **Protection is against** the State's **executive and legislative** action (Laxmikanth). *(Since **Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP, 2023**, Arts. 19 and 21 can also be enforced against private persons.)*
[11:4:5] - **Unguided, uncontrolled executive discretion** breaks **Article 14** (arbitrary).
[11:4:6] - **Capital punishment** does not violate Art. 21 – **Bachan Singh (1980)**, "rarest of rare"; so it is "not within the purview" of Art. 21 rights.
[11:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.205-206; Laxmikanth ch. Fundamental Rights (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt); UPSC CSP 2023 answer key; app notes 2:11 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Right to Die and Euthanasia
[11:5:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Ruling
  [11:5:0.0] Maruti Shripati Dubal (Bombay HC) | 1987 | Right to die part of Art. 21; Sec. 309 IPC unconstitutional
  [11:5:0.1] Chenna Jagadeeswar (AP High Court) | 1988 | Art. 21 gives no right to die; Sec. 309 upheld
  [11:5:0.2] P. Rathinam | 1994 | Sec. 309 IPC (attempted suicide) unconstitutional
  [11:5:0.3] Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab | 1996 | Overruled Rathinam: "right to life" does not include "right to die" (only a right to die with dignity); Sec. 309 valid
  [11:5:0.4] Aruna Shanbaug | 2011 | Nurse in a vegetative state for 42 years after a 1973 assault – face of the euthanasia debate; plea rejected but passive euthanasia under High Court supervision allowed
  [11:5:0.5] Common Cause | 2018 | Dying with dignity an FR under Art. 21; living will / advance directive upheld
[11:5:1] - **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017:** attempted suicide effectively decriminalised. **BNS, 2023** (in force **1 July 2024**): no general offence of attempted suicide.
[11:5:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.205-206; sci.gov.in Gian Kaur (1996), Common Cause (2018); app notes 2:11 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Articles 20 and 21 During an Emergency
[11:6:0] - **44th Amendment (1978):** the enforcement of **Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended** under Art. 359 even during a National Emergency – the only such FRs (Arts. 14, 19, 22 can be).
[11:6:1] - So "right to life and personal liberty" can never be suspended; freedom of movement, residence, profession (Art. 19) can.
[11:6:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.223-225 (Art. 359); Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.38-40; app notes 2:11 sub 9

=== NOTES 2:12 | Right Against Exploitation – Articles 23-24; Right to Freedom of Religion – Articles 25-28
## SUB 0 | Article 25 – Freedom of Conscience and Religion
[12:0:0] # Text and limits
[12:0:1] - **25(1):** "all persons are equally entitled to **freedom of conscience** and the right freely to **profess, practise and propagate** religion" – subject to **public order, morality and health** and to the **other provisions of Part III**. Quoted text → **Art. 25(1)**.
[12:0:2] - **Grounds of restriction:** public order, morality, health – **humanism is not** a ground. So the right to religion is **not without limitations**.
[12:0:3] - Right to religion is a **Fundamental Right** (Arts. 25–28), available to **all persons**, citizens and foreigners. Freedom of conscience = **Art. 25**; "freedom to practise any religion" = **Art. 25**.
[12:0:4] - **Prisoners** do not lose FRs merely by lawful detention (**Sunil Batra**).
[12:0:5] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [12:0:5.0] Conscience | Inner freedom to mould one's relation with God; includes freedom to follow no religion
  [12:0:5.1] Profess | Declare one's beliefs openly
  [12:0:5.2] Practise | Worship, rituals, ceremonies
  [12:0:5.3] Propagate | Spread one's beliefs – not a right to convert another (it would impinge on the other's freedom of conscience)
[12:0:6] # State powers – 25(2)
[12:0:7] - **25(2)(a):** regulate **economic, financial, political or other secular activity** associated with religion – not spiritual belief.
[12:0:8] - **25(2)(b):** **social welfare and reform**, and **throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus** (temple entry). The State may step in to root out a social evil.
[12:0:9] # Explanations
[12:0:10] - **Explanation I:** wearing and carrying **kirpans** is part of the profession of the **Sikh** religion – a **Right to Freedom of Religion** (Art. 25).
[12:0:11] - **Explanation II:** "**Hindus**" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists** – **not Parsis**.
[12:0:12] > Asked as: which Article (conscience, kirpan, temple entry 25(2)(b)), quoted text 25(1), "not a ground" (humanism), what freedom of religion is subject to (I, II, III – not defamation, an Art. 19 ground), "without limitations" is wrong.
[12:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.211-212; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) (Art. 25, kirpan); app notes 2:12 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Articles 23-24 – Right Against Exploitation
[12:1:0] # Article 23
[12:1:1] - **23(1):** prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar** and other **forced labour**; available to **citizens and non-citizens**, and protects against the **State and private persons**.
[12:1:2] - **Begar** = involuntary forced labour **without payment**, exacted by officials/zamindars.
[12:1:3] - **23(2):** State may impose **compulsory service for public purposes** (military/social service); it need not pay in every case, but may **not discriminate on religion, race, caste or class**.
[12:1:4] # Article 24
[12:1:5] - **No child below 14** shall be employed in any **factory, mine or other hazardous employment** – an **absolute prohibition**; harmless or innocent work is not barred.
[12:1:6] - Child labour in hazardous work is prohibited by the **Constitution (Art. 24)** and by the **Supreme Court (M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, 10 Dec 1996)**; the international instrument is the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989, Art. 32)** – not the UN Charter.
[12:1:7] - Art. 24 is the FR **directly related to the exploitation of children**. Related DPSPs: **39(e), 39(f)**.
[12:1:8] - **Arts. 21A and 24** together (education + no hazardous work) make the right meaningful for children (**APPSC G1 2023**).
[12:1:9] TABLE head: Law | Year | Scope
  [12:1:9.0] Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act | 1956 | Trafficking for prostitution
  [12:1:9.1] Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act | 1976 | Debt bondage (not 1977–79)
  [12:1:9.2] Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act | 1986 | 2016 amendment → Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act: below 14 banned except family work after school; adolescents 14–18 barred from hazardous work
  [12:1:9.3] Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act | 2005 | NCPCR, SCPCRs
  [12:1:9.4] POCSO | 2012 | Sexual offences against children
  [12:1:9.5] BNS | 2023 | Trafficking = Sec. 143 BNS; victim's consent immaterial
[12:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.209-211; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) (Art. 23 begar); M.C. Mehta v. State of T.N. (1996) 6 SCC 756; labour.gov.in; app notes 2:12 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Secularism – Meaning and the Indian Model
[12:2:0] - **Secularism** = delinking of the State from religion: **no official (state) religion**, **equal status/respect for all religions**, no religious discrimination, freedom of religion – India is secular for **all** these reasons. It is **not** anti-God, anti-religion or atheist.
[12:2:1] - **Applies to all**, including **irreligious persons** – "not applicable to irreligious persons" is NOT a component.
[12:2:2] - **Modern Indian concept:** **principled distance** – the State **intervenes when a religious practice violates fundamental rights** (reform, Art. 25(2)); not complete distance, not protection of minorities only.
[12:2:3] - **Articles 25–28** emphasise the secular character of Part III; also Arts. 14–16, 29–30, **325** (no exclusion from rolls on religion).
[12:2:4] - 'Secular' added to the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**; the Constituent Assembly **rejected 'God'** in the Preamble (1949). Roots: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, Nehru Report (1928).
[12:2:5] - **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** = state neutrality + **positive intervention for reform**.
[12:2:6] TABLE head: Indian (positive) | Western (negative)
  [12:2:6.0] Principled distance, equal respect | Strict separation
  [12:2:6.1] State may reform, temple entry | Religion purely private
  [12:2:6.2] Aid allowed (Haj, minority institutions) | No state aid
[12:2:7] - **Theocratic state**: an official religion guides law and policy – **not** India.
[12:2:8] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [12:2:8.0] Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Basic structure doctrine
  [12:2:8.1] S.R. Bommai (1994) | Secularism a basic feature; anti-secular State govts can be dismissed under Art. 356
  [12:2:8.2] Abhiram Singh (2017) | Widened Sec. 123(3) RPA – appeals to religion, caste etc. = corrupt practice
  [12:2:8.3] Shakti Vahini (2018) | Khap interference, honour killings illegal
  [12:2:8.4] Amit Sahni (2020) (Shaheen Bagh) | Peaceful protest, but public ways cannot be occupied indefinitely
[12:2:9] - Indian pluralism also protects language: **Art. 343** – **Hindi** (Devanagari) is the **official language of the Union**; India has **no national language**.
[12:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.230 (secular state; Art. 25(2)(a)); Laxmikanth ch. Preamble/Secularism (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt); app notes 2:12 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Articles 26-28 and the Group at a Glance
[12:3:0] - **Right against Exploitation** = Arts. **23–24** (two Articles); **Right to Freedom of Religion** = Arts. **25–28** (**four** Articles) – both Fundamental Rights.
[12:3:1] TABLE head: Article | Right | Limits / note
  [12:3:1.0] 23 | Traffic in human beings, forced labour | All persons
  [12:3:1.1] 24 | Child labour in factories, mines, hazardous work | All
  [12:3:1.2] 25 | Conscience; profess, practise, propagate | Public order, morality, health + other Part III
  [12:3:1.3] 26 | Freedom to manage religious affairs – (a) establish and maintain religious/charitable institutions; (b) manage own affairs in religion; (c) own and acquire property; (d) administer it according to law | For religious denominations or sections; only public order, morality and health (not "other Part III")
  [12:3:1.4] 27 | No one compelled to pay taxes whose proceeds promote a particular religion | All persons; bars taxes, not fees
  [12:3:1.5] 28(1) | No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds | —
  [12:3:1.6] 28(2) | 28(1) does not apply to a State-administered institution set up under an endowment/trust requiring it | —
  [12:3:1.7] 28(3) | In State-recognised or aided institutions attendance is voluntary; minor needs guardian's consent | —
  [12:3:1.8] 29 | Protection of interests of minorities (language, script, culture) | 30 = minorities' educational institutions
[12:3:2] - **State-neutrality provisions:** Art. 27 and Art. 28(1). Art. 26 protects **collective** freedom; Art. 25 the individual.
[12:3:3] - Match drill: **Art. 26** religious affairs; **Art. 40** village panchayats; **Art. 98** Secretariat of Parliament; **Art. 239** administration of UTs.
[12:3:4] - 12 May 2026: SC left it to the **Ministry of Education** whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under **Art. 26(a)**.
[12:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.212-214; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) (Art. 28); app notes 2:12 sub 0, 3
## SUB 4 | Religion Cases – ERP Test, Sabarimala, Anthem, Conversion Laws
[12:4:0] - **Essential Religious Practice (ERP)** test: court-made, **Shirur Mutt (1954)**.
[12:4:1] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [12:4:1.0] Shirur Mutt | 1954 | Origin of ERP; defined "religious denomination"
  [12:4:1.1] Ramji Lal Modi v. UP | 1957 | Sec. 295A IPC upheld on public-order grounds (now Sec. 299 BNS)
  [12:4:1.2] Rev. Stanislaus v. MP | 1977 | Propagate ≠ convert; upheld Orissa (1967) and MP (1968) anti-conversion Acts
  [12:4:1.3] Bijoe Emmanuel v. Kerala | 1986 | No one compelled to sing the National Anthem – violates Art. 19(1)(a) and Art. 25(1); no law obliges anyone to sing it
  [12:4:1.4] St. Stephen's | 1992 | Minority institutions keep autonomy, subject to regulation
  [12:4:1.5] Javed | 2003 | Polygamy not an ERP
  [12:4:1.6] Shayara Bano | 2017 | Instant triple talaq invalid
  [12:4:1.7] Sabarimala (Indian Young Lawyers Assn.) | 28 Sep 2018 | 5 judges, 4:1 – women's age bar struck ("devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination"); Ayyappa devotees not a separate denomination; exclusion not an ERP
[12:4:2] - **Sabarimala** temple: **Pathanamthitta** district, Kerala. **Jan 2019:** **Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga** – first women of the barred age to enter.
[12:4:3] - **2026 review:** nine-judge Bench headed by **CJI Surya Kant** on ERP (Apr 2026). **Karnataka HC (2022):** hijab **not an ERP**.
[12:4:4] - **Anti-conversion laws:** **Jharkhand Freedom of Religion Bill, 2017** – to **stop forcible/fraudulent conversions**. **Punjab** Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act (Apr 2026): sacrilege up to **life imprisonment**.

  [12:5:2.2] Revivalism | Restoring a golden past – Arya Samaj "Back to the Vedas"

=== OWN MCQs of 2:12 (112)
[n57495642107] sub0
  How is the Right to Freedom of Religion under Articles 25 to 28 classified?
  *Fundamental Right | Directive Principle of State Policy | Legal right | Constitutional convention
  x: The freedoms guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 constitute Fundamental Rights and are not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.
[ncb24c3e22b6] sub0
  Which of the following is NOT correct about the terms in Article 25(1)?
  Worship, rituals and ceremonies integral to the religion fall under 'practise' | The freedom to follow no religion falls under 'conscience' | Wearing a turban, crucifix or kirpan is an instance of 'profess' | *'Propagate' means the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God
  x: Propagate means spreading one's beliefs to others; the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God is conscience.
[neb28b33c277] sub0
  Besides public order, morality and health, to what are the freedoms in Article 25(1) subject?
  Security of the State | *The other provisions of Part III | Friendly relations with foreign States | Sovereignty and integrity of India
  x: Article 25(1) expressly subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
[na0f45f3e201] sub0
  Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 25(2)?
  25(2)(a) lets the State regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religion | 25(2)(b) lets the State provide for social welfare and reform | 25(2)(b) lets the State throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus | *25(2)(a) lets the State regulate only spiritual beliefs, not secular activities
  x: Article 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity associated with religion, not spiritual belief.
[n87c606613fb] sub0
  What may the State do where a religious practice involves a social evil?
  Can never intervene in religious matters | Must leave reform entirely to the religious denomination | *May intervene to root it out, subject to constitutional limits | Can intervene only through Parliament
  x: Freedom of religion is not absolute; the State can intervene to root out social evils while respecting constitutional restrictions.
[n125a69e7596] sub0
  Propagation under Article 25 does not include a right to convert another person, because it would affect which right of the other person?
  Right to equality | *Freedom of conscience | Freedom of movement | Right to privacy
  x: Propagation means spreading one's beliefs; a right to convert another would impinge on that person's freedom of conscience.
[f9c59c3dd5640] sub0
  Which of the following does freedom of conscience under Article 25 include?
  Refuse all taxes | Carry on secular activity free of regulation | *Follow no religion at all | Convert another person
  x: Conscience includes the freedom to follow no religion; propagation does not include a right to convert another.
[n8c22e8508c2] sub0

=== NOTES 2:13 | Cultural and Educational Rights – Articles 29-30; the Right to Property and the 44TH Amendment
## SUB 0 | Right to Property Deleted – the 44th Amendment
[13:0:0] # What was deleted, by whom, when
[13:0:1] - **Amendment:** the **44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978** deleted the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights – not the 42nd (1976), 43rd, 24th, 25th or 62nd.
[13:0:2] - **Articles omitted:** **Art. 19(1)(f)** (acquire, hold and dispose of property) and **Art. 31** (compulsory acquisition) were taken out of **Part III**; a new **Art. 300A** was inserted in **Part XII (Chapter IV)**.
[13:0:3] - **Government:** passed under the **Janata Party government of Morarji Desai** (1977-79) – not Indira Gandhi, Narasimha Rao or Vajpayee; nor a "Congress Government".
[13:0:4] - **Date:** the Act is "of 1978" (exam answer for "which year": **1978**); it got assent on **30 April 1979**, and the omission of Art. 31 (s.6) took effect from **20 June 1979** – so property **ceased to be an FR from 1979**.
[13:0:5] - **Why:** property rights were the most litigated FR and kept blocking **land reform** and acquisition for public use.
[13:0:6] - **Result:** FRs were **originally seven, now six**; property is the **only FR ever deleted** (not speech, religion, equality or constitutional remedies).
[13:0:7] > Asked as: "Which amendment deleted property?" (44th – APPSC G2 2008, MPDO 1998; SSC 2008, 2017; MPPSC 2020; UPPSC; CGPSC), "The right to ___ has ceased to be an FR" (property – G2 2011), "Which is not an FR?" (property), A-R "300A because 44th removed it from Part III" (A and R true, R explains A – APPSC G2, NDA 2000).
[13:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.13, p.170-172, p.200; Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.38, p.56; PMF Polity Part 1 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt) p.59, p.72; constitutionofindia.net Art. 31 note (omitted by s.6, w.e.f. 20-6-1979)
## SUB 1 | Right to Property Today – Article 300A, a Legal Right
[13:1:0] # Article 300A
[13:1:1] - **Text:** "**No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law**" – the Article that bars the State from taking property except by law (**300A**, not Art. 300 = suits by/against Government, Art. 299 = contracts, Art. 301 = freedom of trade; there is no 299A).
[13:1:2] - **Status:** a **legal right** (also called a **constitutional right**, since it is in the Constitution) – **not a Fundamental Right**, not a DPSP, not a natural right.
[13:1:3] - **Who:** **any person** – citizens, non-citizens and **companies** (UPSC 2021: "legal right available to any person").
[13:1:4] - **Enforcement:** through **Art. 226** or an ordinary suit – **not Art. 32**; it protects against **executive** action without law, not against legislation; the State is not constitutionally bound to pay compensation.
[13:1:5] - **Human right:** the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the right to property is **also a human right** (forcible dispossession without due process = human-rights violation); UDHR 1948 Art. 17 recognises it.
[13:1:6] - **Not basic structure:** in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** the Court held the right to property is **not part of the basic structure** – so "right to property is part of the basic structure" is the **wrong** statement.
[13:1:7] - **AP angle:** **GGR Housing v. State** (AP High Court, May 2026) – strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Art. 300A.
[13:1:8] > Asked as: "At present, the right to property is a…" (legal right – APPSC AEE 2012, AMVI; UPPCS 1992, 1996; UKPSC 2021; MPPSC 2025), "Which Article?" (300A – APPSC G1, AD Economics), UPSC 2005 statements (only "legal right, not FR" correct: Art. 301 is trade; 300A came from the Janata government).
[13:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.42 (Kesavananda: property not basic structure), p.170; Indian Polity Part 1 (src/polity/indian-polity-part1.txt) p.115-116 (300A; human right); PMF Polity Part 1 p.72, p.75 (UPSC 2021: any person); app notes 2:13 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Cultural and Educational Rights – Articles 29 and 30
[13:2:0] # Article 29 – protection of interests of minorities
[13:2:1] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [13:2:1.0] 29(1) | Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it (not limited to minorities)
  [13:2:1.1] 29(2) | No citizen denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided institution on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language (sex and place of birth are not in the list)
[13:2:2] - **Marginal heading:** Art. 29 = "**Protection of interests of minorities**" – the Article that "protects the interests of minorities" (not 30, 28 or 32).
[13:2:3] - **Objective of the group:** to help **minorities conserve their culture** – not to evolve a single culture or eradicate illiteracy.
[13:2:4] # Article 30 – minority educational institutions
[13:2:5] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [13:2:5.0] 30(1) | All minorities, religious or linguistic, may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice – the "Charter of Education Rights"; madrasas run under it
  [13:2:5.1] 30(1A) (44th Amendment, 1978) | On compulsory acquisition of a minority institution's property, the amount fixed must not restrict or abrogate the Art. 30 right
  [13:2:5.2] 30(2) | No discrimination in grant of aid because an institution is under minority management
[13:2:6] - Art. 29 applies to **citizens only**; Art. 30's text is not confined to citizens.
[13:2:7] - Art. 30 is **not absolute**: the State may regulate **standards**, but may **not take away the minority character** ("right to administer is not a right to maladminister").
[13:2:8] - **Spreading religion** (propagation) is **Art. 25** – a right of all persons, minorities included.
[13:2:9] # Article 350A – mother tongue
[13:2:10] - **Art. 350A:** every State and local authority to provide **instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage** to children of **linguistic minority** groups (not 300A, 351A, 301A); **Art. 350B** = Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
[13:2:11] > Statement trap (APPSC ATWO): "only religious minorities may set up institutions" ✗ (linguistic too); "religious minorities are defined in Art. 350A" ✗; "religious minorities may establish and administer educational institutions" ✓; "minorities may spread their religion" ✓ → **3 and 4 only**.
[13:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.170, p.214-215, p.251 (Art. 350A); PMF Polity Part 1 p.67, p.81; Indian Polity Part 1 p.113; app notes 2:13 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Legal Right or Fundamental Right? – Vote and Information
[13:3:0] # The distinction
[13:3:1] - **Every FR is a constitutional right, but not every constitutional right is an FR**; a **legal right** comes from ordinary law and can be changed by it; every FR is a human right, but not the reverse.
[13:3:2] TABLE head: Right | Status | Where
  [13:3:2.0] Property | Legal (constitutional) right | Art. 300A
  [13:3:2.1] Vote and to be elected | Constitutional right – UPSC 2017 official key; statutory/legal right – Kuldip Nayar (2009), UPPCS keys and NextGen | Art. 326 (adult suffrage, 18+); Sec. 62 RPA 1951; registration Sec. 19 RPA 1950
  [13:3:2.2] Information | Legal right under the RTI Act, 2005; the Supreme Court also reads it into Art. 19(1)(a) (so "both fundamental and legal" is also accepted – NDA 2010) | RTI Act 2005; Art. 19(1)(a)
  [13:3:2.3] Work | DPSP | Art. 41
  [13:3:2.4] Education (6-14) | Fundamental Right | Art. 21A
[13:3:3] - **Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2009)**: voting is only a **statutory/legal** right.
[13:3:4] - **Voting paradox**: voting is statutory, yet the **right to know candidate details, NOTA and ballot secrecy** are recognised under **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
[13:3:5] > Read the options: if "constitutional right" and "legal right" both appear for the vote, UPSC (2017) keyed constitutional; UPPCS (2010, 2015) keyed legal. For RTI with no "both" option, the answer is **legal right**.
[13:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.174 (vote: statutory, s.62 RPA; FR vs constitutional vs human right); upsc.gov.in CSP 2017 answer key; app notes 2:13 sub 5, 2:8 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Who Is a Minority?
[13:4:0] - **Not defined:** "minority" is used in **Arts. 29, 30, 350A, 350B** but **not defined** in the Constitution (Art. 30 does not define it); no 10% or 10,000 population test exists.
[13:4:1] - **Recognised kinds:** the Constitution recognises **religious and linguistic** minorities only – not ethnic minorities (UPSC 1999).
[13:4:2] - **NCM Act, 1992:** "minority" = a community **notified by the Central Government**; the **NCM** is a **statutory** body (quasi-judicial, civil-court powers), not constitutional.
[13:4:3] - **Unit = the State:** religious and linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise** (**T.M.A. Pai, 2002**); tests: numerical inferiority, non-dominance, distinct identity.
[13:4:4] TABLE head: Basis | Determined by
  [13:4:4.0] Religious minority | NCM, Ministry of Minority Affairs – national notification
  [13:4:4.1] Linguistic minority | State-wise
[13:4:5] - **Six notified minorities:** **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains** (Jains added 2014); linguistic minorities are not among these religious categories.
[13:4:6] - National notification brings a group within NCM and central schemes (scholarships, **PMJVK**, **PM VIKAS**).
[13:4:7] - **Mar 2026:** Kerala's **Malayalam Bhasha Bill** contested as harming the **Kannada** linguistic minority in **Kasaragod**.
[13:4:8] > A-R (UPPCS 2019): "Art. 30 does not define minorities" ✓; "the Constitution recognises only linguistic and religious minorities" ✓ – but R does not explain A.
[13:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.215; PMF Polity Part 1 p.52, p.67; Indian Polity Part 1 p.113 (NCM Act 1992); app notes 2:13 sub 1
## SUB 5 | Land Acquisition Laws and Enemy Property
[13:5:0] # Land Acquisition Act, 1894 → LARR Act, 2013
[13:5:1] - **1894 Act:** made by the **British**; in force **1 March 1894**; purpose was **not land reform** but acquisition for public purposes, institutions and companies; became disputed and was **replaced** by the **LARR Act, 2013**.
[13:5:2] - **LARR Act, 2013:** **Social Impact Assessment compulsory**; compensation up to **4x** market value (**rural**), **2x** (**urban**); **unused land returned after 5 years**.
[13:5:3] # Enemy Property (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2017 (Bill of 2016)
[13:5:4] - Enemy property stays **vested in the Custodian**; **the law of succession/inheritance does not apply** to it, and no legal heir can claim it – it is **not returned to heirs**.
[13:5:5] ~~ Sources: Indian Polity Part 1 p.116; app notes 2:13 sub 4; prsindia.org Enemy Property (Amendment and Validation) Bill 2016 (new s.5B)
## SUB 6 | Before 1978 – Saving Clauses and Ninth Schedule
[13:6:0] # The journey of Article 31
[13:6:1] TABLE head: Stage | Position
  [13:6:1.0] 1950 | FR under Art. 19(1)(f) + Art. 31 – the most disputed FR
  [13:6:1.1] 1st Amendment, 1951 | Arts. 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws
  [13:6:1.2] 4th (1955), 17th (1964), 25th (1971) | Narrowed compensation; 17th: land under personal cultivation acquired only on paying market value
  [13:6:1.3] 44th Amendment, 1978 | Deleted 19(1)(f) and 31 → Art. 300A
[13:6:2] # Saving clauses – 31A, 31B, 31C
[13:6:3] TABLE head: Article | Inserted by | Saves
  [13:6:3.0] 31A | 1st, 1951 | Laws on acquisition of estates etc.
  [13:6:3.1] 31B | 1st, 1951 | Acts in the Ninth Schedule – immune from FR challenge
  [13:6:3.2] 31C | 25th, 1971 | Laws giving effect to Arts. 39(b), 39(c); the 42nd's extension to all DPSPs struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)
[13:6:4] - **I.R. Coelho (2007)**, 9 judges: Ninth Schedule laws inserted **after 24 April 1973** are open to **basic structure** review.
[13:6:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Part 1 p.72; Indian Polity Part 1 p.115; app notes 2:13 sub 3
## SUB 7 | Minority Institution Cases
[13:7:0] TABLE head: Case | Year | Holding
  [13:7:0.0] In re Kerala Education Bill | 1958 | Presidential reference on State control over aided/recognised institutions
  [13:7:0.1] St. Stephen's College | 1992 | Minority-institution autonomy (5-judge bench)
  [13:7:0.2] T.M.A. Pai Foundation | 2002 | 11-judge bench; minority status decided State-wise
  [13:7:0.3] P.A. Inamdar | 2005 | 7 judges; no State reservation in unaided private colleges → led to the 93rd Amendment (Art. 15(5), which exempts minority institutions)
  [13:7:0.4] Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust | 2014 | RTE Act's 25% quota does not apply to minority schools
