=== NOTES 2:14 | Right to Constitutional Remedies – Article 32; the Five Writs and Their Scope
## SUB 0 | The Five Writs – Literal Meaning and Purpose
[14:0:0] - **Article 32(2)** names **five writs**: **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto** (not "Quid Warranto", not injunction). Both the **Supreme Court (Art. 32)** and the **High Courts (Art. 226)** issue **all five**.
[14:0:1] - Writs began as **prerogative writs of English common law**; before 1950 only the **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** High Courts could issue them.
[14:0:2] TABLE head: Writ | Literal meaning | Purpose | Lies against
  [14:0:2.0] Habeas Corpus | "To have the body (of)" / "you may have the body" | Detained person produced before the court; release from illegal detention; court inquires into the legality of detention | Public authorities and private individuals
  [14:0:2.1] Mandamus | "We command" (an order) | Orders a public official, body, inferior court or government to perform a public duty it refused or neglected; can also order it not to enforce an unconstitutional law | Public officials, statutory bodies, govt companies, inferior courts, tribunals, government
  [14:0:2.2] Prohibition | "To forbid" / restrain | Higher court stops a lower court/tribunal exceeding its jurisdiction while the case is pending | Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only
  [14:0:2.3] Certiorari | "To be certified" / informed | Higher court calls up the record of a lower court/tribunal for review; quashes an order already passed; also transfers a pending case | Judicial, quasi-judicial and (since 1991) certain administrative bodies
  [14:0:2.4] Quo Warranto | "By what authority (or warrant)?" / "what is your authority" | Court asks a holder to show his right to a public office; ousts an ineligible person / usurper | Holder of a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution
[14:0:3] - **Habeas Corpus** = the writ of **personal liberty** – the "**bulwark of individual liberty**", the **greatest safeguard of personal liberty**; also used to produce a person **missing or in custody**. The term belongs to **law**.
[14:0:4] - **Mandamus** = Judiciary **orders the Executive to perform its duty**; "an order to act legally and abstain from an unlawful act". **Mandamus directs activity; Prohibition directs inactivity.**
[14:0:5] - **Certiorari** = the "**postmortem**" writ – examines the working of **subordinate courts**; brought to get an order **quashed**. Grounds: lack/excess of jurisdiction, **error of law on the face of the record**.
[14:0:6] - **Wrong pairs** asked: "Quo Warranto – certify the proceedings" (certify = Certiorari); "Prohibition – ban on liquor"; "Mandamus – produce the body".
[14:0:7] TABLE head: Match (APPSC G2 Mains 2025) | Meaning
  [14:0:7.0] Quo Warranto | ii. by what authority
  [14:0:7.1] Mandamus | iii. we command
  [14:0:7.2] Habeas Corpus | iv. to have the body of
  [14:0:7.3] Certiorari | i. to be certified
[14:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.218-222 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.111-112 (Sheet #42 Writs); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.67-69
## SUB 1 | Heart and Soul – Article 32 as a Fundamental Right
[14:1:0] - **Right to Constitutional Remedies = Article 32** – the right to **move the Supreme Court directly** when a Fundamental Right is violated (not Arts. 14, 15, 17, 19, 21, 29-31, 33, 34 or 36). It is **itself a Fundamental Right**.
[14:1:1] - **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**: Art. 32 is "**the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it**" – the Article without which the Constitution would be a **nullity** (not Freedom of Speech, Equality, Religion or Property).
[14:1:2] - **Why**: "a right without a remedy is a **worthless declaration**" – Art. 32 gives an **effective remedy** against violation of FRs (A-R: A true, R true, R explains A).
[14:1:3] - "**Soul**" alone is also used for the **Preamble** (Thakur Das Bhargava; Rocket: "key / soul of the Constitution"); with Ambedkar or "heart and soul" the answer is always **Art. 32 / Right to Constitutional Remedies**.
[14:1:4] - **Basic structure**: judicial review under **Art. 32** (SC) and **Arts. 226 and 227** (HCs) is part of the **inviolable basic structure** (Kesavananda Bharati 1973, 13 judges; **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**); Art. 245 is not.
[14:1:5] - The power of **judicial review** of the Supreme Court is exercised through **Art. 32** (not 131, 132, 134); the two provisions that most clearly express judicial review = **Arts. 32 and 226**. Judicial review rests on **Arts. 13, 32, 226** – **not Art. 225** (jurisdiction of existing HCs).
[14:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.73, p.77, p.215-218; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.67-68; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.37 (Preamble), p.111
## SUB 2 | Writ Jurisdiction – Article 32 vs Article 226; Guardian of Fundamental Rights
[14:2:0] - Citizens move the **Supreme Court (Art. 32)** or the **High Court (Art. 226)** for infringement of FRs – **Arts. 32 and 226** (not 33/227, 34/228). **Only the SC and HCs** issue writs – not "all courts", Parliament or the President.
[14:2:1] - **Article 226** empowers the **High Courts** to issue writs (not 213, 225, 227, 228, 249, 262).
[14:2:2] - **Guardian / protector of Fundamental Rights = the Judiciary** (Supreme Court as "protector and guarantor") – **not the President**, Parliament, Executive, Cabinet or parties. The **Supreme Court** is also the **custodian / guardian of the Constitution**.
[14:2:3] - The SC's writ power is **original but not exclusive** – "SC has exclusive power to issue writs" is **false**; HCs also decide the **validity of Central laws** (A false, R true – UPPCS 2019; official key (a) was wrong).
[14:2:4] TABLE head: Point | Art. 32 (SC) | Art. 226 (HC)
  [14:2:4.0] Nature | Itself a Fundamental Right – SC cannot refuse when an FR is shown | Constitutional, discretionary remedy
  [14:2:4.1] Scope | Only Fundamental Rights (narrower) | FRs and "any other purpose" – constitutional and statutory (legal) rights (wider)
  [14:2:4.2] Territory | Whole of India (wider) | Own territory; beyond it if the cause of action arises inside (15th Amendment, 1963)
  [14:2:4.3] Writs | Five | Five
[14:2:5] - So **High Courts are in a better position** to protect citizens' rights, **because the SC issues writs only for FRs** (A and R true, R explains A). The HC writ power covers **constitutional, statutory and fundamental rights** (all).
[14:2:6] - A right that is **not an FR** – e.g. the **right to vote** – is enforced in the **High Court under Art. 226**, not Art. 32.
[14:2:7] - **Art. 226 is ordinarily refused** where an **alternative and equally efficacious remedy** exists (rule of prudence; T.R. Verma 1957) or where **disputed questions of fact** need trial; it is **not** barred merely because no FR is involved ("any other purpose").
[14:2:8] - **Match (APPSC G2 Mains 2025):** **Art. 137** = SC **reviews** its own judgment; **Art. 226** = HCs issue writs; **Art. 13** = SC declares a law **unconstitutional**; **Art. 32** = SC restores FRs by writs.
[14:2:9] - **Res judicata**: an HC dismissal **on merits** bars the same plea under Art. 32 (remedy: appeal).
[14:2:10] - **20 Jan 2026**: SC (Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma) agreed to examine whether the **Enforcement Directorate** can invoke writ jurisdiction (appeals by Kerala and Tamil Nadu). **16 Jul 2026**: SC studied an **SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings** under Arts. 32 and 226 in threats to **life and liberty**.
[14:2:11] # Amendments
[14:2:12] TABLE head: Amendment | Year | Point
  [14:2:12.0] 42nd | 1976 | Inserted Art. 32A (no challenge to State laws under Art. 32); curbed Art. 226
  [14:2:12.1] 43rd | 1977 | Omitted Arts. 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A, 228A
  [14:2:12.2] 44th | 1978 | Restored Art. 226
[14:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.39, p.180, p.215-219; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.68-69; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.111; Union of India v. T.R. Verma (1957)
## SUB 3 | Scope and Limits of Each Writ
[14:3:0] # Habeas Corpus
[14:3:1] - The **only writ that lies against private persons** as well as the State; safeguards the liberty of **all persons** in the territory, citizens or not.
[14:3:2] - Not issued where detention is **lawful**, by a **competent court** (judicial custody), for contempt of court/legislature, or outside the court's territory. A habeas corpus petition is **not dismissed for imperfect pleadings**.
[14:3:3] - **Wrong statement** (asked twice): "Habeas corpus lies against the executive only, not against private persons".
[14:3:4] # Mandamus
[14:3:5] - Lies against **public officials, government, public corporations and government companies** performing public duties, inferior courts and tribunals.
[14:3:6] - Does **not** lie against: a **private individual or body** (unless entrusted with a **public duty** or **colluding with a public authority**); the **President or Governors** (**Art. 361**); a **contractual** obligation; a **discretionary** duty; non-statutory instructions; a Chief Justice acting judicially.
[14:3:7] - **UPSC 2022**: A (no mandamus against a private body unless it has a public duty) – correct; B (no mandamus against a government company) – **wrong**; C (any public-minded person may seek Quo Warranto) – correct → **A and C only**.
[14:3:8] - "Mandamus cannot be issued against the **Government**" is the **incorrect** statement; it can lie against a public servant; it cannot against a private individual.
[14:3:9] - **Law and policy**: mandamus **cannot compel the Government to make a law or a policy** (e.g. to **appoint a commission to study climate change**), but **enforces a policy once laid down**; it does lie to compel statutory/public duties (filling seats, cleanliness, cyclone shelters). A-R: both true, R explains A.
[14:3:10] # Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
[14:3:11] - **Prohibition**: only against **judicial and quasi-judicial bodies** – not administrative authorities, legislatures, private persons. It goes to the **lower court**, not to Parliament, an officer or the Government.
[14:3:12] - **Certiorari**: not against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**; since **1991** also against administrative bodies affecting rights.
[14:3:13] - **Quo Warranto**: **any public-minded person** may seek it (need not be aggrieved); not for **ministerial or private** office.
[14:3:14] TABLE head: Prohibition vs Certiorari | Prohibition | Certiorari
  [14:3:14.0] Stage | While proceedings are pending | After an order is passed (also transfers a pending case)
  [14:3:14.1] Nature | Preventive only | Preventive and curative
  [14:3:14.2] Effect | Stops the lower body | Quashes the order ("postmortem")
[14:3:15] - **Similarity**: both lie (traditionally) **only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies**; both check excess of jurisdiction; both are issued by SC and HCs.
[14:3:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.218-220; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.67-69 (UPSC 2022 Q with explanation p.72-73); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.111-112; Constitution of India, Art. 361
## SUB 4 | Clauses of Article 32 – What It Enforces
[14:4:0] TABLE head: Clause | Provision
  [14:4:0.0] 32(1) | Right to move the SC by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of Part III rights – itself guaranteed
  [14:4:0.1] 32(2) | SC may issue directions, orders or writs, including the five writs
  [14:4:0.2] 32(3) | Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise these powers within its local limits – no such law made yet
  [14:4:0.3] 32(4) | The right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides (Art. 359)
[14:4:1] - **Only Fundamental Rights** can be enforced under Art. 32 – not constitutional, statutory or other rights. So the SC can **refuse relief** if **no Fundamental Right has been infringed** – not because another court can give relief, facts are disputed or the wrong writ was named.
[14:4:2] - **Right to property** is no longer an FR (**44th Amendment, 1978**; now **Art. 300A**) – its violation **cannot** be challenged by a **writ under Art. 32**, only under Art. 226, a civil suit etc.
[14:4:3] - Both SC and HCs share jurisdiction over **enforcement of Fundamental Rights** (Centre-State and inter-State disputes = SC only, Art. 131).
[14:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.216-218; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.67-68; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.111
## SUB 5 | Suspension during Emergency; Articles 33-35
[14:5:0] - **Who suspends FRs? The President** – under **Art. 359**, during a National Emergency, by order suspending the right to move courts for named FRs (not Parliament, SC or PM). **Art. 358** suspends Art. 19 automatically (war/external aggression).
[14:5:1] - **Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended** – added by the **44th Amendment (1978)** to undo **ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976)**, which had upheld suspension of habeas corpus/Art. 21 in the Emergency.
[14:5:2] - Limits on FRs are imposed by **Parliament** by law; the **Judiciary only judges their reasonableness** – "the power to limit FRs is with the Supreme Court" is false.
[14:5:3] - **Art. 33**: **Parliament** (not State legislatures) may restrict or abrogate FRs of the **armed forces, paramilitary/forces for public order (police), intelligence or counter-intelligence bodies** and persons in **telecommunication systems set up for those forces** – not people of the communication sector in general.
[14:5:4] - **Art. 34**: restrictions while **martial law** is in force; Parliament may **indemnify** acts done under it. Martial law is not defined in the Constitution.
[14:5:5] - **Art. 35**: **Parliament alone** legislates on matters under Arts. 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and **prescribes punishment for Part III offences** – a **State legislature cannot**.
[14:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.218, p.223-224; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.69-70, p.129 (Arts. 358-359); Constitution of India, Arts. 33-35 (legislative.gov.in)
## SUB 6 | Public Interest Litigation
[14:6:0] - **No Article mentions PIL** – it is a judge-made tool (borrowed from the **USA**), filed under **Arts. 32 and 226**; PIL is **not itself an FR**.
[14:6:1] - PIL relaxes **locus standi** (only the aggrieved may sue): any **public-spirited person** may move the court for those unable to – giving the **poor and weak access to justice**, essential for the **rule of law** (A and R true, R explains A).
[14:6:2] - **Epistolary jurisdiction**: letters/postcards treated as writ petitions – **Sunil Batra** (prisoner's letter). **S.P. Gupta (1981)** – key PIL case; Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
[14:6:3] - Judicial review lets the SC strike down laws that **violate the Fundamental Rights of Scheduled Tribes** and weaker sections; courts do not enact laws.
[14:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.218-219; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.68

  x: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes the right to a remedy itself a Fundamental Right, giving direct access to the Supreme Court.
[f66bfa9268f6d] sub1
  How many judges decided Kesavananda Bharati, which made judicial review under Articles 32, 226 and 227 basic structure?
  7 | *13 | 9 | 11
  x: Kesavananda Bharati was a 13-judge Bench.
[g172bcc1c2918] sub1
  Who described Article 32 as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'?
  Jawaharlal Nehru | *B.R. Ambedkar | K.M. Munshi | Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar
  x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the very soul and heart of the Constitution.
[g27b57b1f2470] sub1
  Which Article of the Constitution gives the power of judicial review to the Supreme Court and the High Courts?
  Article 131 | *Article 13 | Article 143 | Article 368
  x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, giving the Supreme Court and High Courts the power of judicial review.
[n346aea7fcda] sub1

  x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
[n7f5ab8cdff3] sub2

  x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
[gbe21223cc44c] sub2

  x: The Supreme Court is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights; the Judiciary is their guardian.
[nindian-polity-15-6] sub2

  x: Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', while the Supreme Court under Article 32 acts only for Fundamental Rights.
[n8576d4137da] sub2

  x: A High Court ordinarily exercises Article 226 jurisdiction within its territory, but may do so beyond that territory where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territorial jurisdiction. This position followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.
[n248aef544a0] sub2

  x: Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue all five writs.

  x: The proposed SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings concerns threats to life and liberty, strengthening access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
[na18ffb1eae7] sub2

  x: After a dismissal on merits, the same plea ordinarily cannot be raised under Article 32; the remedy is an appeal. If the dismissal was not on merits, Article 32 may be invoked.

=== NOTES 2:15 | Directive Principles of State Policy – Articles 36-51, Classification, Implementation
## SUB 0 | Article-wise Directives – Articles 38 to 51
[15:0:0] # Article → Directive (the most-asked angle: "which Article…?")

  [15:0:1.0] 38 | Social order for the welfare of the people – justice, social, economic and political; 38(2) (44th Amendment): minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities
  [15:0:1.1] 39 | Principles of policy – clauses (a) to (f) (table below)
  [15:0:1.2] 39A | Equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amendment, 1976)
  [15:0:1.3] 40 | Organisation of village panchayats as units of self-government
  [15:0:1.4] 41 | Right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement
  [15:0:1.5] 42 | Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
  [15:0:1.6] 43 | Living wage, decent standard of life, leisure; promote cottage industries (individual or co-operative basis) in rural areas
  [15:0:1.7] 43A | Participation of workers in management of industries (42nd Amendment) – industries, not agriculture
  [15:0:1.8] 43B | Promotion of co-operative societies (97th Amendment, 2011)
  [15:0:1.9] 44 | Uniform Civil Code for the citizens throughout India
  [15:0:1.10] 45 | Early childhood care and education for all children until six years (86th Amendment, 2002; originally free and compulsory education till 14)
  [15:0:1.11] 46 | Educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections; protect them from social injustice and exploitation
  [15:0:1.12] 47 | Nutrition, standard of living, public health; prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health
  [15:0:1.13] 48 | Agriculture and animal husbandry on modern scientific lines; prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle
  [15:0:1.14] 48A | Protect and improve the environment; safeguard forests and wildlife (42nd Amendment)
  [15:0:1.15] 49 | Protection of monuments, places and objects of artistic or historic interest of national importance
  [15:0:1.16] 50 | Separation of judiciary from executive in the public services of the State
  [15:0:1.17] 51 | Promotion of international peace and security; just and honourable relations, respect for international law, arbitration – the DPSP behind foreign policy; last Article of Part IV
[15:0:2] # Article 39 – clauses
[15:0:3] TABLE head: Clause | Directive
  [15:0:3.0] 39(a) | Adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally
  [15:0:3.1] 39(b) | Ownership and control of material resources distributed to subserve the common good
  [15:0:3.2] 39(c) | Economic system not to result in concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment
  [15:0:3.3] 39(d) | Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
  [15:0:3.4] 39(e) | Health and strength of workers and tender age of children not abused
  [15:0:3.5] 39(f) | Children to develop in freedom and dignity; protected against exploitation and abandonment (42nd Amendment)
[15:0:4] - **Concentration of wealth** violates the **DPSPs – Arts. 39(b) and 39(c)** (UPSC 2021), not the Right to Equality; land reforms (zamindari abolition, ceilings) implement 39(b) and (c).
[15:0:5] - **Gender equality / women:** asked as Art. **39** (39(a) livelihood, 39(d) equal pay) – "equal pay for equal work" is a **DPSP**, not an FR.
[15:0:6] - **Close pairs:** 46 (weaker sections) vs 47 (nutrition, prohibition) vs 48 (cows) vs 49 (monuments); 43 (living wage) vs 43A (workers in management) vs 43B (co-operatives); 48 vs 48A (environment – "Article 48" is the nearest option when 48A is missing).
[15:0:7] > Asked as: "Which Article…?" – 40 (village panchayats, ~15 times), 51 (international peace, ~10), 46 (~6), 44 (UCC, 4), 50 (4), 48/49/48A/43A/41/45/47/38 (1-3 each); match lists (APPSC ASO: 46-47-40, 39-48-47; APSLPRB SI 2019: 50-IV, 48-III, 42-II, 47-I).

[15:0:9] - **Planning Commission (Mar 1950):** set up by a Cabinet resolution in pursuance of the DPSPs – **Art. 39** (and the Art. 38 aim) – not by any Article or Act.
[15:0:10] - **State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (Oct 2016):** "equal pay for equal work" applies to **temporary employees** doing the same work as regular ones.
## SUB 1 | Is It a DPSP? – Lists and Odd Ones Out
[15:1:0] TABLE head: Is a DPSP (Article) | Is NOT a DPSP (where it is)
  [15:1:0.0] Right to work, employment to all (41) | Abolition of untouchability – FR, Art. 17
  [15:1:0.1] Maternity relief (42) | Ban on child labour in factories/mines – FR, Art. 24
  [15:1:0.2] Equal pay for equal work (39(d)) | Ban on begar / forced labour – FR, Art. 23
  [15:1:0.3] Prohibition of liquor / intoxicants (47) | Equality before law (14), non-discrimination (15), life and liberty (21), conviction protection (20) – FRs
  [15:1:0.4] Cow protection (48), environment (48A) | Protection of interests of minorities – FR, Art. 29
  [15:1:0.5] Uniform Civil Code (44) | Right to Information – legal right, RTI Act 2005
  [15:1:0.6] Living wage (43), free legal aid (39A), monuments (49) | Free education up to 14 – FR, Art. 21A since 2002; "up to 16" – nowhere
  [15:1:0.7] Village panchayats (40), separation of judiciary (50) | Mother-tongue instruction at primary stage – Art. 350A (outside Part IV)
  [15:1:0.8] International peace and security (51) | Increasing international trade; small family norm; adult education; uniform criminal code; national service in army; vegetarian habits
[15:1:1] - **Employment to all** and **maternity benefits** come under the **DPSPs** (APPSC G2 2003, JL 2004, AEE 2009).
[15:1:2] - **Promotion of international peace and security** is in the **DPSPs (Art. 51, Part IV)** – not the Preamble, FDs or Ninth Schedule (UPSC 2014).
[15:1:3] - **Separation of judiciary from executive** is enjoined by a **DPSP (Art. 50)** – not the Preamble, Seventh Schedule or convention (UPSC 2020).
[15:1:4] - **Social and economic planning** is **not** in Part IV: "**Economic and social planning**" is **Entry 20 of the Concurrent List**.
[15:1:5] > Odd-one-out PYQs: "adult education" (silent – UP 2008), "free education up to 16" (UP 2013), "free education to 14" (UDA/LDA 2010, after 2002), "RTI" (UPPCS 2006), "untouchability" (State PSC), "increasing international trade" (APPSC G2 Mains 2017).
[15:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.248-251 (Part IV list), p.312 (Concurrent List Entry 20 "Economic and social planning"), p.294 (PYQ 140: Concurrent); Rocket Polity Part 2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt) "Economic and Social Planning: Concurrent List"; PMF Polity Part 1 p.85 (UPSC 2020 separation of judiciary); app notes 2:15 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Part IV Basics – Articles 36-51, Welfare State and Aims
[15:2:0] # Where and what
[15:2:1] - **Part IV**, **Articles 36 to 51** (16 Articles) – not Part III (12-35, FRs), Part I (1-4), Part II (5-11), Part IVA (FDs).
[15:2:2] - **Article 36:** "State" has the **same meaning as in Part III** (Art. 12).
[15:2:3] - **Aim:** **social and economic democracy** (not political democracy, which FRs secure) and a **welfare state** – a **secular** welfare state, **not a religious State** and not a capitalist, police or communist State.
[15:2:4] - **Welfare state:** its ideal is enshrined in the **DPSPs** (UPSC 2015, 2020); "**The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap**" describes a welfare State; it gives **special care to the welfare of weaker sections**.
[15:2:5] - **Economic justice:** in the **Preamble and the DPSPs** (UPSC 2013); **economic democracy** is envisaged through the DPSPs; **social justice** runs through the Preamble, FRs, DPSPs and the special provisions for Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
[15:2:6] - **Economic goals:** from the DPSPs flow two dominant goals of economic policy – **increasing national income** and **improving its distribution**.
[15:2:7] - **Nature:** **positive** and **expansive** (they widen the State's role; FRs are restrictive/negative); their spirit is welfare and **humanism** (APPSC key).
[15:2:8] > Asked as: "Which Part?" (IV – ~10 times), "Articles 36 to 51 cover…", "goal of DPSP" (welfare state), "not an objective" (religious State), "purpose" (social and economic democracy – UPSC 2002).
[15:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.245 (Part IV, aims, positive obligations), p.247; PMF Polity Part 1 p.77 (Police State into Welfare State), p.84 (UPSC 2020); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.45, p.47; app notes 2:15 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Article 37 – Non-justiciable, yet Fundamental in Governance
[15:3:0] # The text
[15:3:1] - **Article 37:** the provisions of Part IV "**shall not be enforced by any court**", but the principles are "**fundamental in the governance of the country**" and "it shall be the **duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws**".
[15:3:2] - So DPSPs are **non-justiciable** – not enforceable, no justiciable rights for individuals, **no legal duty** on the State; their sanction is **moral and political** (public opinion, elections).
[15:3:3] - They are **not limitations** on the legislative or executive function (UPSC 2017: "neither") – they are **guide-posts for legislation** and a **positive mandate** to the State, not prohibitions or "mere moral precepts".
[15:3:4] - "Fundamental in the governance of the country" = **DPSPs** (UPSC 2013) – not FRs or FDs.
[15:3:5] # FR vs DPSP
[15:3:6] TABLE head: Basis | Fundamental Rights | Directive Principles
  [15:3:6.0] Place | Part III, Arts. 12-35 | Part IV, Arts. 36-51
  [15:3:6.1] Courts | Justiciable | Non-justiciable (Art. 37)
  [15:3:6.2] Character | Negative – restrain the State | Positive – exhort the State to act
  [15:3:6.3] Aim | Political democracy | Social and economic democracy, welfare state
  [15:3:6.4] Sanction | Legal | Moral and political
  [15:3:6.5] Conflict | Generally prevail (Champakam Dorairajan 1951) | Subordinate; laws for 39(b), (c) protected by Art. 31C
[15:3:7] - **Minerva Mills (1980):** **harmony and balance** between Part III and Part IV is part of the **basic structure**.
[15:3:8] - **Kesavananda Bharati (1973):** Justices Shelat and Grover listed "the **mandate to build a welfare State contained in Part IV**" among basic features – the basis for NDA 2012's "all of the above".
[15:3:9] > A-R (APPSC G2): "DPSPs are not independently enforceable" + "they serve as guide-posts for legislation" → both true, R explains A (official key). Odd one out: "They impose a legal duty on the State" ✗; "directed at making India an advanced capitalist country" ✗.
[15:3:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.13, p.245-246, p.248 (Art. 37; FR negative, DPSP positive); PMF Polity Part 1 p.77, p.82-83 (sanction; Champakam, Minerva), p.84 (UPSC 2020); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.46
## SUB 4 | Amendments that Added or Changed DPSPs
[15:4:0] TABLE head: Amendment | Year | Change
  [15:4:0.0] 42nd | 1976 (in force 3 Jan 1977) | Four new DPSPs: 39(f) (children), 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 43A (workers in management), 48A (environment, forests, wildlife)
  [15:4:0.1] 44th | 1978 | 38(2) – the second aspect of Art. 38: minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities
  [15:4:0.2] 86th | 2002 | Changed the subject of Art. 45 – now early childhood care and education until six; 6-14 education became FR Art. 21A; FD 51A(k) added
  [15:4:0.3] 97th | 2011 | Art. 43B – co-operative societies (the last DPSP added)
[15:4:1] - **Count:** the 42nd added **four** DPSPs (Laxmikanth's count; Rocket and PMF list the three new Articles 39A, 43A, 48A plus the recast 39(f)); with the 44th's 38(2), **five** new DPSPs in all.
[15:4:2] - **NOT by the 42nd:** cow-slaughter ban (48, original), UCC (44, original), equal pay (39(d), original), right to work (41, original), living wage (43, original), 38(2) (44th), 43B (97th), ECCE (86th).
[15:4:3] - **Chronology:** **48A/39A/43A (1976) → 38(2) (1978) → Art. 45 changed (2002) → 43B (2011)** (APPSC G1 Screening 2024).
[15:4:4] - **First Amendment, 1951:** added the **Ninth Schedule** and Arts. 31A, 31B (to protect land reforms after Champakam Dorairajan).
[15:4:5] > Asked as: "Which was added by the 42nd?" (43A – UPSC 2017, UPPCS 2019; 39A – NDA 2020; free legal aid "later date" – UPRO 2014), "year of free legal aid" (1976 – RAS 2024), "86th altered…" (ECCE till six – WBCS 2019).
[15:4:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.46, p.48 (amendment table); PMF Polity Part 1 p.81-82 (amendment table; 42nd strengthened 39(f)), p.82 (Champakam → 1st Amendment); NextGen Polity p.250 (Art. 45, 43A); M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. "Directive Principles" (42nd added four DPSPs); app notes 2:15 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Sources and Antecedents; Jammu and Kashmir
[15:5:0] # Foreign source
[15:5:1] - Borrowed from the **Irish Constitution of 1937** ("Directive Principles of Social Policy"), which copied the **Spanish Constitution** – not the USA, USSR, France, Japan, Australia, England or Switzerland.
[15:5:2] - **Constitution match (APPSC G2 Mains 2025):** UK – **rule of law**; Ireland – **DPSP**; USA – **judicial review**; Canada – **residual powers**.
[15:5:3] # Indian antecedents
[15:5:4] TABLE head: Antecedent | Contribution
  [15:5:4.0] Nehru Report (1928) | Early charter of rights and welfare goals
  [15:5:4.1] Karachi Resolution (1931) | Socialist-nationalist economic programme of the freedom struggle
  [15:5:4.2] Instrument of Instructions (GoI Act, 1935) | Instructions to Governors – incorporated as the DPSPs (UPSC 2010); DPSPs are called the "Instrument of Instructions"
  [15:5:4.3] Sapru Committee (1945) | Split rights into justiciable and non-justiciable
  [15:5:4.4] Gandhian ideals; traditional Hindu outlook | Village self-government, cottage industries, prohibition, cow protection
[15:5:5] # Jammu and Kashmir (before 2019)
[15:5:6] - Under the **Constitution (Application to J&K) Order, 1954**, **Part IV (DPSP)** – and also **Part IVA (Fundamental Duties)** – did **not apply** to J&K; Part III applied with exceptions.
[15:5:7] - **C.O. 272 of 5 August 2019** superseded the 1954 Order and applied **all provisions** of the Constitution to J&K (now a Union Territory since 31 Oct 2019).
[15:5:8] > APPSC G1 2003 asked "not applicable to J&K" with both DPSP and FD among the options – both were true then; today nothing in Part IV is excluded.
[15:5:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.245 (Irish 1937 from Spain), p.34 (DPSP did not apply in J&K), p.306 (Part IV and Part IVA not applicable to J&K); PMF Polity Part 1 p.77 (Instrument of Instructions); app notes 2:15 sub 1
## SUB 6 | Implementation – Panchayats, Legal Aid, UCC, Cow Protection
[15:6:0] # Article 40 – village panchayats
[15:6:1] - **Panchayati Raj** is laid down under the **DPSPs (Art. 40)**; Art. 40 was given practical shape by the **73rd Amendment, 1992** (Part IX) – because the DPSP-only system had **no uniform pattern across States and elections were not regularly held**.
[15:6:2] - **Nyaya Panchayats** (village courts): justified by **Art. 39A** (equal justice, access to justice) – the Gram Nyayalayas idea of cheap local justice.
[15:6:3] # Article 39A – legal aid
[15:6:4] - **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** – in force **9 November 1995** (**National Legal Services Day**); **NALSA** → SLSAs → DLSAs; **Lok Adalats**.
[15:6:5] # Article 41 – work
[15:6:6] - **MGNREGA, 2005** (also linked to Art. 43) – replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act** (2025); **National Social Assistance Programme (15 August 1995)** meets Art. 41.
[15:6:7] # Article 44 – Uniform Civil Code
[15:6:8] - **Goa** follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**; **Uttarakhand** – first State UCC (in force 27 Jan 2025, STs exempt); **Gujarat** – second (Gujarat UCC Bill, 2026: Scheduled Tribes exempted).
[15:6:9] - **21st Law Commission (B.S. Chauhan, 2018):** UCC "**neither necessary nor desirable**" at this stage.
[15:6:10] - **2026:** Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (Jun 2026) – SC suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination; Mar 2026 – a 3-judge bench considered deferring to Parliament on Art. 44. Art. 44 is **not enforceable** in court.
[15:6:11] - **Hindu Code Bill:** introduced 1951 (Ambedkar resigned); passed as **four Acts (1955-56)** – Hindu Marriage (divorce for both spouses, monogamy), Succession, Minority and Guardianship, Adoptions and **Maintenance** – codified Hindu law; they did **not** create a uniform civil code.
[15:6:12] # Article 48 – cow protection
[15:6:13] - Art. 48 is only a directive; laws on **cow slaughter** are made by **States** (**State List Entry 15**, preservation of stock); the **Centre** legislates through **Concurrent List Entry 17 – prevention of cruelty to animals** (PCA Act 1960 and its 2017 cattle-market rules).
[15:6:14] # Other laws
[15:6:15] - **48A:** Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Environment (Protection) Act 1986; **45/21A:** RTE Act 2009; **47:** prohibition laws, public health; **39(b), (c):** land reforms.
[15:6:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.388 (Art. 40 → 73rd Amendment), p.326; PMF Polity Part 1 p.79 (73rd gave practical shape to Art. 40), p.81 (Uttarakhand UCC 27 Jan 2025), p.83 (implementation laws); PMF Polity Part 2 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt) (Nyaya Panchayats); en.wikipedia.org Hindu code bills (four Acts 1955-56); app notes 2:15 sub 9
[15:6:17] - **AP (Mar 2023):** Cabinet approved Mandal Legal Services Committees for **Anaparthi, Piduguralla and Mydukur** (Palnadu is a district, not a mandal).
[15:6:18] - **NALSA:** free and competent legal services to the weaker sections on the basis of **equal opportunity**; issues **guidelines to SLSAs**; organises Lok Adalats.
[15:6:19] - **Education across the Constitution** (UPSC 2012 – all five): DPSP Art. 45; Panchayats/Municipalities (11th, 12th Schedules); Fifth and Sixth Schedules (tribal areas); Seventh Schedule (Concurrent Entry 25).
[15:6:20] - **First national meet of DLSAs:** 30-31 July **2022**, Vigyan Bhawan, **New Delhi** (NALSA).
## SUB 7 | Classification – Socialist, Gandhian, Liberal-intellectual
[15:7:0] - The **Constitution does not classify** DPSPs; the three-fold grouping (**socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual**) is an **academic** one for convenient study – "all of the above" (UPPCS 2018).
[15:7:1] TABLE head: Group | Articles | Ideas
  [15:7:1.0] Socialistic (economic and social principles) | 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47 | Welfare, livelihood, equal pay, legal aid, right to work, living wage, workers in management
  [15:7:1.1] Gandhian (6) | 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48 | Village panchayats, cottage industries, co-operatives, weaker sections, prohibition, cow protection
  [15:7:1.2] Liberal-intellectual (7) | 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51 | UCC, ECCE, modern agriculture, environment, monuments, separation of judiciary, international peace
[15:7:2] - **Overlaps:** 43 and 47 are Socialist and Gandhian; 48 is Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual; 43B is Gandhian.
[15:7:3] - **Not Gandhian:** **UCC** (liberal-intellectual) and **right to work** (socialist); "reasonable leisure and cultural opportunities" for workers (43) is asked as socialist.
[15:7:4] > UPSC 2012: Gandhian = village panchayats + cottage industries (**2 and 3**); State PSC: not Gandhian = UCC + right to work (**2 and 4**); APPSC JA (NTRUHS): "economic and social principles" = livelihood (39(a)) + equal pay (39(d)).
[15:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.247-248 (three groups), p.165; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.45, p.47 (Gandhian 6, Liberal 7); PMF Polity Part 1 p.77-79 (not watertight; overlaps)
## SUB 8 | Criticism – Who Said What
[15:8:0] TABLE head: Person | Remark
  [15:8:0.0] Dr. B.R. Ambedkar | "Novel feature" of the Constitution – the only approving one
  [15:8:0.1] Granville Austin | FRs and DPSPs together the "conscience of the Constitution"
  [15:8:0.2] K.T. Shah | "A cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank"
  [15:8:0.3] T.T. Krishnamachari | "A veritable dustbin of sentiments"
  [15:8:0.4] Nasiruddin | "No better than New Year's resolutions" broken on the second of January
  [15:8:0.5] K.C. Wheare | "Manifesto of aims and aspirations"
  [15:8:0.6] Sir Ivor Jennings | "Pious aspirations" (pious = devoutly religious / well-meant but unrealistic)
[15:8:1] - Most criticism targets **non-justiciability** (Art. 37); the right-to-work debate (FR or DPSP) pitted **K.T. Shah** against **Ambedkar** in the Constituent Assembly.
[15:8:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity p.165 (Ambedkar "novel feature"), p.245; PMF Polity Part 1 p.77, p.83; app notes 2:15 sub 7
[15:8:3] - **Granville Austin:** DPSPs and FRs are "aimed at furthering the goals of the **social revolution**" (APPSC G2 2008).
[15:8:4] - **'New Magna Carta' for DPSPs:** attribution **unsettled** (key grids give Pylee/Ambedkar); 'Magna Carta of India' usually = **Part III (FRs)**.
[15:8:5] - **B.N. Rau (1946):** DPSPs are "in the nature of **moral precepts for the authorities of the State**" – they have at least an educative value.

  *C, D, B, A | D, C, B, A | C, B, D, A | C, D, A, B
  x: 42nd Amendment (1976) added 39A, 43A, 48A; 44th (1978) added 38(2); 86th (2002) substituted Article 45; 97th (2011) added Article 43B.

=== NOTES 2:17 | Fundamental Duties – Article 51A, Swaran Singh Committee, Enforceability
## SUB 0 | Basics – Part IVA, Article 51A, 42nd and 86th Amendments
[17:0:0] - **Fundamental Duties = Part IVA**, which has **only one Article – Article 51A** (not Part IV, VI-A, III; not Arts. 49, 50, 51, 52). Opening words: "It shall be the duty of **every citizen of India**".
[17:0:1] - The **original Constitution had no Fundamental Duties** (not in the text completed in Nov 1949 or on 26 Jan 1950); they are a **separate Part**, **not part of the Fundamental Rights**.
[17:0:2] - Added by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** (Indira Gandhi govt; "Mini Constitution"), on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**; in force **3 January 1977**. Not the 24th, 31st, 38th, 41st, 44th or 46th.
[17:0:3] - **Number**: **10** duties in 1976 (clauses a–j – the "**10 commandments**") → **11 at present**; the **11th duty, 51A(k)**, added by the **86th Amendment Act, 2002** (not 87th, 96th or "2001").
[17:0:4] TABLE head: Particular | 42nd CAA, 1976 | 86th CAA, 2002
  [17:0:4.0] Duties | Inserted Part IVA, Art. 51A, clauses (a)–(j) | Added 51A(k) – parent/guardian to give education to child 6–14 years
  [17:0:4.1] Same Act also | Added DPSP Art. 48A; moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A, 17B) | Inserted Art. 21A (Right to Education as an FR); substituted Art. 45
[17:0:5] - **51A(g)** (environment) came in 1976, after the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.
[17:0:6] - Part IVA is one of **four Parts added after 1950**: **IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA**. Other Parts: **Part VI = The States**; **Part IXA = The Municipalities** (Part XI is Centre–State relations).
[17:0:7] - Number game: **8** suggested (Swaran Singh) – **10** added (1976) – **11** now (2002).
[17:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.158, p.252-253 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.42-44 (Sheets #17-18); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.87-88 (file pages)
## SUB 1 | The Eleven Duties – Clause-wise
[17:1:0] TABLE head: Clause | Fundamental Duty | Nature
  [17:1:0.0] 51A(a) | Abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and National Anthem | Civic
  [17:1:0.1] 51A(b) | Cherish and follow the noble ideals of the national struggle for freedom | Moral
  [17:1:0.2] 51A(c) | Uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India | Civic
  [17:1:0.3] 51A(d) | Defend the country and render national service when called upon | Civic
  [17:1:0.4] 51A(e) | Promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic, regional or sectional diversities; renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women | Civic/Moral
  [17:1:0.5] 51A(f) | Value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture | Moral
  [17:1:0.6] 51A(g) | Protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife; compassion for living creatures | Civic
  [17:1:0.7] 51A(h) | Develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform | Moral
  [17:1:0.8] 51A(i) | Safeguard public property and abjure violence | Civic
  [17:1:0.9] 51A(j) | Strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity | Moral
  [17:1:0.10] 51A(k) | Parent/guardian to provide opportunities for education to child or ward aged 6–14 | Civic
[17:1:1] - **Moral duties: (b), (f), (h), (j)**; civic duties: (a), (c), (d), (g), (i).
[17:1:2] - The **first duty**: respect the ideals of the **Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem** (all three) – so respecting the National Flag is a **fundamental duty** (not a right, DPSP or "ordinary/statutory" duty).
[17:1:3] - Weaker sections / STs: the duty closest to social justice is **51A(e) – fraternity and common brotherhood**; protecting cultural diversity = **51A(f) – composite culture**.
[17:1:4] - **Protection** of **wildlife** is a duty (51A(g)); the Flag is to be **respected**, not "protected".
[17:1:5] - **Fraternity**: 51A(e) speaks of harmony and common brotherhood; the Preamble speaks of fraternity.
[17:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.253; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.42-44; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.87-88 (UPSC 2012, 2015 PYQs)
## SUB 2 | What Is Not a Fundamental Duty
[17:2:0] TABLE head: Not a duty | Where it really is
  [17:2:0.0] To vote in public/general elections | Nowhere (a statutory right)
  [17:2:0.1] To pay taxes | Swaran Singh proposal not accepted
  [17:2:0.2] Family planning / population control | Nowhere
  [17:2:0.3] Compulsory military service | 51A(d) says only "when called upon"
  [17:2:0.4] Protect weaker sections from social injustice / their educational and economic interests | DPSP Art. 46
  [17:2:0.5] Protect monuments and places of national importance | DPSP Art. 49
  [17:2:0.6] Organise village panchayats | DPSP Art. 40
  [17:2:0.7] Abolition of untouchability | FR Art. 17
  [17:2:0.8] Abolition of titles | FR Art. 18
  [17:2:0.9] Separation of judiciary; free and compulsory education (as a State duty) | DPSP Arts. 50, 45
[17:2:1] - Also **not** duties: "to protect the **elderly, differently abled and children**" (51A(k) only covers a parent's duty to educate), "to **respect parents and teachers**".
[17:2:2] - **48A vs 51A(g)**: environment as a **DPSP** (State) = **Art. 48A**; as a **citizen's duty** = **Art. 51A(g)**. Public property by citizens = 51A(i), not 48A.
[17:2:3] - Scientific temper (51A(h)) and public property (51A(i)) are **only duties**, with no DPSP look-alike.
[17:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.249-254; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.89-91 (UPSC 2011, 2012 PYQs); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.46
## SUB 3 | Swaran Singh Committee (1976)
[17:3:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [17:3:0.0] Set up | 1976 by the Congress party (Indira Gandhi govt)
  [17:3:0.1] Chairman | Sardar Swaran Singh
  [17:3:0.2] Members | 12 – incl. A.R. Antulay, S.S. Ray, C.M. Stephen, H.R. Gokhale, Dinesh Goswami, Rajni Patel, V.N. Gadgil, Vasant Sathe
  [17:3:0.3] Not members | Haridev Joshi, M.N. Venkatachaliah (later CJI; Constitution Review Commission 2000)
  [17:3:0.4] Context | Need felt during the Internal Emergency (1975–77)
  [17:3:0.5] Duties suggested | 8
  [17:3:0.6] Duties added (42nd CAA) | 10
[17:3:1] - Fundamental Duties came from the **Swaran Singh Committee** – not Sarkaria, Rajamannar, ARC, Verma, Balwant Rai Mehta, Narasimham, Rangarajan, Fazl Ali, Thakkar, Shekatkar etc.
[17:3:2] - **Recommendations NOT accepted**: (1) Parliament to impose **penalty/punishment** for non-compliance; (2) such penalty laws **not to be questioned in any court** for violating FRs; (3) **duty to pay taxes**.
[17:3:3] - Accepted duties include "**strive towards excellence**" (51A(j)); the committee list was taken in a **modified form**.
[17:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.252; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.88; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.42; R.A.S. 2018 key (members)
## SUB 4 | Nature, Enforceability, Source and Criticism
[17:4:0] - **Non-justiciable** (like DPSPs): **cannot be enforced by writs**; the Constitution gives **no legal sanction** for violation – **only FRs are justiciable** (enforceable in courts; not DPSPs, the Preamble or Duties).
[17:4:1] - **Parliament may enforce them by legislation**; courts use them to **interpret ambiguous laws**, test **constitutionality** and judge the **reasonableness** of a law restricting an FR.
[17:4:2] - **UPSC 2017**: "a legislative process has been provided to enforce them" and "they are correlative to legal duties" – **both false**.
[17:4:3] - **Citizens only** – not foreigners (no exception, not even 51A(i)); FRs such as Arts. 14, 20, 21, 25 extend to foreigners too. **51A(k)** is the only duty addressed to **parents/guardians**.
[17:4:4] - **Source: Constitution of the former USSR** (Russian); among major democracies only **Japan** has a comparable list. India was **not** the first country to adopt duties.
[17:4:5] # Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) – laws already giving effect to duties
[17:4:6] TABLE head: Law | Duty

[17:4:7] - The Verma Committee was set up to **operationalise** duties and **identified existing legal provisions** – it did not ask for implementation "irrespective of" them.
[17:4:8] - Imputations prejudicial to national integration (51A(c)): now **Sec. 197, BNS 2023** (earlier IPC 153B). **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** rests on **Art. 253**.
[17:4:9] # Criticism and significance
[17:4:10] - Criticism: **not exhaustive** (omits voting, taxes, family planning); **vague** ("noble ideals", "scientific temper"); a "**code of moral precepts**" (non-justiciable); **superfluous**; an **appendage to Part IV** instead of following Part III.
[17:4:11] - Significance: reminder of obligations; warning against anti-national acts; **help courts on reasonableness**; promote discipline and participation.

## SUB 5 | Rights and Duties – Correlation and Cases
[17:5:0] - **Rights are correlative with duties** (UPSC 2017) – every right implies a duty; **Holland**: others' forbearance from interfering with a right is called a duty. "**Rights without duties are like men without shadows**."
[17:5:1] - Example: **Art. 19(1)(a)** (free speech) goes with **51A(c)** (sovereignty, unity, integrity).
[17:5:2] TABLE head: Case | Year | Held
  [17:5:2.0] AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS | 2001 (reported 2002) | Duties are as important as Fundamental Rights; rights and duties correlative
  [17:5:2.1] Mohan Kumar Singhania v. Union of India | 1991 | Art. 51A may be used to interpret laws and test their validity
  [17:5:2.2] Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala | 1986 | Duties cannot override FRs; respect for the Anthem needs no compelled singing
  [17:5:2.3] M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India | – | CSR includes environmental protection, linked to 51A(g)
  [17:5:2.4] SC on corporations | Mar 2026 | Corporations, as legal persons, also carry the 51A(g) duty (CSR = at least 2% of average net profit, Sec. 135, Companies Act 2013)
  [17:5:2.5] SC on Pollution Control Boards | Aug 2025 | Linked PCB enforcement to 51A(g)
[17:5:3] - **Ramlila Maidan case (2012)**: Parts III, IV and IVA are to be read together. **Subhash Kumar (1991)**: clean environment is part of **Art. 21**.
[17:5:4] - **Vande Mataram** recitation debate (Aug 2026): duties under 51A **cannot curtail Arts. 25 and 26** (freedom of religion).
[17:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.88-90 (Mohan Kumar Singhania, AIIMS, Ramlila Maidan; UPSC 2017 PYQ); old app notes row 17 (2025-26 rulings, as of 2026)

=== NOTES 2:18 | Amendment of the Constitution – Article 368, Majorities, Procedure, Limitations
## SUB 0 | Article 368 – Where It Is, What It Says, Nature of the Procedure
[18:0:0] - **Article 368**, the **only Article of Part XX**, gives Parliament the **power to amend the Constitution and the procedure** for it (not Arts. 14, 320, 330, 352, 356, 360, 366, 367, 369, 370 or 395).
[18:0:1] - Wording: Parliament may, "in exercise of its **constituent power**, amend by way of **addition, variation or repeal** any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down" – subject to the **basic structure** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
[18:0:2] - **Art. 368 itself provides for two types** of amendment – **special majority**, and **special majority + ratification by half the States**. The **simple-majority** changes (Arts. 2-4, 169 etc.) lie **outside Art. 368**, so books also speak of "three ways" of amending the Constitution.
[18:0:3] - **Art. 13(4)** (added by the **24th Amendment, 1971**): an amendment made under Art. 368 is **not "law"** under Art. 13, so **Art. 13(2) does not apply** to it (it still applies to laws of Parliament, ordinances and executive orders).
[18:0:4] - Art. 368 has itself been amended by the **24th (1971)** and the **101st (2016**, GST Council Art. 279A added to the ratification list) Amendments – both statements true (MPPSC 2020).
[18:0:5] - Borrowed from **South Africa** (with the election of Rajya Sabha members).
[18:0:6] - Nature: **neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis of both** – "partly rigid, partly flexible". Dual nature shown by: some provisions need a **special majority**, some only a **simple majority** like ordinary laws, and the **federal structure cannot be altered easily** (State ratification). FRs are **not** amendable "without judicial review".
[18:0:7] - **K.C. Wheare**: the amending process strikes a **good balance between rigidity and flexibility** ("variety in the amending process is wise but rarely found"); he called the Constitution **quasi-federal**.
[18:0:8] - **Granville Austin**: the process "appears **complicated**" but is "**merely diverse**" – one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution.
[18:0:9] - Latest enacted amendment (as of Nov 2026): the **106th (2023)**, women's reservation; the 129th and 130th are pending Bills and the 131st Bill was defeated (Apr 2026).
[18:0:10] > Exam angle: "Which Article/Part deals with amendment?" is the single most repeated PYQ – Art. 368, Part XX.
[18:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.161, p.256 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.92-95; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.53-55; Constitution of India Arts. 13(4), 368
## SUB 1 | Procedure under Article 368 – Step by Step
[18:1:0] - 1. Initiated **only by a Bill in either House of Parliament** (Lok Sabha **or** Rajya Sabha) – **not** in a State Legislature and **not** by the President.
[18:1:1] - 2. Moved by a **minister or a private member**; **no prior permission/recommendation of the President**.
[18:1:2] - 3. Passed in **each House separately** by a **special majority** – a majority of the **total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting**.
[18:1:3] - 4. **No joint sitting** (Art. 108 does not apply): if either House rejects it, the Bill **fails**.
[18:1:4] - 5. If it touches a **federal provision**, it must also be **ratified by the legislatures of half the States** by a **simple majority** (not all States).
[18:1:5] - 6. The **President must give assent** – he can neither withhold assent nor return the Bill; made obligatory by the **24th Amendment, 1971** (368(2) "**shall give his assent**").
[18:1:6] - So "prior recommendation of the President" is **false**, "President must assent" is **true**, "special majority in both Houses, no joint sitting" is **true** (UPSC 2022). "Initiated in Lok Sabha only" and "ratified by all the States" are **false** (UPSC 2013).
[18:1:7] TABLE head: Basis | Ordinary Bill | Money Bill | Constitution Amendment Bill
  [18:1:7.0] Articles | 107, 108 | 109, 110 | 368
  [18:1:7.1] Origin | Either House | Lok Sabha only | Either House
  [18:1:7.2] President's prior recommendation | Not required | Required | Not required
  [18:1:7.3] Majority | Simple | Simple | Special, in each House separately
  [18:1:7.4] Deadlock | Joint sitting (Art. 108) | No joint sitting (LS prevails) | No joint sitting – Bill fails
  [18:1:7.5] President | Assent, withhold or return once | Assent or withhold, never return | Must assent
[18:1:8] - **Financial Bill (I)**: starts only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation, but the Rajya Sabha **may reject or amend** it.
[18:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.256 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.93; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Amendment of the Constitution
## SUB 2 | Three Kinds of Amendment and the Simple-Majority Provisions
[18:2:0] TABLE head: Route | Requirement | Examples
  [18:2:0.0] Simple majority of Parliament (outside Art. 368) | Majority of members present and voting; such laws are not deemed amendments under Art. 368 | Arts. 2, 3, 4; 169; citizenship; Fifth and Sixth Schedules; quorum
  [18:2:0.1] Special majority of Parliament | Majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting, each House | Fundamental Rights (incl. Art. 32), DPSPs, all provisions not in the other two groups
  [18:2:0.2] Special majority + ratification by half the States | As above + simple majority in half the State legislatures | Federal provisions (next sub-section)
[18:2:1] - **New States** (admission/establishment, Art. 2), **formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names** (Art. 3) – by a **simple majority**, ordinary law; **Art. 4(2)**: such laws (and the consequent changes to the **First and Fourth Schedules**) are **not amendments for the purpose of Art. 368**. No State ratification is needed.
[18:2:2] - **Art. 3 proviso**: the Bill needs the **President's recommendation** and is **referred to the State legislature** for its views – so "boundaries may be altered without intimation to the States" is **false**.
[18:2:3] - **Legislative Council** (Art. 169): the **State Assembly passes a resolution by special majority** (majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting), **followed by an Act of Parliament** by simple majority – not an Art. 368 amendment.
[18:2:4] - Other simple-majority matters: **acquisition and termination of citizenship**; **Second Schedule** emoluments; **quorum**; MPs' salaries; rules of procedure; privileges; use of English in Parliament; **number of puisne judges of the SC** and more SC jurisdiction; **official language**; elections and **delimitation**; **Union Territories**; **Fifth Schedule** and **Sixth Schedule**.
[18:2:5] - **Article 32** is amended by a **special majority ("two-thirds")**, **without** State ratification (APPSC G2 2017) – though the SC's power under it is part of the basic structure.
[18:2:6] - Provisions that **cannot** be amended by simple majority and need **no** ratification → **special majority** (not ordinances, Cabinet decisions or Presidential orders).
[18:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.256-257 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.92; Constitution of India Arts. 3, 4, 169
## SUB 3 | Federal Provisions Needing Ratification by Half the States
[18:3:0] - Special majority **plus** ratification by the legislatures of **not less than one-half of the States**, by **simple majority**:
[18:3:1] TABLE head: Provision | Articles / Schedule
  [18:3:1.0] Election of the President and its manner | 54, 55
  [18:3:1.1] Extent of the executive power of the Union and the States | 73, 162
  [18:3:1.2] Supreme Court and High Courts | Part V ch. IV, Part VI ch. V, 241
  [18:3:1.3] Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and States | Part XI ch. I
  [18:3:1.4] Any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule (e.g. the Union List) | Seventh Schedule
  [18:3:1.5] Representation of States in Parliament | Fourth Schedule
  [18:3:1.6] GST Council (added by the 101st Amendment, 2016) | 279A
  [18:3:1.7] Article 368 itself | 368
[18:3:2] - **Not** in the list: **qualifications, tenure, conditions of office of the President**; **conditions of the Governor's office**; Fundamental Rights; DPSPs; formation of new States; abolition of Legislative Councils; creation of UTs.
[18:3:3] - So for **I. Union List, II. extent of a State's executive power, III. conditions of the Governor's office**, only **I and II** need ratification (UPSC 2025).
[18:3:4] - **Not all States**: half the States are enough – it is **not necessary that all State legislatures act** on the Bill; **no time limit** for ratification.
[18:3:5] - **First amendment ratified by the States: the 3rd Amendment (1954)** – re-enacted **Entry 33 of the Concurrent List** (trade and commerce in essential commodities).
[18:3:6] - **Rajendra N. Shah (2021)**: Part IXB (97th, co-operatives) **struck down for State co-operatives** for **want of ratification**.
[18:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.256-257 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.93; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.55
## SUB 4 | Majorities in Parliament
[18:4:0] TABLE head: Majority | Meaning | Used for
  [18:4:0.0] Simple | Majority of members present and voting | Ordinary, Money and Financial Bills; confidence motions; Arts. 2-4, 169 laws
  [18:4:0.1] Absolute | Majority of the total membership | Never alone – always with another majority
  [18:4:0.2] Effective | Majority of the House's effective strength (total minus vacancies) | Removal of the Vice-President (RS), Deputy Chairman, Speaker/Deputy Speaker
  [18:4:0.3] Special – Art. 249 type | Two-thirds of members present and voting, Rajya Sabha only | Parliament legislating on a State List subject in the national interest (Art. 249); new All-India Services (Art. 312)
  [18:4:0.4] Special – Art. 368 type | Majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting, each House | Amendment; removal of SC/HC judges (124, 217), CAG (148), CEC (324), SEC (243K); approval of National Emergency (352)
  [18:4:0.5] Special – Art. 61 type | Two-thirds of the total membership of the House | Impeachment of the President – the strictest
[18:4:1] - **High Court judges** (incl. the CJ) are removed by the **President** after an **address by Parliament** passed by a special majority (total membership + two-thirds present and voting) in each House – not by the Governor or the CJI.
[18:4:2] - Worked example (2026): the 131st Amendment Bill got **298 for, 230 against**; two-thirds of **528 present and voting = 352**, so it **failed**.
[18:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.161-162 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.92-93; Constitution of India Arts. 61, 217(1)(b), 124(4), 249; Praveen CA360 Apr 2026 p.6
## SUB 5 | Limits on the Amending Power – FRs and the Basic Structure
[18:5:0] TABLE head: Case / Act | Year | Held
  [18:5:0.0] Shankari Prasad | 1951 | Parliament can amend FRs; an amendment is not "law" under Art. 13(2); upheld the 1st Amendment
  [18:5:0.1] Sajjan Singh | 1965 | Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad
  [18:5:0.2] Golaknath | 1967 | Parliament cannot abridge FRs; an amendment is law – first to limit the power
  [18:5:0.3] 24th Amendment | 1971 | Parliament can amend any part incl. FRs; Art. 13(4), 368(3); assent obligatory
  [18:5:0.4] Kesavananda Bharati | 24 April 1973 | 13 judges, 7:6; FRs amendable but not the basic structure; upheld the 24th; overruled Golaknath
  [18:5:0.5] Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain | 1975 | Doctrine first applied to strike down an amendment clause (39th)
  [18:5:0.6] 42nd Amendment | 1976 | Added 368(4), (5): no limit on constituent power, no judicial review
  [18:5:0.7] Minerva Mills | 1980 | Struck down 368(4), (5); limited amending power is itself a basic feature
  [18:5:0.8] Waman Rao | 1981 | Doctrine applies to amendments after 24 April 1973
[18:5:1] - So the power of Parliament to amend is **limited by the Constitution itself** (its basic structure); the "**unquestioned right of Parliament to amend any part**" is **not** a basic feature – FRs, independence of the judiciary and federalism are.
[18:5:2] - **Who amends FRs?** **Parliament** (special majority) – not the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha alone, and not the Supreme Court, which only reviews.
[18:5:3] - Sequence: **Shankari Prasad → Golaknath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda**.
[18:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.258-262 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.93-94
## SUB 6 | Criticism of the Procedure and Amendment Bills in News
[18:6:0] - **No special body** (convention, as in the USA) and **no referendum**; constituent power lies with **Parliament**.
[18:6:1] - **States cannot initiate** an amendment (only a resolution for a Legislative Council under Art. 169); their role is **only to ratify** certain Bills; most of the Constitution is amended by Parliament alone.
[18:6:2] - **No time limit** for ratification; silent on **withdrawal** of ratification; **no joint sitting**; provisions **too sketchy**.
[18:6:3] TABLE head: Bill | Subject | Status (Nov 2026)
  [18:6:3.0] 129th, 2024 | Simultaneous elections (One Nation, One Election) – new Art. 82A; amends 83, 172, 327 | With JPC (chair P.P. Chaudhary)
  [18:6:3.1] 130th, 2025 | Removal of PM, CMs, Ministers detained 30 consecutive days; Arts. 75, 164, 239AA | With JPC (chair Aparajita Sarangi)
  [18:6:3.2] 131st, 2026 | Lok Sabha ceiling 550 → 850; delimitation on 2011 data to speed up women's quota | Defeated in Lok Sabha (298-230), 17 Apr 2026
[18:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.259-260 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Lens Apr 2026 (1) p.1.10; Praveen CA360 Apr 2026 p.6 and Sep 2026 p.14

  x: Representation of States in Parliament (Rajya Sabha seats) is in the Fourth Schedule, a federal provision needing ratification by half the States.
[n3feb16e2d69] sub4

  265 | 298 | 330 | *352
  x: Two-thirds of 528 is 352; with only 298 votes in favour the Bill failed the two-thirds requirement.

  x: Under the Article 61 type of majority, impeachment of the President requires two-thirds of the total membership of the House concerned.
[n349f795d7ee] sub4

  x: The Article 368 type of majority is used for removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, the CAG, the CEC and State Election Commissioners, constitutional amendment, and approval of a National Emergency. The relevant provisions include Articles 124, 217, 148, 324, 243K and 352.
[n620a638c542] sub4

  x: Article 312 deals with creating new All-India Services. The Article 368 type majority is for constitutional amendment, the Article 61 type for impeaching the President, and Article 249 for legislating on a State List subject.

[n195d712c8b3] sub5

  x: The basic structure cannot be amended even by the special procedure; the other three are simple-majority matters outside Article 368.
[nindian-polity-67-12] sub5

  x: Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh held so; Golaknath barred abridging FRs, Kesavananda allowed amendment within the basic structure, and Minerva Mills held limited amending power basic.
[n75d04b498e8] sub5

  x: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368, empowered Parliament to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), under which an amendment made under Article 368 is not ‘law’ for Article 13.

  x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges) held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

  x: Both are true: Minerva Mills struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 (added by the 42nd Amendment) because a limited amending power is itself a basic feature. R explains A.

=== NOTES 2:19 | Important Constitutional Amendments
## SUB 0 | 61st Amendment – Voting Age 18
[19:0:0] - The **61st Amendment** amended **Article 326**: voting age lowered from **21 to 18** for elections to the **Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies** (not for local bodies alone).
[19:0:1] - Introduced in the Lok Sabha on **13 December 1988** by **B. Shankaranand** as the **Constitution (Sixty-second Amendment) Bill, 1988**; titled the **61st Amendment Act, 1988**; assent and in force **28 March 1989** – so options read "61st, 1988" or "61st, 1989". First used in the **1989 general election**.
[19:0:2] - Not the 57th, 60th, 62nd, 63rd, 64th, 65th or 66th; not emergency powers or President's Rule.
[19:0:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.5, p.56, p.63 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.337; Constitution (Sixty-first Amendment) Act, 1988 (legislative.gov.in); Wikipedia, Sixty-first Amendment (citing the Bill)
## SUB 1 | 42nd Amendment, 1976 – the "Mini-Constitution"
[19:1:0] - Passed during the **Emergency** (PM **Indira Gandhi**); Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha on **1 September 1976**.
[19:1:1] - Called the **Mini-Constitution** because it changed the **Preamble**, the **Seventh Schedule** and **54 Articles** (A and R true, R explains A).
[19:1:2] TABLE head: Area | Change
  [19:1:2.0] Preamble | Added "Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity" ("Justice" was already there)
  [19:1:2.1] Fundamental Duties | Part IVA, Art. 51A – 10 duties (on the Swaran Singh Committee) – first inserted by the 42nd, not from the beginning
  [19:1:2.2] State List → Concurrent | Education, forests, weights and measures, wild animals and birds, administration of justice
  [19:1:2.3] DPSP | New 39A, 43A, 48A, 39(f); wider 31C
  [19:1:2.4] Courts | Part XIVA tribunals (323A, 323B); 368(4), (5) barred review of amendments
  [19:1:2.5] Executive | Ministerial advice binding on the President
  [19:1:2.6] Others | Lok Sabha/Assembly term 6 years; seat allocation frozen on the 1971 Census (till 2001); Emergency in part of India
[19:1:3] - Undone later: 44th restored the **5-year term**; Minerva Mills struck 368(4), (5). The Preamble words and the Duties **remain**.
[19:1:4] - The **number of Lok Sabha seats per State** is still based on the **1971 Census** (freeze extended by the **84th**, 2001).
[19:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.226 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.37, p.53, p.56; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.44
[19:1:6] - The Supreme Court holds **secularism** to be part of the **basic structure** (S.R. Bommai 1994), though the word came only with the 42nd.
## SUB 2 | 73rd and 74th Amendments – Local Government
[19:2:0] TABLE head: Item | 73rd (1992) – Panchayats | 74th (1992) – Municipalities
  [19:2:0.0] Part | IX (243–243O) | IXA (243P–243ZG)
  [19:2:0.1] Schedule | Eleventh – 29 subjects | Twelfth – 18 subjects
  [19:2:0.2] In force | 24 April 1993 | 1 June 1993
[19:2:1] - Together the **73rd and 74th** are the **local-governance** amendments (not 63rd/64th, 42nd/43rd, 86th/87th).
[19:2:2] - 73rd: constitutional status to **Panchayati Raj** (not the 71st, 72nd, 75th or 76th); three tiers; one-third seats for **women** (243D); State Finance Commission (243I); State Election Commission (243K).
[19:2:3] - 74th: added a **new Schedule** (Twelfth), **restructured municipalities**, **one-third seats for women** (243T); it applies to **all States** – not "only some specified States".
[19:2:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.11, p.58, p.95 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.62, p.399
## SUB 3 | Amendments 1951–1978 – Number and Year
[19:3:0] TABLE head: No. | Year | Key change
  [19:3:0.0] 1st | 1951 | Ninth Schedule, Arts 31A, 31B, 15(4); new 19(2) grounds
  [19:3:0.1] 3rd | 1954 (assent 22 Feb 1955) | Entry 33, Concurrent List – first ratified by States
  [19:3:0.2] 4th, 5th | 1955 | Compensation (Art. 31); time limit for State views on Art. 3 Bills
  [19:3:0.3] 7th | 1956 | States reorganisation; Part A/B/C/D States abolished
  [19:3:0.4] 12th | 1962 | Goa, Daman and Diu into the Union
  [19:3:0.5] 15th | 1963 | HC judges' retirement 60 → 62
  [19:3:0.6] 24th | 1971 | Parliament can amend any part incl. FRs; 13(4); President "shall give his assent"
  [19:3:0.7] 25th | 1971 | "Amount" for "compensation"; Art. 31C
  [19:3:0.8] 26th | 1971 | Privy purses and privileges of former rulers abolished
  [19:3:0.9] 32nd | 1973 | Arts 371D, 371E (Andhra Pradesh)

  [19:3:0.11] 42nd | 1976 | Mini-Constitution
  [19:3:0.12] 44th | 1978 | Emergency safeguards; property out of FRs
[19:3:1] - **1955**: the 4th and 5th were passed, and the 3rd (Act of 1954) got assent on 22 Feb 1955 – so "**all the above**" is keyed.
[19:3:2] - Match: **1st – Ninth Schedule; 12th – Goa, Daman and Diu; 15th – retirement age 62; 24th – power to amend any part**.
[19:3:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.53-56 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); List of amendments of the Constitution of India (Wikipedia, citing the Gazette)
[19:3:4] - **58th (1987)** authoritative Hindi text; **96th (2011)** "Oriya" → "Odia" – with **12th** Goa, Daman and Diu and **15th** HC retirement age 62 (match).
## SUB 4 | 44th Amendment, 1978
[19:4:0] - Enacted by the **Janata government** (PM **Morarji Desai**); a corrective to the 38th, 39th and 42nd.
[19:4:1] - President may **return the advice of the Council of Ministers once** for reconsideration (Art. 74(1)); he must act on the reconsidered advice – not the 39th, 40th or 42nd.
[19:4:2] - **Right to Property**: Arts 19(1)(f) and 31 deleted → legal right under **Art. 300A**.
[19:4:3] - National Emergency: "internal disturbance" → "**armed rebellion**"; only on the **written recommendation of the Cabinet**; **Lok Sabha** can disapprove it; **Arts 20 and 21** cannot be suspended.
[19:4:4] - Restored the **5-year term** of the Lok Sabha/Assemblies and courts' power over election disputes of the President, VP, PM and Speaker.
[19:4:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.53-56 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.226
## SUB 5 | First Amendment, 1951
[19:5:0] - The **first Amendment Bill was presented in 1951** and enacted by the **Provisional Parliament** (PM **Jawaharlal Nehru**); assent by President Rajendra Prasad on **18 June 1951**.
[19:5:1] - Widely seen as enacted to **overcome judicial interpretations of FRs** (Kameshwar Singh – zamindari; Champakam Dorairajan – Art. 15(4); Romesh Thappar – new 19(2) grounds).
[19:5:2] - Added **Arts 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**; validity upheld in **Shankari Prasad (1951)**.
[19:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.258, p.261 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.53
[19:5:4] - **Art. 31B** validates Acts placed in the **Ninth Schedule**; **31A** saves estate-acquisition laws.

  [19:6:0.1] 58th | 1987 | Authoritative Hindi text of the Constitution

  [19:6:0.7] 91st | 2003 | Ministers ≤ 15% of the Lok Sabha/Assembly (75(1A), 164(1A)); defectors barred from ministership
[19:6:1] - The 35th (1974) had an earlier Tenth Schedule on **Sikkim**; the present anti-defection Tenth Schedule is the **52nd**.
[19:6:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.54-57 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.226

[19:7:1] - All of 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th upheld in **M. Nagaraj (2006)**.

=== NOTES 2:20 | Recent Amendments – 97TH to 106TH
## SUB 0 | 97th Amendment, 2011 – Co-operative Societies
[20:0:0] - Passed in **2011**, notified **12 January 2012** (hence "97th Amendment Act of 2012" in some papers); gave **constitutional status and protection to co-operative societies** – not education, terrorism or Lokpal.
[20:0:1] TABLE head: Provision | Content
  [20:0:1.0] Art. 19(1)(c) | Right to form co-operative societies made a Fundamental Right
  [20:0:1.1] Art. 43B (DPSP) | Promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, professional management of co-operatives
  [20:0:1.2] Part IXB | Arts 243ZH–243ZT – a new Part
  [20:0:1.3] 243ZJ | Board of max 21 directors; one SC/ST seat and two women seats; term 5 years
  [20:0:1.4] 243ZM | Accounts audited within six months of the close of the financial year
  [20:0:1.5] 243ZP | Returns filed within six months of the close of every financial year (not two months)
[20:0:2] - So of "A. Part added by the 97th; B. audit in six months; C. returns in two months; D. six-year term", only **A and B** are correct.
[20:0:3] - **Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)**: Part IXB **struck down for State co-operatives** (no State ratification); it still applies to **multi-State co-operatives**.
[20:0:4] - The **15% cap on Ministers** is the **91st (2003)**, not the 97th.
[20:0:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.41, p.45-48, p.57-58 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); Constitution of India Arts. 243ZJ, 243ZM, 243ZP
## SUB 1 | Recent Amendments in Order (97th to 106th)
[20:1:0] TABLE head: No. | Year | Subject
  [20:1:0.0] 97th | 2011 | Co-operative societies
  [20:1:0.1] 98th | 2012 | Art. 371J – Hyderabad-Karnataka region
  [20:1:0.2] 99th | 2014 | NJAC – struck down 2015 (the only recent one struck down as a whole)
  [20:1:0.3] 100th | 2015 | India-Bangladesh LBA – 111 Indian, 51 Bangladeshi enclaves
  [20:1:0.4] 101st | 2016 | GST
  [20:1:0.5] 102nd | 2018 | NCBC constitutional – Art. 338B
  [20:1:0.6] 103rd | 2019 | 10% EWS
  [20:1:0.7] 104th | 2019 | SC/ST seats to 2030; Anglo-Indian nomination ended
  [20:1:0.8] 105th | 2021 | States/UTs again identify their own SEBCs
  [20:1:0.9] 106th | 2023 | Women's reservation – assent 28 Sept 2023
[20:1:1] - The **106th (2023)** is the **latest enacted** amendment (as of Nov 2026).
[20:1:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); List of amendments of the Constitution of India (Wikipedia)
## SUB 2 | 101st Amendment, 2016 – GST
[20:2:0] - Assent **8 September 2016**; GST from **1 July 2017**.
[20:2:1] - Inserted **246A** (Parliament and States both make GST laws), **269A** (GST on inter-State supply), **279A** (**GST Council**: chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**; decisions by **three-fourths** weighted votes).
[20:2:2] - Omitted **Art. 268A** (service tax); added the GST Council to the provisions needing **State ratification** (amended Art. 368).
[20:2:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.93
## SUB 3 | 102nd and 105th Amendments – Backward Classes
[20:3:0] TABLE head: Item | 102nd (2018) | 105th (2021)
  [20:3:0.0] Bill | Constitution (123rd Amendment) Bill, 2017 | 127th Bill, 2021
  [20:3:0.1] Assent | 11 August 2018 | 18 August 2021
  [20:3:0.2] Change | Art. 338B – National Commission for Backward Classes made constitutional; 342A – President notifies SEBC list | 342A(3) – States/UTs again identify their own SEBCs
[20:3:1] - A paper asking about "the Constitution Bill (103rd Amendment), 2017" means this Bill: it **empowers the National Commission for Backward Classes** (not a "Council", not the SC body).
[20:3:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); PRS Legislative Research, Constitution (123rd Amendment) Bill, 2017
## SUB 4 | 103rd and 104th Amendments, 2019
[20:4:0] - **103rd**: passed as the **124th Amendment Bill, 2019**; assent **12 January 2019**; inserted **15(6)** and **16(6)** – up to **10%** for EWS (income limit ₹8 lakh, fixed by notification).
[20:4:1] - **Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (7 Nov 2022)**: upheld **3:2**; the 50% ceiling does not apply to EWS.
[20:4:2] - **104th**: SC/ST seat reservation (Art. 334) extended to **2030**; **Anglo-Indian nomination** to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies ended (**January 2020**).
[20:4:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022)
## SUB 5 | 106th Amendment, 2023 – Women's Reservation
[20:5:0] - **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**; **assent 28 September 2023** (so "2023", not 2020-2022).
[20:5:1] - One-third seats for women in the **Lok Sabha (330A)** and **State Assemblies (332A)**; **334A** on timing; 239AA amended for **Delhi**.
[20:5:2] - Starts only after **delimitation** on the first Census after commencement; lasts **15 years**, extendable by Parliament by law; **not yet in force** (Nov 2026).
[20:5:3] - Debates: **no OBC sub-quota**; **southern States** fear a smaller share after delimitation.
[20:5:4] - Local bodies have had **one-third for women** since **1992** (**243D, 243T**).
[20:5:5] - **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** (early delimitation on 2011 data, Lok Sabha to 850) was **defeated** in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026.
[20:5:6] ~~ Sources: Praveen CA360 Apr 2026 p.6 (src/current-affairs/praveen-ca360-2026-04-magazine.txt); PMF Lens Apr 2026 (1) p.1.10; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.57
## SUB 6 | Pending Amendment Bills (as of Nov 2026)
[20:6:0] TABLE head: Bill | Subject | Status
  [20:6:0.0] 129th, 2024 | One Nation, One Election – new Art. 82A; amends 83, 172, 327 | JPC, chair P.P. Chaudhary
  [20:6:0.1] 130th, 2025 | Removal of PM, CMs, Ministers detained 30 consecutive days on serious charges; Arts 75, 164, 239AA | JPC, chair Aparajita Sarangi
  [20:6:0.2] 131st, 2026 | Lok Sabha ceiling 550 → 850; delimitation | Defeated 17 Apr 2026
[20:6:1] ~~ Sources: Praveen CA360 Sep 2026 p.14 (src/current-affairs/praveen-ca360-2026-09-magazine.txt); PMF Lens Apr 2026 (1) p.1.10
