=== NOTES 2:21 | Basic Structure Doctrine – Kesavananda Bharati and After
## SUB 0 | Kesavananda Bharati (1973) – Where the Doctrine Was Propounded
[21:0:0] - The **basic structure doctrine** was **first propounded** in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** – not in Golaknath (1967), Sajjan Singh (1965), Shankari Prasad (1951), Champakam Dorairajan, Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi, Minerva Mills, Bommai or Indra Sawhney. Where Kesavananda is not among the options, the answer is "**None of the above**".
[21:0:1] - Decided **24 April 1973** by **13 judges** (the largest bench ever), majority **7:6**, headed by **CJI S.M. Sikri**.
[21:0:2] - Held: Parliament under **Art. 368** may amend **any part** of the Constitution, **including Fundamental Rights**, but **cannot alter, damage or destroy its basic structure**.
[21:0:3] - **Overruled Golaknath** and **upheld the 24th Amendment** (1971), which had amended Arts. 13 and 368.
[21:0:4] - Held the **Preamble** to be **part of the Constitution** and amendable, but its objectives embody the basic structure – the Preamble is regarded as **part of the basic structure** (Kesavananda, not Berubari, Gopalan or the Privy Purse case).
[21:0:5] - Struck down the part of **Art. 31C** (25th Amendment) that barred courts from asking whether a law really gives effect to the Directive Principles – so **judicial review** of amendments stays.
[21:0:6] - Basic features named by the judges included **supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, unity and sovereignty, parliamentary system, welfare state, dignity of the individual**.
[21:0:7] - Landmark for "**the basic structure of the Constitution, as defined in the Preamble, cannot be changed**" (CDS 2010) – not for religion in politics, untouchability or the non-suspension of Art. 21.
[21:0:8] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [21:0:8.0] Dietrich Conrad | German jurist; argued in India (1965) that the amending power has implied limits, drawing on Germany's Basic Law
  [21:0:8.1] Justice Mudholkar | Dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) – first judicial reference to "basic features"
  [21:0:8.2] CJI S.M. Sikri | Headed the 13-judge Kesavananda bench
[21:0:9] - Country the idea is traced to: **Germany**.
[21:0:10] > Exam angle: "Which case propounded the basic structure doctrine?" is asked again and again (×18 PYQs) – Kesavananda Bharati, 1973.
[21:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.258-262, p.326 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.94, p.97-98 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.59-61
## SUB 1 | What the Basic Structure Means
[21:1:0] - Basic structure = the **core features** of the Constitution that **cannot be amended or altered by Parliament** in exercise of the power under **Art. 368** (APPSC G1 2018) – "certain features are so essential that they **cannot be abrogated**" (IAS 1994).
[21:1:1] - It is **not** "what can be amended by simple majority", **not** "Directive Principles only" or "Fundamental Rights only", **not** "the order of Articles cannot be altered" and **not** "amendments only on procedural matters".
[21:1:2] - Source of the theory = **judicial interpretation** – **judge-made**, nowhere defined in the text; **not** inserted by any **Act of Parliament** or amendment (APPSC G1 2024 statement I false).
[21:1:3] - **Not exhaustive**: the Supreme Court has never fully listed it; the list grows **case by case**.
[21:1:4] - What limits Parliament's power to amend the Constitution = the **basic structure** (not FRs as such, customs or distribution of powers).
[21:1:5] - Present position: Parliament can amend **any part** of the Constitution, **including FRs**, **without affecting the basic structure** (APPSC G1 2024 statement II true); FRs can still be amended after Kesavananda.
[21:1:6] - **Parliament's limited amending power** is itself a basic feature (**Minerva Mills, 1980**; statement III true).
[21:1:7] - As a principle of judicial review, the doctrine **accepts the supremacy of the Constitution and of the courts** (the American principle of judicial supremacy, accepted "to a limited extent"). It goes beyond "**procedure established by law**", under which a court only checks whether a law is within the authority's powers.
[21:1:8] TABLE head: Statement (APPSC G1 2024) | Verdict
  [21:1:8.0] Doctrine incorporated by an Act of Parliament | False – judge-made
  [21:1:8.1] Parliament may amend any part without affecting the basic structure | True
  [21:1:8.2] Limited amending power is a basic feature | True – Minerva Mills
  [21:1:8.3] Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) declared the welfare state basic | False – welfare state: Kesavananda / Bhim Singhji (1981); Kumar Padma Prasad was about judicial independence in appointing judges
[21:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.180, p.259, p.262-263, p.324-325 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.94, p.98-99 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 2 | Evolution – Shankari Prasad to the NJAC Case
[21:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Case / event | Contribution
  [21:2:0.0] 1951 | Shankari Prasad | Art. 368 includes power to amend FRs; an amendment is not "law" under Art. 13
  [21:2:0.1] 1965 | Sajjan Singh | Upheld the 17th Amendment; reaffirmed Shankari Prasad; Mudholkar dissent
  [21:2:0.2] 1967 | Golaknath | Challenged the 17th (not the 24th); 11 judges, 6:5; FRs "transcendental and immutable"; amendment is "law"; Parliament cannot amend (abridge) FRs; first use of prospective overruling
  [21:2:0.3] 1971 | 24th Amendment | Parliament's reply – Art. 13(4), Art. 368: Parliament can abridge FRs
  [21:2:0.4] 1973 | Kesavananda Bharati | Basic structure; Golaknath overruled; 24th upheld
  [21:2:0.5] 1975 | Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain | First application; struck Art. 329A(4) (39th Amendment) putting the PM's and Speaker's election beyond courts; free and fair elections, rule of law, democracy basic
  [21:2:0.6] 1976 | 42nd Amendment | Art. 368(4), (5): no limit on the amending power, no court review
  [21:2:0.7] 1980 | Minerva Mills | Struck 368(4), (5) and the widened 31C; judicial review, limited amending power, FR–DPSP harmony basic
  [21:2:0.8] 1981 | Waman Rao | Doctrine applies to amendments after 24 April 1973
  [21:2:0.9] 1994 | S.R. Bommai | Nine judges; secularism, federalism basic
  [21:2:0.10] 2007 | I.R. Coelho | Nine judges; post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws reviewable
  [21:2:0.11] 2015 | NJAC case (SC Advocates-on-Record Assn.) | 99th Amendment (2014) and NJAC Act struck, 4:1 – judicial independence
[21:2:1] - **1967** key judgment on FRs = **Golak Nath v. State of Punjab** – the case that said **Fundamental Rights cannot be amended**.
[21:2:2] - Case by which Parliament got (back) the right to amend FRs = **Kesavananda Bharati** – it upheld the 24th Amendment after Golaknath had denied the power (Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh had also allowed it before 1967).
[21:2:3] - **Judicial review** was **explicitly held a basic feature in Minerva Mills (1980)** – the 42nd Amendment's bar on review was struck "as it excludes judicial review, which is a basic feature"; reaffirmed in S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) and **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
[21:2:4] - The term "**judicial review**" is **nowhere defined or used** in the Constitution; Arts. 13, 32, 226 confer the power.
[21:2:5] - **Election bar** for the PM was the **39th Amendment** (not the 42nd) – struck in Raj Narain; the **99th (NJAC)** was struck for violating **judicial independence** (UPSC 2019: only II correct).
[21:2:6] - Benches: Golaknath **11, 6:5** | Kesavananda **13, 7:6** | NJAC **4:1** | Bommai and Coelho **9**.
[21:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.180-182, p.258-262, p.326 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.93-94, p.98 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.59-61 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 3 | Elements Declared Basic Structure → Case
[21:3:0] TABLE head: Element | Case
  [21:3:0.0] Supremacy of Constitution; sovereign democratic republic; secularism; federalism; separation of powers; parliamentary system; unity and sovereignty; welfare state; individual dignity | Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
  [21:3:0.1] Free and fair elections, democracy, rule of law, equality | Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
  [21:3:0.2] Judicial review, limited amending power, FR–DPSP harmony | Minerva Mills (1980)
  [21:3:0.3] Welfare state | Bhim Singhji (1981)
  [21:3:0.4] Rule of law; judicial review | P. Sambamurthy (1987)
  [21:3:0.5] SC powers under Arts. 32, 136, 141, 142 | Delhi Judicial Service Association (1991)
  [21:3:0.6] Principle of equality | Indra Sawhney (1992)
  [21:3:0.7] Secularism (reaffirmed), federalism | S.R. Bommai (1994)
  [21:3:0.8] HC powers under Arts. 226, 227; judicial review | L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
  [21:3:0.9] Independent judiciary | Kumar Padma Prasad (1992); All India Judges Assn. (2002); NJAC (2015)
  [21:3:0.10] Free and fair elections, democracy | Kuldip Nayar (2006)
[21:3:1] - **S.R. Bommai** = the case in which **secularism** was upheld as a basic feature (not liberalism, dignity or freedom of religion; not D.S. Nakara, Common Cause or Sajjan Singh).
[21:3:2] - Secularism was basic **even before the 42nd Amendment (1976)** put "secular" in the Preamble.
[21:3:3] - Basic features **not amendable** under Art. 368 include **sovereignty, territorial integrity, federal system, judicial review and parliamentary system** – all five (SSC 2007).
[21:3:4] - **Judicial activism** is a judicial practice, **not a basic feature**; federation, secularism and judicial review are.
[21:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.259, p.262-263, p.327 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.98-99 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 4 | Ninth Schedule, Articles 31A–31C and the Coelho Case
[21:4:0] - Created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B** (and 31A); it also added **Art. 15(4)** and new **Art. 19(2)** grounds (public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence). Purpose: protect **land-reform** laws.
[21:4:1] - Covers **Central and State** laws; entries made **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment** (UPSC 2018 statement I true) – not by ordinary law, a State Legislature or a Presidential order.
[21:4:2] - Example: **76th Amendment, 1994** placed **Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation** Act. Entries: **13** at the start → **282** now (more than 280).
[21:4:3] TABLE head: Case | Year | Rule
  [21:4:3.0] Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Amendments, including inclusions, cannot destroy the basic structure
  [21:4:3.1] Waman Rao | 1981 | Cut-off 24 April 1973; later entries open to challenge
  [21:4:3.2] I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu | 2007 | Nine judges; no blanket immunity; "rights test / direct impact test" on the essence of Arts. 14, 19, 21
[21:4:4] - So "the validity of a law placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be examined by any court" is **false** – UPSC 2018 answer **"1 only"**.
[21:4:5] - **Coelho** = the "**Ninth Schedule case**" (not the Seventh, Eighth or Tenth).
[21:4:6] - Sequence: **1st Amendment (1951) → Kesavananda (1973) → Waman Rao (1981) → Coelho (2007)**.
[21:4:7] TABLE head: Article | Saves | Inserted by
  [21:4:7.0] 31A | Estate acquisition, agrarian reform laws from Arts. 14, 19 | 1st Amendment, 1951
  [21:4:7.1] 31B | Ninth Schedule laws | 1st Amendment, 1951
  [21:4:7.2] 31C | Laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c) from Arts. 14, 19 | 25th Amendment, 1971 (not the First); widened by the 42nd
[21:4:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.70, p.99-101 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.258 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt)
## SUB 5 | Supreme Court vs Parliament – Doctrines, Supremacy, Criticism
[21:5:0] TABLE head: Doctrine / rule | Origin
  [21:5:0.0] Basic structure | Supreme Court – Kesavananda (1973)
  [21:5:0.1] Eclipse, severability, pith and substance, colourable legislation, harmonious construction, territorial nexus | Supreme Court (interpretive doctrines)
  [21:5:0.2] Prospective overruling | Supreme Court – Golaknath (1967)
  [21:5:0.3] DPSP primacy over Arts. 14, 19 (Art. 31C) | Parliament – 25th Amendment (1971)
  [21:5:0.4] Art. 13(4) | Parliament – 24th Amendment
  [21:5:0.5] Unlimited amending power (Art. 368(4), (5)) | Parliament – 42nd; struck in Minerva Mills
[21:5:1] - The doctrine rests on **supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts**.
[21:5:2] - Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**: written supreme Constitution, FRs, judicial review, federal division, **limited** amending power. India = a **synthesis** of American judicial supremacy and British parliamentary supremacy.
[21:5:3] - The **43rd Amendment (1977)** removed the 42nd Amendment's bar on High Courts reviewing central laws.
[21:5:4] TABLE head: View | Argument
  [21:5:4.0] Criticism | No textual definition; "judicial rewriting" by unelected judges; open-ended list; "judicial supremacy"
  [21:5:4.1] Defence | Shield against majorities; checks misuse of Art. 368
[21:5:5] - **2026**: free and fair elections and democracy as basic features cited in the debate on making **voting** more than a statutory right.
[21:5:6] - **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** (simultaneous polls), JPC: ex-CJI **B.R. Gavai** – no violation of basic structure; ex-CJIs **U.U. Lalit** and **Sanjiv Khanna** raised doubts (as of 2026).
[21:5:7] - Cannot be done even by an Art. 368 amendment: **destroying the basic structure** (amending FRs, the Preamble or adding to the Ninth Schedule can be done).

=== NOTES 2:24 | Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
## SUB 0 | Constitutional Government = Limited Government
[24:0:0] - **Constitutional government** by definition = **limited government** – a government **limited by the terms of the Constitution** (UPSC 2020, 2021 ×2) – not "government by the legislature", "popular", "multi-party", "federal structure" or a head with nominal/real powers.
[24:0:1] - "**Persons may change but rules should not change**" = principle of **constitutional government** (rule of law, not of persons).
[24:0:2] - In a democracy the powers of the government are limited by the **Constitution**.
[24:0:3] - **Constitutionalism**: limits + rule of law + checks and balances + judicial review + FRs; a **legislative majority cannot override constitutional limitations**.
[24:0:4] - Not an indication of true democracy: "**rule by majority only**" – free and fair elections, respect for the individual and equality before law are.
[24:0:5] - **PIL** is **not indispensable** for the rule of law, which existed before PIL through **Arts. 14, 32, 226**.
[24:0:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.21 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.325 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); app notes 2:24
## SUB 1 | Separation of Powers – Montesquieu and the Indian Degree
[24:1:0] - **Montesquieu**: **division of powers** best protects liberty; "**The Spirit of Laws**" (**1748**); drew on the **British** constitution.
[24:1:1] - **Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy = separation of powers** (UPSC 2021) – not a committed judiciary, centralisation or an elected government.
[24:1:2] - **Presidential** government operates on **separation of powers**; **parliamentary** = **fusion** (ministers drawn from and responsible to the legislature). Division of powers between Centre and States = federalism.
[24:1:3] - The organ made up of the **people's elected representatives** = the **legislature** (judges are appointed; the media is not an organ of government).
[24:1:4] - India: **Nominal head** President; **real executive** Council of Ministers. **Ambedkar** preferred **responsibility over stability**; reasons: familiarity (1919/1935 Acts), diversity, avoiding American-style deadlock.
[24:1:5] - India: **no rigid separation** – implicit, not absolute, **functional**; overlaps → checks and balances (**Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955**). Separation of powers = basic feature (**Kesavananda, 1973**).
[24:1:6] - **Art. 50 (DPSP)**: separate the judiciary from the executive **in the public services of the State**. Judiciary insulated: **Arts. 50, 121, 211, 235**.
[24:1:7] - **Munro's Madras Regulations (1816)** reversed the Cornwallis separation – the **Collector** again got **magisterial and police powers**.
[24:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.105 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.325 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); app notes 2:24
## SUB 2 | Legislature Over Executive
[24:2:0] - In India the **executive is subordinate to the legislature** – the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
[24:2:1] TABLE head: Device | Purpose
  [24:2:1.0] Question Hour, Zero Hour | Daily watch
  [24:2:1.1] No-confidence motion | Removes the government – Lok Sabha only
  [24:2:1.2] Impeachment (Art. 61) | Removes the President
  [24:2:1.3] Collective responsibility | Art. 75(3) Lok Sabha; 164(2) Assembly
[24:2:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.105 (src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); app notes 2:24
## SUB 3 | Executive Over Legislature
[24:3:0] TABLE head: Power | Union | State
  [24:3:0.0] Summon/prorogue; max 6-month gap | Art. 85 | Art. 174
  [24:3:0.1] Dissolve lower House | Art. 85(2) | Assembly (174(2))
  [24:3:0.2] Address / messages | 86, 87 | 175, 176
  [24:3:0.3] Ordinance | 123 | 213
  [24:3:0.4] Assent / veto | 111 | 200; reserve 201
[24:3:1] - Ordinance only when the legislature is **not in session**; subject to judicial review; laid before the House.
[24:3:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 2:24 (old-notes.txt); Constitution of India Arts. 85, 123, 174, 200, 213
## SUB 4 | Judicial Checks and Overriding a Judgment
[24:4:0] - **Judicial review** of laws and executive action: **Arts. 13, 32, 226**; an ultra vires law is **void**.
[24:4:1] - **Art. 121**: no discussion in Parliament on an SC/HC judge's conduct except on a removal motion; **Art. 211** for States. **Arts. 122, 212**: courts cannot question legislative proceedings for irregular procedure.
[24:4:2] - **Art. 142** complete justice – fills gaps (Vishaka before the POSH Act, 2013).
[24:4:3] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [24:4:3.0] Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) | No rigid separation
  [24:4:3.1] Kesavananda (1973) | Separation of powers = basic feature
  [24:4:3.2] Raj Narain (1975) | Legislature cannot decide an election dispute; 39th Amendment validation of PM's election struck
  [24:4:3.3] Minerva Mills (1980) | 42nd Amendment bar on review struck
  [24:4:3.4] I.R. Coelho (2007) | Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries reviewable
[24:4:4] - Ways the legislature can respond to a judgment, and their limits:
[24:4:5] TABLE head: Option to override a judgment | Limit
  [24:4:5.0] Constitutional amendment | Basic structure
  [24:4:5.1] Validating law | Must remove the basis; cannot simply declare the judgment void
  [24:4:5.2] Ninth Schedule (76th, TN 69%) | Coelho review
  [24:4:5.3] Review Art. 137; reference Art. 143 | Art. 143 advice not binding
  [24:4:5.4] 1st / 24th / 26th / 77th Amendment | Overrode Champakam / Golaknath / Madhav Rao (privy purses) / Indra Sawhney
[24:4:6] - Parliament overrides a judgment by **changing the law or constitutional basis** – not by a simple resolution.
[24:4:7] - **One Nation One Election Bill** (129th Amendment Bill, 2024): amends **Arts. 83, 172, 327** (and adds 82A).
[24:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.324 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.105; app notes 2:24
## SUB 5 | Thinkers on the State and Limited Government
[24:5:0] TABLE head: Thinker / school | View
  [24:5:0.0] Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) | Absolute sovereign power of the monarch
  [24:5:0.1] John Locke | Limited government, natural rights (life, liberty, property)
  [24:5:0.2] J.-J. Rousseau | The Social Contract (1762); general will, popular sovereignty
  [24:5:0.3] D.G. Ritchie | Customary (historical) rights – rights grow out of custom
  [24:5:0.4] Individualists | State a necessary evil – keep it minimal
  [24:5:0.5] Anarchists | State an unnecessary evil – abolish it
[24:5:1] ~~ Sources: Britannica, Leviathan, The Social Contract (britannica.com); D.G. Ritchie, Natural Rights (1895)

=== NOTES 2:25 | President of India – Election, Term, Impeachment and Powers
## SUB 0 | Election – Electoral College, Value of Votes, Disputes (Arts. 54, 55, 71)
[25:0:0] TABLE head: Votes in the Presidential election | Does NOT vote
  [25:0:0.0] Elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) | Nominated members of Parliament and of State Assemblies
  [25:0:0.1] Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies | All members of State Legislative Councils (elected or nominated) – a CM who sits in the Council also cannot vote
  [25:0:0.2] Elected members of the Assemblies of NCT Delhi and Puducherry (added by the 70th Amendment, 1992) | Governors, Lt. Governors; UTs without Assemblies (e.g. Chandigarh, Daman and Diu)
[25:0:1] - **Art. 54** = the electoral college; **Art. 55** = manner of election; Arts. 54 and 55 together = **election of the President** (not Arts. 49, 56, 62, 74, 78, 103).
[25:0:2] - **Keyword – "elected" members**: "all the members of the two Houses" is **wrong** (nominated MPs are out); the correct code is **elected MPs + elected MLAs** (States, Delhi, Puducherry).
[25:0:3] - **Indirect election**: the President is chosen by the elected representatives, not directly by the people, and not by Parliament or the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha alone.
[25:0:4] - **Art. 55(3)**: **proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote**, by **secret ballot** – method borrowed from **Ireland**.
[25:0:5] - PR-STV is also used for the **Vice-President**, **Rajya Sabha** members and **Legislative Council** members; **Lok Sabha** and State Assembly members are elected directly (first-past-the-post).
[25:0:6] TABLE head: Elector | Value of vote | Effect
  [25:0:6.0] MLA | Population of the State ÷ elected MLAs × 1/1000 | Varies from State to State (uniformity among States, Art. 55(1))
  [25:0:6.1] MP | Total value of all MLAs' votes ÷ total elected MPs | Same for every MP, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (parity between the Union and the States)
[25:0:7] - **Population base: 1971 Census** – frozen by the 42nd Amendment (till 2000) and then by the **84th Amendment (2001)** till the first Census after **2026**.
[25:0:8] - **Vote value depends on the population–seats ratio, not on the number of seats**: Puducherry MLA **16** > Arunachal Pradesh MLA **8**; Kerala MLA **152** > Madhya Pradesh MLA **131** (2022 values). So "more Assembly seats → higher MLA vote value" is **wrong**.
[25:0:9] - **Nomination**: at least **50 electors as proposers and 50 as seconders** (since 1997; **10 + 10** from 1974 to 1997); deposit ₹15,000. Vice-President: **20 + 20**.
[25:0:10] - **Quota**: more than half of valid vote value; lowest candidate eliminated and votes transferred by preference (V.V. Giri, 1969, won on **second-preference** votes).
[25:0:11] - **Art. 71**: all doubts and disputes about the election are decided **only by the Supreme Court**, whose decision is **final** (not the Election Commission or the RS Chairman).
[25:0:12] - **Acts done before the election is declared void remain valid** ("not invalidated").
[25:0:13] - **Art. 71(4)**: the election **cannot be challenged or postponed** because of **vacancies in the electoral college** – members of a **dissolved Assembly** simply do not vote.
[25:0:14] - **Election vs impeachment**: **elected MLAs vote in the election but take no part in impeachment** (Parliament alone impeaches); **nominated MPs** do the reverse. **Legislative Councils** do neither.
[25:0:15] > UPSC 1996 (twice) and State PSCs: "part of the electoral college but not of impeachment" = **State Legislative Assemblies**.
[25:0:16] - **Electoral colleges compared**: President = elected MPs + elected MLAs; Vice-President = all MPs; Rajya Sabha = elected MLAs; Lok Sabha = the people – so a **Lok Sabha member** shares no electoral college with the others.
[25:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.370-373 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.136-137 (file pages, src/polity/pmf-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.1, p.6-7 (file pages, src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.22-23 (Sheet #8); Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (1974 and 1997 amendments); ECI, Presidential Election 2022 value-of-vote table
## SUB 1 | Qualifications, Term, Re-election, Oath, Resignation, Emoluments (Arts. 56–60)
[25:1:0] TABLE head: Article | Provision
  [25:1:0.0] 56 | Term: 5 years from the date he enters upon his office; resignation in writing to the Vice-President; continues until the successor enters office
  [25:1:0.1] 57 | Eligibility for re-election – any number of times, no upper limit
  [25:1:0.2] 58 | Qualifications: citizen of India; 35 years completed; qualified for election to the Lok Sabha; no office of profit
  [25:1:0.3] 59 | Conditions of office: not a member of any legislature; no office of profit; rent-free residence; emoluments cannot be diminished
  [25:1:0.4] 60 | Oath before the CJI (in his absence the senior-most SC judge)
[25:1:1] - **Art. 58 – what is NOT required**: **education**, citizenship **by birth** (any citizen), a **maximum age** (there is none). Qualified for the **Lok Sabha** (House of the People), not the Rajya Sabha or a State legislature.
[25:1:2] - **Office of profit**: a person holding an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local authority is **not eligible**; the offices of President, VP, Governor and Union/State Minister are not offices of profit.
[25:1:3] - **Art. 59**: an MP or MLA may contest, but his **seat is deemed vacated on the date he enters upon his office** as President (no prior resignation needed).
[25:1:4] - **Resignation**: addressed to the **Vice-President**, who **communicates it to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha** (not to the CJI, PM, RS Chairman or the electoral college).
[25:1:5] - **Oath (Art. 60)**: to **faithfully execute the office**, **preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law**, and devote himself to the **service and well-being of the people of India** – administered by the **CJI**, not the Vice-President.
[25:1:6] - **Emoluments**: fixed by **Parliament by law**, originally listed in the **Second Schedule**; charged on the Consolidated Fund; **cannot be diminished during the term**. Salary **₹5 lakh per month** (Finance Act, 2018, w.e.f. 1 January 2016).
[25:1:7] - **Term continues**: if the successor has not entered office when the 5 years end, the **outgoing President continues** – the VP or the CJI does not step in.
[25:1:8] - No term limit in India (USA: two terms, 22nd Amendment); only **Rajendra Prasad** has been elected twice (1952, 1957).
[25:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.373-375; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.137-138 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.22; President's Emoluments and Pension Act, 1951 (Finance Act, 2018)
## SUB 2 | Powers of the President
[25:2:0] - **Art. 53**: the **executive power of the Union is vested in the President**, exercised directly or through subordinate officers **in accordance with the Constitution** – so his power is **not unlimited** (Art. 74: aid and advice).
[25:2:1] - **Art. 53(2)**: **Supreme Command of the Defence Forces** is vested in the **President** (regulated by law) – not the Defence Minister, Army Chief or a Field Marshal.
[25:2:2] - **Union executive**: **President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers and Attorney General** (Part V, Chapter I) – not the Speaker or the RS Deputy Chairman.
[25:2:3] TABLE head: Power | Examples
  [25:2:3.0] Executive | Appoints the PM and on his advice other Ministers; Governors (Art. 155), CAG (Art. 148), AG (Art. 76), Election Commissioners (Art. 324), UPSC, Finance Commission; Ambassadors and High Commissioners; administers UTs; Art. 240 regulations for A&N, Lakshadweep, DNH and Daman & Diu, and Puducherry when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved
  [25:2:3.1] Legislative | Integral part of Parliament (Art. 79: President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha); summons and prorogues the Houses, dissolves the Lok Sabha (Art. 85); summons a joint sitting (Art. 108 – presided over by the Speaker); addresses and sends messages (Art. 86); special address (Art. 87); nominates 12 to the Rajya Sabha; assent to Bills; ordinances
  [25:2:3.2] Financial | Budget laid in his name; Money Bills and demands for grants only on his recommendation; advances from the Contingency Fund; constitutes the Finance Commission
  [25:2:3.3] Judicial | Appoints SC/HC judges (Third Judges Case 1998: CJI + four senior-most judges collegium); Art. 143 advisory opinion – not binding; Art. 72 pardon
  [25:2:3.4] Diplomatic and military | Treaties in his name; sends and receives envoys; declares war and concludes peace on the Council's advice
  [25:2:3.5] Emergency | Art. 352 National, Art. 356 President's Rule, Art. 360 Financial
[25:2:4] - **Prior recommendation of the President** is needed for: **Money Bills (Art. 117)**, **Art. 3 Bills** (new States, boundaries), Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, State Bills restricting trade (Art. 304) – not for Constitution Amendment Bills or every private member's Bill.
[25:2:5] - **Reports laid before Parliament by the President**: **Finance Commission** recommendations (Art. 281), **CAG** reports (Art. 151), **National Commission for SCs** (Art. 338), UPSC, Linguistic Minorities – but **not the PAC** report (a committee of Parliament itself).
[25:2:6] - **Art. 78 (PM's duties)**: communicate **all decisions of the Council of Ministers** on administration and **proposals for legislation**; furnish information the President calls for; place before the Council a matter **decided by a single Minister** if the President so requires. With **Art. 86** (address and messages) – all four CDS 2013 statements are correct.
[25:2:7] - **Address to Parliament (Art. 87)**: at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**; the speech is **prepared by the Union Cabinet** (Council of Ministers).
[25:2:8] - **When the Lok Sabha is dissolved** the Council of Ministers continues (Art. 75 needs a Council at all times), and the President still **acts on its advice**.
[25:2:9] - **First citizen** of India; "**represents the nation but does not lead the nation**" (the PM leads).
[25:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.378-386; PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.1-4 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.23-24; Constitution of India Arts. 53, 78, 79, 86, 87, 117, 151, 281, 338
## SUB 3 | Vacancy and Acting President (Arts. 62, 65)
[25:3:0] - **Causes of vacancy**: expiry of term, **death**, **resignation**, **removal by impeachment**, disqualification, election declared void.
[25:3:1] - **Art. 62(1) – expiry**: the election must be **completed before the term expires**; if delayed, the **outgoing President continues** (no vacancy, so the VP does **not** act).
[25:3:2] - **Art. 62(2) – death, resignation, removal or otherwise**: election **within six months** of the vacancy (the office can stay vacant at most 6 months); the new President gets a **full five-year term**, not the remainder.
[25:3:3] - **Art. 65(1)**: in a vacancy by **death, resignation or removal**, the **Vice-President acts as President** until the new President enters office; **Art. 65(2)**: the VP also **discharges the functions** when the President is absent, ill or otherwise unable.
[25:3:4] - While acting, the VP has all the powers, immunities and emoluments of the President and does **not** act as RS Chairman – the **Deputy Chairman presides** over the Rajya Sabha.
[25:3:5] - **Both offices vacant**: the **Chief Justice of India**, and in his absence the **senior-most SC judge**, discharges the President's functions – **President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969** – not the PM, Speaker, AG or CEC.
[25:3:6] TABLE head: Acting President | When | Why
  [25:3:6.0] V.V. Giri (VP) | 3 May – 20 July 1969 | Zakir Husain died in office
  [25:3:6.1] M. Hidayatullah (CJI) | 20 July – 24 August 1969 | Giri resigned as VP to contest; both offices vacant
  [25:3:6.2] B.D. Jatti (VP) | February – July 1977 | Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office
  [25:3:6.3] M. Hidayatullah (VP) | 6–31 October 1982 | Discharged the functions while Zail Singh was abroad for surgery
[25:3:7] - **M. Hidayatullah** – the **only CJI to act as President** (first and only, 1969); the only person who has been **CJI, acting President and Vice-President (1979–84)**; he performed the President's functions **twice** (1969 as CJI, 1982 as VP).
[25:3:8] - **Not CJIs who acted**: P.N. Bhagwati, P.B. Gajendragadkar.
[25:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.376-377; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.138 (file pages); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.10-11 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.23; President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969; presidentofindia.gov.in (former Presidents); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Hidayatullah (acting President 1969 and 1982)
## SUB 4 | Impeachment (Art. 61)
[25:4:0] - **Art. 61** = procedure for **impeachment** (removal) of the President (not Arts. 53, 60, 63, 71, 72, 74, 78); Art. 56(1)(b) refers to it.
[25:4:1] - **Only ground: "violation of the Constitution"** – not corruption, misbehaviour, criminal offence, moral degradation, unsoundness of mind or professional misconduct (the Constitution does not define the term).
[25:4:2] - **Who removes him**: **Parliament** (the two Houses) – not the PM, the CJI, the party in power, a court, or the Lok Sabha alone.
[25:4:3] - **Initiated in either House of Parliament** (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) – not only the Lok Sabha and not a joint sitting.
[25:4:4] TABLE head: Step | Requirement
  [25:4:4.0] Notice | 14 days' written notice, resolution signed by one-fourth of the total members of the initiating House
  [25:4:4.1] Initiating House | Passes the charge by two-thirds of its total membership
  [25:4:4.2] Other House | Investigates the charge (President may appear or be represented) and sustains it by two-thirds of its total membership → removed from that date
[25:4:5] - **Quasi-judicial procedure**; borrowed from the **USA**. **No President has ever been impeached.**
[25:4:6] - **Nominated MPs take part**; **elected MLAs (States, Delhi, Puducherry) do not** – the President is removed by the national Parliament alone, keeping removal free from narrow regional considerations.
[25:4:7] - "Impeachment" is used **only for the President**; judges and the Vice-President are "removed". **VP removal**: Rajya Sabha resolution by a majority of all its then members, agreed to by the Lok Sabha; **no ground** is specified.
[25:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.375-376; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.138 and Part 2 p.1, p.8-10 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.22-23

[25:5:4] - **State with most Presidents**: **Tamil Nadu** – S. Radhakrishnan, R. Venkataraman, A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

## SUB 6 | Constitutional Position, Article 74 and Discretion
[25:6:0] - **Nominal / de jure** executive and **constitutional head of the State**; the **PM and Council of Ministers** are the **real / de facto** executive. A-R: "the Constitution vests executive power in the President" (A) because "he is the constitutional Head of the State" (R) – both true, R explains A.
[25:6:1] - **Art. 74(1)**: a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President. **42nd Amendment (1976)**: advice made **binding** ("shall act"). **44th Amendment (1978)**: he may **return the advice once for reconsideration**, then must act on it.
[25:6:2] - So the President's influence on ministers = he **may seek reconsideration once** before putting his seal on a matter.
[25:6:3] - **Art. 74(2)**: whether and what advice was tendered **cannot be inquired into by any court**.
[25:6:4] - **Art. 361**: President/Governor not answerable to any court for official acts; no criminal proceedings during the term; **civil proceedings only after two months' written notice**; no court can compel a Governor to perform a duty.
[25:6:5] - **Situational discretion** (no constitutional discretion): appointing a PM when no party has a clear majority; dismissing a Ministry that has lost confidence; dissolving the Lok Sabha if the Ministry lost its majority; day-to-day decisions under a **caretaker government**; **suspensive veto** (returning a Bill), **pocket veto** (keeping a Bill pending); asking the Council to **reconsider** advice.
[25:6:6] - **Not discretionary**: **summoning and proroguing Parliament**, appointing Ministers, appointing the majority leader as PM (a convention), assent to Bills.
[25:6:7] - **PM** = "keystone of the Cabinet arch" – the President is only the formal head.
[25:6:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.377-378; PMF Polity Notes Part 1 p.138 and Part 2 p.4-5 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.24
## SUB 7 | Articles 52–78 and President vs Vice-President
[25:7:0] - **Arts. 52–78 = Part V, Chapter I – the Union Executive** (Chapter II = Parliament; Part VI = the States).
[25:7:1] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [25:7:1.0] 52 / 53 | There shall be a President / executive power of the Union vested in him
  [25:7:1.1] 54 / 55 | Election (electoral college) / manner of election
  [25:7:1.2] 56 / 57 / 58 | Term / re-election / qualifications
  [25:7:1.3] 59 / 60 / 61 / 62 | Conditions of office / oath / impeachment / time of election to fill vacancy
  [25:7:1.4] 63 / 64 | There shall be a Vice-President / VP ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
  [25:7:1.5] 65 | Vice-President to act as President
  [25:7:1.6] 66 / 67 / 68 | Election of VP / term and removal of VP / time of election to fill VP vacancy
  [25:7:1.7] 71 | Election disputes (Supreme Court)
  [25:7:1.8] 72 | Pardon
  [25:7:1.9] 74 / 75 | Council of Ministers to aid and advise / other provisions – 75(1A) Council not above 15% of Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003)
  [25:7:1.10] 76 / 77 / 78 | Attorney General / conduct of business / PM's duty to keep the President informed
[25:7:2] - **President vs Vice-President** – the most-tested differences:
[25:7:3] TABLE head: Basis | President | Vice-President
  [25:7:3.0] Electors | Elected MPs + elected MLAs | All MPs, elected and nominated (no MLAs)
  [25:7:3.1] Qualified for | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
  [25:7:3.2] Nomination | 50 + 50 | 20 + 20
  [25:7:3.3] Removal | Impeachment (Art. 61) | Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha
  [25:7:3.4] Resigns to | Vice-President | President
  [25:7:3.5] Part of Parliament | Yes | No
  [25:7:3.6] Vacancy | Election within 6 months | No six-month deadline (Art. 68)
[25:7:4] - **11th Amendment (1961)** ended the joint-meeting method for electing the VP (now an electoral college of all MPs).
[25:7:5] - **2022 VP election**: electoral college of **788** members.
[25:7:6] - **July 2025**: VP **Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned** (addressed to the President); **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected in September 2025 – **Arts. 65 and 68** in action.
[25:7:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.369, p.387; PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.7-10 (file pages); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.7-8 (Articles list), p.25-26 (Sheet #9); Constitution of India Part V
## SUB 8 | Veto, Ordinance and Pardon – Summary (details in row 26)
[25:8:0] TABLE head: Veto | Meaning | Indian President?
  [25:8:0.0] Absolute | Withholds assent – private members' Bills; Government Bills after the Cabinet resigns | Yes
  [25:8:0.1] Suspensive | Returns once; must assent if re-passed – not for Money Bills | Yes
  [25:8:0.2] Pocket | Keeps the Bill pending – the Constitution fixes no time limit | Yes
  [25:8:0.3] Qualified | Overridable by a higher majority (USA) | No
[25:8:1] - **Constitution Amendment Bill**: must give assent (**24th Amendment, 1971**). The **2025 Presidential Reference** (opinion of 20 November 2025) held courts cannot fix timelines or create "deemed assent".
[25:8:2] - **Ordinance (Art. 123)**: only when Parliament (either House) is not in session; must be laid and **lapses six weeks after reassembly**; may be **withdrawn at any time**; subject to **judicial review**. **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)**: re-promulgation in Bihar a fraud on the Constitution; **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**: **seven judges**, laying is mandatory.
[25:8:3] - **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** (President Droupadi Murmu): SC judges **33 → 37, excluding the CJI** (38 with the CJI).
[25:8:4] TABLE head: Pardon term | Meaning
  [25:8:4.0] Pardon | Removes both sentence and conviction
  [25:8:4.1] Commutation | Lighter form (death → rigorous life imprisonment)
  [25:8:4.2] Remission | Shorter period, same character
  [25:8:4.3] Respite | Lesser sentence for special reasons (pregnancy, disability)
  [25:8:4.4] Reprieve | Temporary stay of execution
[25:8:5] - **Art. 72** (President): **court-martial**, offences against **Union law**, **all death sentences**; **Art. 161** (Governor): State laws; the Governor **cannot pardon a death sentence or a court-martial** sentence (he may suspend, remit or commute a death sentence).
[25:8:6] - **Cases**: **Maru Ram (1980)** – exercised on the Council's advice; **Kehar Singh (1989)** – may examine evidence afresh, **no right of oral hearing**; **Epuru Sudhakar (2006)** – **limited judicial review** on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds.
[25:8:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.380-383, p.386; PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.2-5, p.79-80 (file pages); PMF Lens June 2026 1.13 (src/current-affairs/pmf-lens-2026-06-02.txt); Praveen CA360 May 2026 (Supreme Court judges strength)

=== NOTES 2:26 | Veto Powers, Ordinance-making Power (art. 123) and Pardoning Power (art. 72)
## SUB 0 | Veto Power of the President – Types and Article 111
[26:0:0] - **Article 111**: a Bill passed by both Houses is presented to the President, who **declares assent**, **withholds assent** or (for a **non-Money Bill**) **returns** it for reconsideration. So the power to withhold assent is in **Art. 111** (not Arts. 63, 108 or 109).
[26:0:1] - Does the Indian President have a veto? **Yes** – three of the four kinds: **absolute, suspensive and pocket**; **no qualified veto**.
[26:0:2] TABLE head: Veto | Meaning | Applies to
  [26:0:2.0] Absolute | Withholds assent; the Bill ends and never becomes an Act | Private members' Bills; Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent and the new Cabinet advises against it – not "at all times"
  [26:0:2.1] Suspensive | Returns the Bill once; if re-passed (with or without amendment) he must assent | Ordinary Bills (and Financial Bills) – not Money Bills
  [26:0:2.2] Pocket | Neither assents, rejects nor returns – keeps the Bill pending indefinitely | Possible because Art. 111 prescribes no time limit
  [26:0:2.3] Qualified | Can be overridden only by a higher (two-thirds) majority | USA – not India
[26:0:3] - **Veto by type of Bill:**
[26:0:4] TABLE head: Bill | President (Union) | President (State Bill reserved, Art. 201)
  [26:0:4.0] Ordinary | Assent, withhold or return once – must assent if re-passed | Assent, withhold or direct return – not bound to assent even if re-passed
  [26:0:4.1] Money | Assent or withhold; cannot return (usually assents – introduced on his prior recommendation) | Assent or withhold – so he can veto a State Money Bill
  [26:0:4.2] Constitutional Amendment | Must assent (24th Amendment, 1971); cannot reject or return | Cannot be introduced in a State Legislature
[26:0:5] - The one-time return power can apply to **Financial Bills of Categories I and II**; a Money Bill and a Constitutional Amendment Bill cannot be returned.
[26:0:6] - APPSC G1 2024 statements: "suspensive veto in Money Bills but not Finance Bills" – **false** (the reverse); "absolute veto on Government Bills at all times" – **false**; "**pocket veto indefinitely; the American President has a qualified veto**" – **true**; "objective = checks and balances between the President's office and Parliament" – **false** (the stated objects are to **prevent hasty, ill-considered or unconstitutional legislation**) → **only III**.
[26:0:7] TABLE head: Feature | India | USA
  [26:0:7.0] Absolute veto | Yes | No
  [26:0:7.1] Qualified veto | No | Yes – Congress overrides by two-thirds
  [26:0:7.2] Pocket veto | Yes – no time limit | Yes – President must act within 10 days (the 10-day rule is American)
[26:0:8] > Exam angle: Art. 111; Money Bill cannot be returned; amendment Bill must be signed; India has no qualified veto.

## SUB 1 | Vetoes Actually Used – Pocket Veto and the Indian Post Office Bill
[26:1:0] - **Pocket veto** = the President **keeps a Bill pending with him, without any time limit**, neither approving, rejecting nor returning it – not the Speaker blocking a Bill, the PM dropping ministers or the Rajya Sabha rejecting a Bill.
[26:1:1] TABLE head: Veto | President | Bill
  [26:1:1.0] Pocket | Giani Zail Singh | Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 (power to intercept mail)
  [26:1:1.1] Absolute | Dr. Rajendra Prasad (on the Council of Ministers' advice) | PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954
  [26:1:1.2] Absolute | R. Venkataraman | Salary, Allowances and Pension of MPs (Amendment) Bill, 1991
[26:1:2] - The Post Office Bill question is asked in every form – "refused to sign / did not assent / did not give assent / first to use the power on it" → **Zail Singh** (not Radhakrishnan, V.V. Giri, Zakir Hussain, R. Venkataraman, K.R. Narayanan, Rajendra Prasad or A.P.J. Abdul Kalam). He **did not return** it; he simply kept it pending, and it was never enacted (later withdrawn).
[26:1:3] - Pocket veto used **only once** at the Union level; "the only instance of the President's veto" in older keys means this Bill, though the **PEPSU (1954)** and **1991** Bills were absolute vetoes.
[26:1:4] - **2002**: the **Representation of the People (Amendment) Ordinance** on **electoral reforms** was returned by **President Kalam**; the Union Cabinet sent it back unchanged and he **assented under Art. 123**.
[26:1:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 p.51 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.2; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.23, p.381; Sunday Guardian, "The President who used 'pocket veto'" (sundayguardianlive.com); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. President
## SUB 2 | Ordinance-making Power – Article 123: Basis, Nature, Scope
[26:2:0] - **Art. 123** (Part V): the **President** promulgates ordinances during the **recess of Parliament** – not the Speaker, the RS Chairman or the Attorney-General. Governor: **Art. 213** (Part VI). Not Arts. 161, 200, 201, 356 or 360.
[26:2:1] - Nature: the **most important legislative power of the President** – a **legislative power of the Executive** (President is part of Parliament, Art. 79), not an executive order. Among his legislative powers (summoning, proroguing, assent), the ordinance is the one examiners key; pardon is a judicial power; **adjourning** a sitting is the presiding officer's job.
[26:2:2] - When: only when **both Houses, or either House, are not in session** and he is **satisfied** that circumstances need **immediate action**; none while both Houses sit. Exercised on the **Council of Ministers' advice**.
[26:2:3] - Force: the **same force and effect as an Act of Parliament** and the same limits; **co-extensive** with Parliament's legislative power but **not a parallel** power.
[26:2:4] TABLE head: Can | Cannot
  [26:2:4.0] Amend or repeal any Central Act (or an earlier ordinance) | Amend the Constitution (Art. 368)
  [26:2:4.1] Operate retrospectively (from a back date) | Abridge Fundamental Rights – it is "law" under Art. 13(2)
  [26:2:4.2] Introduce or change tax provisions | Go beyond Parliament's legislative competence
[26:2:5] - UPSC 2025: "amend any Central Act" and "come into effect from a back date" true; "abridge a FR" false → **I and III only**.
[26:2:6] - Origin: a **relic of the Government of India Act, 1935** (Governor-General's ordinance power).
[26:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.386 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.2-3; Rocket Polity Part 1 p.23-24, Part 2 p.82-84 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); Constitution of India Art. 123
## SUB 3 | Ordinance – Life, Lapse, Withdrawal and Judicial Review
[26:3:0] - 1. Promulgated during recess. 2. **Laid before both Houses** on reassembly. 3. **Ceases six weeks after reassembly** unless approved – if the Houses reassemble on **different dates**, the six weeks run from the **later date**. 4. Ends **earlier** if **both Houses pass resolutions disapproving** it (within those six weeks – not "six months"), or if the President **withdraws** it.
[26:3:1] - The President **can withdraw an ordinance at any time** – "once promulgated it cannot be withdrawn / the President can never repeal it" is **false**.
[26:3:2] - **Maximum life = six months + six weeks**: maximum gap between sessions is **six months** (**Art. 85**; States **Art. 174**) + the six-week window – so neither "six months", "three months" nor "indefinitely".
[26:3:3] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [26:3:3.0] Lapse | 6 weeks after reassembly
  [26:3:3.1] Maximum gap between sessions | 6 months
  [26:3:3.2] Maximum life | 6 months + 6 weeks
  [26:3:3.3] Linked limit – Art. 101(4) | MP's unexcused absence for 60 days vacates the seat (prorogation and adjournments of more than four consecutive days excluded)
[26:3:4] - **Satisfaction and judicial review:**
[26:3:5] TABLE head: Year | Event | Effect
  [26:3:5.0] 1975 | 38th Amendment | Satisfaction under Arts. 123, 213, 352 made final
  [26:3:5.1] 1978 | 44th Amendment | Reversed the 38th – satisfaction justiciable
  [26:3:5.2] 1987 | D.C. Wadhwa v State of Bihar | Routine re-promulgation without placing before the legislature = fraud on the Constitution
  [26:3:5.3] 2017 | Krishna Kumar Singh v State of Bihar | Seven judges; re-promulgation may be a fraud on the Constitution; laying is mandatory
[26:3:6] - Ordinances are **subject to judicial review**; criticism – they **bypass parliamentary deliberation**.
[26:3:7] - In news (2026): the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** (judges 33 → 37 besides the CJI) revived the debate on **ordinance misuse and executive overreach**.
[26:3:8] - AP: the State used a Governor's ordinance (**Art. 213**) on **organ-transplant committees**.
[26:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.386 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.3; Rocket Polity Part 2 p.52, p.82-84; PMF Lens June 2026 (2) 1.13 p.3; Constitution of India Arts. 85, 123(2)
## SUB 4 | Pardoning Power – Article 72: Forms and Nature
[26:4:0] - **Art. 72**: the President may "grant **pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions** of punishment or **suspend, remit or commute** the sentence of any person convicted of any offence" – not Arts. 62, 63, 70, 71, 73, 74 or 75.
[26:4:1] TABLE head: Form | Meaning
  [26:4:1.0] Pardon | Removes both sentence and conviction – as if the offence was never committed
  [26:4:1.1] Commutation | Substitutes a lighter form of punishment (death → rigorous life imprisonment)
  [26:4:1.2] Remission | Reduces the period without changing its character (2 years RI → 1 year RI)
  [26:4:1.3] Respite | A lesser sentence for special reasons – pregnancy, physical or mental disability
  [26:4:1.4] Reprieve | Temporary stay of execution (esp. death) to allow time to seek a pardon
[26:4:2] - Commutation changes the **form**; remission reduces the **duration**.
[26:4:3] - Covers: (a) sentence by a **court-martial**; (b) offence against a **Union law**; (c) every **death sentence**. Amnesty is outside Art. 72.
[26:4:4] - Nature: listed among the President's **judicial powers** (UPPCS key: judicial power); strictly it is an **executive power, independent of the judiciary** – he is not a court of appeal.
[26:4:5] - Exercised on the **aid and advice of the Council of Ministers** (**Maru Ram, 1980**) – he **cannot** act without the Central Government's advice; subject to **limited judicial review** (mala fide, arbitrary, irrelevant grounds). So UPSC 2025 → **I only**.
[26:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.383 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.23, p.99-100 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.3-4, p.5 (UPSC 2025 PYQ); Constitution of India Art. 72
## SUB 5 | President (Art. 72) vs Governor (Art. 161) and Clemency Cases
[26:5:0] - **Both the President (Art. 72) and the Governor (Art. 161)** have pardoning power – not the Chief Justice.
[26:5:1] TABLE head: Point | President (Art. 72) | Governor (Art. 161)
  [26:5:1.0] Offences | Against Union laws | Against State laws
  [26:5:1.1] Death sentence | Can pardon | Cannot pardon; can suspend, remit or commute
  [26:5:1.2] Court-martial | Yes | No
[26:5:2] - So "the Governor can pardon a sentence of death" is **false**; the Governor is part of the State Legislature, does not appoint HC judges and has no emergency powers – those statements are true.
[26:5:3] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [26:5:3.0] Maru Ram (1980) | Power exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice
  [26:5:3.1] Kehar Singh (decided 1988, reported AIR 1989) | President may examine the evidence afresh; no right of oral hearing
  [26:5:3.2] Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006) | Limited judicial review – mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds
[26:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.4, p.80 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.297 (Governor, src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.31
## SUB 6 | State Bills Reserved for the President – Articles 200 and 201
[26:6:0] - **Art. 200**: the Governor may **assent, withhold, return** (non-Money Bill) or **reserve** a Bill for the President; the **Governor has no pocket veto**.
[26:6:1] - **Art. 201**: for a reserved Bill the President **declares or withholds assent**, or directs its return (non-Money Bill); no time limit is written in Arts. 200 or 201.
[26:6:2] - **8 April 2025, State of Tamil Nadu v Governor**: indefinite inaction under **Art. 200** held **justiciable**; **ten** TN Bills deemed assented.
[26:6:3] - **Nov 2025, Presidential reference (Art. 143, five judges)**: courts **cannot fix timelines** for the Governor or President; **no deemed assent**; the powers cannot be used arbitrarily.
[26:6:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.2 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.51; old app notes 2:26 sub 3; Praveen CA360 Sep 2026 (Art. 143 reference)

  In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), how many Tamil Nadu Bills were deemed assented?
  *Ten | Twelve | Eight | Fifteen
  x: The April 2025 ruling held indefinite inaction under Article 200 justiciable and deemed ten TN Bills assented.
[g1aa7076f739b] sub6
  Which of the following powers does the Governor NOT have over State Bills?
  *Pocket veto | Withholding assent | Returning a non-money Bill | Reserving a Bill for the President
  x: Under Article 200 the Governor may assent, withhold, return or reserve a Bill, but has no pocket veto.

=== NOTES 2:27 | Vice-president; Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers – Articles 74, 75, 77, 78
## SUB 0 | Vice-President – Office, Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Election (Arts. 63, 64, 66, 71, 79, 89)
[27:0:0] # Office
[27:0:1] - **Article 63**: "There shall be a Vice-President of India" – the **second-highest office** (second highest dignitary) after the President; modelled on the **American Vice-President**, but unlike the US VP he does **not succeed** to the Presidency for the rest of the term – he only **acts** until a new President enters office.
[27:0:2] - **Articles 64 and 89(1)**: the VP is the **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States)** – the VP **presides over the sessions of the Rajya Sabha**. Not the President, PM, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, CJI, CEC or Leader of Opposition; the Chairman is **not separately elected, appointed or nominated**.
[27:0:3] - The VP is **not a member** of either House or of any State Legislature (a member elected VP vacates the seat) – so "VP is a member of the Rajya Sabha" is **false**.
[27:0:4] - As Chairman he does **not vote in the first instance**; he has a **casting vote** in a tie. He does not preside while a resolution for **his own removal** is under consideration.
[27:0:5] - He has a **formal function** – chairing the Rajya Sabha (so "no formal function attached to his office" is **false**). Ex officio **President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA)**.
[27:0:6] - **Article 79**: Parliament = **the President + the Council of States + the House of the People** – the VP, the PM and the Council of Ministers are **not** parts of Parliament.
[27:0:7] # Election (Article 66)
[27:0:8] - **Elected, not appointed** – the only one of VP / PM / Governor / CEC who is **not appointed by the President**.
[27:0:9] - Electoral college = **all members of both Houses of Parliament** – **elected and nominated** MPs (**788** when full). **State Legislative Assemblies and Councils have no role** – so the VP's electoral college is **not** "similar to the President's".
[27:0:10] - **Proportional representation by single transferable vote**, **secret ballot**; each MP's vote has equal value; **20 proposers + 20 seconders**; governed by the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.
[27:0:11] TABLE head: Point | President | Vice-President
  [27:0:11.0] Electoral college | Elected MPs + elected MLAs (States, Delhi, Puducherry) | All MPs (elected + nominated); no MLAs
  [27:0:11.1] Qualified for election as member of | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
  [27:0:11.2] Proposers / seconders | 50 / 50 | 20 / 20
[27:0:12] - **Qualifications**: citizen; **35 years**; qualified for election as a member of the **Rajya Sabha** (not the Lok Sabha); no office of profit.
[27:0:13] - **Article 71**: all doubts and disputes about the VP's election are decided by the **Supreme Court** – final (not the Speaker, President or Parliament); acts done before the election is declared void stay valid. **39th Amendment (1975)** removed the SC's power over President/VP election disputes; **44th Amendment (1978)** restored it.
[27:0:14] > Exam angle: "Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?" → the Vice-President (×10 PYQs); "who elects?" → members of both Houses only.
[27:0:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.8-9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.7-10 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.20-22 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 1 | Vice-President – Term, Oath, Resignation, Removal, Vacancy; Acting President (Arts. 65, 67-70)
[27:1:0] # Term, oath, resignation (Articles 67, 69)
[27:1:1] - Term **5 years**; continues **until his successor enters upon office** (Art. 67(c)); **re-election any number of times**.
[27:1:2] - **Oath** administered by the **President** (or a person appointed by him) – Art. 69.
[27:1:3] - **Resigns** by writing to the **President** (Art. 67(a)) – not the PM or Parliament.
[27:1:4] # Removal (Article 67(b))
[27:1:5] - Resolution moved **only in the Rajya Sabha** (not the Lok Sabha, either House or a joint sitting), passed by a **majority of all the then members** of the Rajya Sabha (effective majority) and **agreed to by the Lok Sabha** (simple majority); **14 days' notice**; **no grounds** stated; not impeachment.
[27:1:6] - "Removed by a two-thirds majority in the Rajya Sabha" – **false** (two-thirds is the President's impeachment).
[27:1:7] # Vacancy (Article 68)
[27:1:8] - Vacancy by expiry: election before the term ends. Casual vacancy (death, resignation, removal): filled **as soon as possible** – **no six-month deadline**; the new VP gets a **full 5-year term**.
[27:1:9] - The Constitution is **silent** on who performs the VP's duties during a vacancy; the **Deputy Chairman** only performs the duties of the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** – he does **not** "act as Vice-President".
[27:1:10] # Acting President (Article 65)
[27:1:11] - On a **vacancy** in the President's office (death, resignation, removal) the VP **acts as President until a new President is elected** and enters office – a **maximum of six months**, because **Art. 62** requires the new President to be elected **within six months** of the vacancy.
[27:1:12] - When the President is **absent, ill or unable**, the VP **discharges his functions** until he resumes.
[27:1:13] - While acting: he gets the **powers, immunities and emoluments of the President**; he does **not perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (the **Deputy Chairman** presides) and draws no Chairman's salary.
[27:1:14] - If both offices are vacant (e.g. the acting VP resigns), the **Chief Justice of India** (then the senior-most SC judge) discharges the President's functions – **President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969**.
[27:1:15] TABLE head: Point | President | Vice-President
  [27:1:15.0] Resigns to | Vice-President (Art. 56(1)(a)) | President (Art. 67(a))
  [27:1:15.1] Removal | Impeachment (Art. 61), two-thirds of total membership of each House | RS resolution (majority of all members) + LS agrees
  [27:1:15.2] Vacancy filled | Within 6 months (Art. 62) | As soon as possible (Art. 68)
[27:1:16] - On the President's resignation, the VP immediately informs the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** (Art. 56(2)).
[27:1:17] > Exam angle: removal starts only in the RS; while acting as President he does not chair the RS but gets the President's emoluments.
[27:1:18] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.8-11 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 (legislative.gov.in)

## SUB 3 | Prime Minister – Appointment, Membership, Tenure (Art. 75)
[27:3:0] # Appointment (Article 75(1))
[27:3:1] - **"The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President"** – **Art. 75(1)** (not Arts. 32, 70, 74, 79, 356, 348); **other Ministers** are appointed by the President **on the advice of the PM**. The PM is **not elected** by Parliament or the Lok Sabha and is not merely "nominated by the majority party".
[27:3:2] - By convention the President appoints the **leader of the majority party / coalition in the Lok Sabha**; in a hung House he uses **discretion** and may ask for a floor test later.
[27:3:3] - The PM has **full discretion** in choosing his Ministers (any person, MP or not) – the President does not counsel him and has no discretion here. The President **cannot appoint a Minister not recommended by the PM**.
[27:3:4] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [27:3:4.0] 54 | Election of the President
  [27:3:4.1] 75 | Appointment of the PM and Council of Ministers
  [27:3:4.2] 155 | Appointment of the Governor
  [27:3:4.3] 164 | Appointment of the CM and State Council of Ministers
[27:3:5] # Membership
[27:3:6] - The PM **need not be an MP when appointed** but must become a member of **either House within six months** (not "of the Lok Sabha" only).
[27:3:7] - May belong to **either House** (UK: Commons by convention); **generally a member of the Lok Sabha**. A PM from the **Rajya Sabha cannot vote in the Lok Sabha** (e.g. on a no-confidence motion) but can speak there.
[27:3:8] # Tenure, salary, death
[27:3:9] - **No fixed tenure**; formally holds office during the **President's pleasure** (not Parliament's); in practice while he has the **Lok Sabha's confidence**. No limit on terms.
[27:3:10] - Salary and allowances fixed by **Parliament** (not the President).
[27:3:11] - **Death or resignation of the PM automatically dissolves the Council of Ministers**; a Minister's death only creates a vacancy.
[27:3:12] - **Convention, not text**: the **PM resigns on losing the majority in the Lok Sabha** (the Constitution does not say so). The Finance Minister's House, regional representation and the Speaker acting as President are not rules at all.
[27:3:13] - The **Prime Minister is the most important political institution in the country** (NCERT Class 9, "Working of Institutions").
[27:3:14] > Exam angle: "appointed by the President" (×8) and "within six months, either House".
[27:3:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9-10 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.13-14 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.20-21 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NCERT Democratic Politics Class 9 ch.4
## SUB 4 | Articles 74, 77, 78 – Advice, Name of the President, Duties of the PM
[27:4:0] TABLE head: Article | Content
  [27:4:0.0] 74(1) | A Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with the advice; he may ask once for reconsideration (44th Amdt, 1978), then the advice is binding
  [27:4:0.1] 74(2) | Advice tendered cannot be inquired into by any court
  [27:4:0.2] 77(1) | All executive action of the Government of India is expressed to be taken in the name of the President (not the PM or "the Government of India")
  [27:4:0.3] 77(2) | Orders authenticated as per rules made by the President
  [27:4:0.4] 77(3) | The President makes rules for the convenient transaction of business and its allocation among Ministers – Allocation of Business Rules and Transaction of Business Rules, 1961
  [27:4:0.5] 78 | Duties of the PM: (a) communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and proposals for legislation; (b) furnish information the President calls for; (c) submit for the Council's consideration a matter decided by a single Minister if the President requires
[27:4:1] - **42nd Amendment (1976)** made the advice **binding** on the President; **44th (1978)** added the one-time reconsideration. **Article 74(3) does not exist.** During a National Emergency the advice stays binding.
[27:4:2] - Under **Art. 78** the PM is the **bridge / link between the President and the Council of Ministers** – not Arts. 76, 79 or 81. Administering Ministers' oaths is **not** an Art. 78 duty (the President does it).
[27:4:3] - **Article 53**: the **executive power of the Union is vested in the President** (not the PM); executive power means **carrying on the business of government** (residuary functions after legislation and adjudication) – true, but not the reason for vesting it in the President.
[27:4:4] - State parallel: executive action of a State is taken in the **name of the Governor** (Art. 166).
[27:4:5] > Exam angle: Art. 78 = PM communicates decisions (×3); Art. 77 = name of the President (×2).
[27:4:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.14-15, p.17-18, p.22 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.2-3 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt)
[27:4:7] - **Ministries / Departments** are created and portfolios allotted by the **President on the PM's advice** under the **Allocation of Business Rules, 1961** (Art. 77(3)) – not by the PM on the Cabinet Secretary's advice.
## SUB 5 | Council of Ministers – Responsibility, Non-member Ministers, Rights in Parliament (Arts. 75, 88)
[27:5:0] # Responsibility
[27:5:1] - **Article 75(3)**: the Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha)** – a **constitutional obligation**; **not to both Houses / "the Parliament"**, even if the PM or Ministers sit in the Rajya Sabha.
[27:5:2] - **Article 75(2)**: Ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President** (not of the PM) – so the **President determines the term and membership** of the Council, on the PM's advice.
[27:5:3] - Members of **both** Houses can be Ministers – true, but that is not why the Council answers to the Lok Sabha.
[27:5:4] # Non-member Ministers (Article 75(5))
[27:5:5] - A person who is not an MP **can be appointed a Minister** (including PM), but a Minister who for **six consecutive months** is not a member of either House **ceases to be a Minister** – **Art. 75(5)** (75(2) = pleasure, 75(3) = collective responsibility, 75(4) = oath).
[27:5:6] - **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)**: a non-member cannot be **re-appointed repeatedly** without getting elected.
[27:5:7] # Ministers in Parliament (Article 88)
[27:5:8] - Every Minister has the **right to speak and take part** in the proceedings of **either House**, any **joint sitting** and any committee of which he is named a member – but **votes only in the House of which he is a member**. So a **Rajya Sabha Minister can take part in Lok Sabha deliberations** (unlike a nominated member, the Deputy Chairman or the Leader of the House in the RS) but **cannot vote** there.
[27:5:9] - **Article 75(1B)**: a member disqualified for **defection** cannot be a Minister until **re-elected**.
[27:5:10] - **July 2026**: a Minister of State's resignation was accepted under **Article 75(2)** after his RS term ended.
[27:5:11] > Exam angle: "responsible to the Lok Sabha" + "pleasure of the President" statement pairs; six consecutive months (×5).
[27:5:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.17-20 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9-10 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.1, p.4 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt)
## SUB 6 | Size of the Council of Ministers – 91st Amendment, 2003
[27:6:0] - Before 2003 the Constitution set **no limit**; the **91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003** inserted **Art. 75(1A)**: total Ministers **including the PM** shall **not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha** (543 → max **81**) – not 10%, 12% or 20%.
[27:6:1] - **Art. 164(1A)** (States): **15% of the Assembly**, including the CM, **minimum 12**; 294-member Assembly → max **44**.
[27:6:2] - Aim: curb jumbo ministries and **strengthen the anti-defection law** (also inserted 75(1B), 164(1B)).
[27:6:3] TABLE head: Amendment | Subject (to avoid the trap)
  [27:6:3.0] 91st (2003) | 15% ceiling on ministries; defectors barred from office
  [27:6:3.1] 92nd (2003) | Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali in the 8th Schedule
  [27:6:3.2] 93rd (2005) | OBC reservation in educational institutions (Art. 15(5))
  [27:6:3.3] 95th (2009) | Extended SC/ST seat reservation
  [27:6:3.4] 97th (2011) | Co-operative societies – Art. 19(1)(c), Art. 43B, Part IXB – not cabinet size
[27:6:4] - **130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025**: a PM/CM/Minister detained for **30 consecutive days** for an offence punishable with **5+ years** is removed on the **31st day**; touches **Articles 75, 164, 239AA**.
[27:6:5] > Exam angle: 91st = 15% (×7 PYQs); the 97th is co-operatives.
[27:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.19 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.21 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 7 | Categories of Ministers; Cabinet; Deputy PM and Other Non-constitutional Posts
[27:7:0] - **Three categories**: **Cabinet Ministers**, **Ministers of State** (incl. **independent charge**), **Deputy Ministers** – the Constitution **does not classify** them; the ranking rests on **convention and the PM's choice**.
[27:7:1] - Hierarchy (top down): **Cabinet Minister → Minister of State → Deputy Minister → Parliamentary Secretary** (Parliamentary Secretaries are **not members** of the Council of Ministers).
[27:7:2] TABLE head: Basis | Council of Ministers | Union Cabinet
  [27:7:2.0] Size | About 60–80 | About 15–20
  [27:7:2.1] Composition | Cabinet Ministers, MoS (independent charge), MoS, Deputy Ministers | PM + Cabinet-rank Ministers only
  [27:7:2.2] Role | Arts. 74–75 body | Core / supreme decision-making body
[27:7:3] - The word **"Cabinet"** was inserted (Art. 352(3)) by the **44th Amendment, 1978** – so the **Cabinet, Council of Ministers and Speaker are mentioned** in the Constitution; the **Deputy Prime Minister is not**.
[27:7:4] TABLE head: Post | Facts
  [27:7:4.0] Deputy PM | Not in the Constitution; appointed for political reasons; oath as an ordinary Minister; confers no power of the PM (K.M. Sharma v. Devi Lal, 1990); first Sardar Patel (1947–50)
  [27:7:4.1] Leader of the House (LS) | Not constitutional; PM if an LS member, else his nominee (Pranab Mukherjee under RS-PM Manmohan Singh)
  [27:7:4.2] PMO | Extra-constitutional staff agency of the PM
[27:7:5] - **AP angle**: **1956 Gentlemen's Agreement** – united AP cabinet **60% Andhra : 40% Telangana**.
[27:7:6] > Exam angle: "how many types of Ministers?" → three; "not mentioned in the Constitution" → Deputy PM.
[27:7:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.18, p.20-21 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams Part 1.2 p.9 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-appsc-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.5 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt)
[27:7:8] - **PM's residence**: **7 Race Course Road** – renamed **7 Lok Kalyan Marg** (Sept 2016).
[27:7:9] - **Deputy PMs in order of appointment**: **Patel (1947) → Morarji Desai (1967) → Charan Singh (1979) → Devi Lal (1989)** → L.K. Advani (2002).
[27:7:10] - **PMO**: the **Prime Minister's Secretariat** (1947) was renamed **Prime Minister's Office in 1977** (Morarji Desai).
[27:7:11] - **Political executive** = PM and Ministers (elected, temporary); **permanent executive** = civil servants such as the **Secretary of a Ministry**.
[27:7:12] - **Sardar Patel** (first Deputy PM) also held **Home, States and Information & Broadcasting** – the **first I&B Minister** of free India.
[27:7:13] - **Deputy PMs (7)**: Sardar Patel (1947–50), Morarji Desai (1967–69), Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram (1979), **Y.B. Chavan (1979–80)**, Devi Lal (1989–91), L.K. Advani (2002–04).

## SUB 10 | Oaths and Resignations – Executive Heads
[27:10:0] TABLE head: Office | Oath Article | Oath by | Resigns to
  [27:10:0.0] President | 60 | CJI | Vice-President
  [27:10:0.1] Vice-President | 69 | President | President
  [27:10:0.2] PM, Union Ministers | 75(4), Third Schedule | President | President
  [27:10:0.3] Governor | 159 | Chief Justice of the High Court | President
  [27:10:0.4] CM, State Ministers | 164(3) | Governor | Governor
[27:10:1] - Oaths of President, VP and Governor are in **Articles 60, 69, 159** – **not** the Third Schedule; Ministers' oaths are in the Third Schedule.
[27:10:2] - **Speaker** resigns to the **Deputy Speaker** (Art. 94).
[27:10:3] - **President**: removed only by **impeachment** (Art. 61) – **14 days' notice**, **two-thirds** of the total membership of each House.
