=== NOTES 2:28 | Cabinet System, Cabinet Committees, Collective and Individual Responsibility; Attorney General of India
## SUB 0 | Attorney General of India – Article 76 and Article 88
[28:0:0] - **Article 76**: office of the **Attorney General (AG) for India** – the **highest (first) law officer** of the country; appointed by the **President** (not by Parliament, the Speaker, the PM or on Parliament's recommendation). Not Arts. 77, 78 or 79.
[28:0:1] - **Qualification**: a person **qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court** – a citizen who has been a High Court judge for 5 years, or a High Court advocate for 10 years, or an eminent jurist in the President's opinion.
[28:0:2] - **Term**: **not fixed** by the Constitution; holds office **during the pleasure of the President** (not the PM, not "for life", not "six years", not "as long as Parliament has confidence"). No procedure or grounds of removal are laid down, so he is **not removed like a Supreme Court judge**. By convention he **resigns when the government changes**.
[28:0:3] - **Remuneration**: such as the **President may determine** (Art. 76(4)) – not Parliament.
[28:0:4] - **Duties** (Art. 76(2)): **advise the Government of India on legal matters** and perform duties of a legal character **referred or assigned by the President** – not a Governor, the CJI or the Law Commission. He appears for the Government in the Supreme Court – the Government's **chief legal adviser and primary lawyer**.
[28:0:5] - **Right of audience** (Art. 76(3)): in **all courts in the territory of India**.
[28:0:6] - **Article 88**: though **not a member**, he may **speak and take part** in the proceedings of **either House**, a **joint sitting** and any **committee** of which he is named a member – **without a right to vote**. So he is the non-member who can participate in Lok Sabha proceedings (not the CJI, the Vice-President, the Solicitor General, the CAG or a Governor).
[28:0:7] - **Article 105(4)**: he enjoys **all the privileges and immunities of an MP** – "not entitled to MP privileges" is false.
[28:0:8] - **Limits**: not a member of the Cabinet; not a full-time government servant – **private practice allowed**, but he cannot advise or brief **against the Government of India**, defend accused persons in criminal cases without permission, or become a company director without permission.
[28:0:9] TABLE head: Item | Attorney General | Solicitor General | Advocate General (State)
  [28:0:9.0] Basis | Art. 76 | Not constitutional (statutory / Law Officers Rules) | Art. 165
  [28:0:9.1] Appointed by | President | Appointments Committee of the Cabinet | Governor
  [28:0:9.2] Tenure | President's pleasure | Fixed at appointment (usually 3 years) | Governor's pleasure
  [28:0:9.3] Rights in the House | Art. 88 (no vote) | None | Art. 177 (no vote)
  [28:0:9.4] Rank | First law officer | Second law officer – assists the AG | State's legal adviser
  [28:0:9.5] First holder | M.C. Setalvad | C.K. Daphtary | –
[28:0:10] - **R. Venkataramani** – AG since **1 October 2022** (after K.K. Venugopal); re-appointed for **two years from 1 October 2025** (as of 2026).
[28:0:11] - AP Animal Husbandry 2023 statements (SC-judge qualification; advise GoI and duties assigned by the President; audience in all courts) – **all three correct**, so "incorrect" = **None of these**.
[28:0:12] > Exam angle: Art. 76 / Art. 88 / Art. 105(4); "pleasure of the President" (not PM); remuneration by the President (not Parliament); non-member who speaks in Parliament.
[28:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.339-340, p.439 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Attorney General of India; Constitution of India Arts. 76, 88, 105(4), 165, 177
## SUB 1 | Collective Responsibility – Article 75(3) and the Parliamentary Principle
[28:1:0] - **Article 75(3)**: the Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha** – not to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole or the President. States: **Art. 164(2)** (to the Legislative Assembly).
[28:1:1] - **Collective responsibility** is the feature that marks India as a **parliamentary (cabinet / responsible / Westminster) system** – not separation of powers, rule of law or judicial review.
[28:1:2] - UPSC 2017: the principle underlying the Cabinet form of government = **a mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people** (not minimising criticism, speeding up work or strengthening the head of government).
[28:1:3] - Features of the parliamentary system: **nominal and real executives**, **majority party rule**, **collective responsibility**, **double membership** (ministers are MPs), **PM's leadership**, **dissolution of the Lok Sabha**. "**Election of the whole Parliament every 5 years**" is **not** a feature – the **Rajya Sabha is permanent** (one-third retire every 2 years).
[28:1:4] TABLE head: Event | Consequence
  [28:1:4.0] No-confidence motion passed (moved only in the Lok Sabha) | Whole Council, incl. RS ministers, resigns – "sink or swim together"
  [28:1:4.1] Union Budget / Money Bill defeated in the Lok Sabha | Loss of confidence – the PM submits the resignation of the Council of Ministers (not just the Finance Minister; the Budget is not sent to the RS or re-presented)
  [28:1:4.2] Government defeated in the Rajya Sabha | None – no resignation, no dissolution, no President's Rule
  [28:1:4.3] PM dies or resigns | Council of Ministers dissolves
  [28:1:4.4] A minister disagrees with a Cabinet decision | Must accept and defend it or resign
[28:1:5] - UPPCS 1993 A-R: "Ministers make policy and civil servants adhere to it" (true) and "parliamentary government works on cabinet collective responsibility" (true), but collective responsibility (ministers to the Lok Sabha) does **not explain** why civil servants carry out policy – **both true, R not the correct explanation**.
[28:1:6] - **Oath of secrecy** (Third Schedule, administered by the **President**) keeps Cabinet deliberations confidential and the ministry united in public.
[28:1:7] - India chose the parliamentary form from experience of the **GoI Acts of 1919 and 1935** and to avoid a personality cult.
[28:1:8] > Exam angle: "responsible to whom?" → Lok Sabha; Budget defeat → whole ministry resigns; RS defeat → nothing.
[28:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.25 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.20 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.3 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliamentary System, Central Council of Ministers
## SUB 2 | Cabinet and Council of Ministers; Individual Responsibility – Article 75(2)
[28:2:0] TABLE head: Council of Ministers | Cabinet
  [28:2:0.0] Wider body – Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers | Nucleus – PM and Cabinet-rank Ministers
  [28:2:0.1] Constitutional – Arts. 74-75 | Word only in Art. 352(3); rest by convention
  [28:2:0.2] Rarely meets as a body | Meets regularly; takes policy decisions
  [28:2:0.3] Collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha | Directs and supervises the Council
[28:2:1] - The word **"Cabinet"** occurs **only once** – in **Article 352(3)** (National Emergency only on the **written advice of the Union Cabinet**), inserted by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978** (not the 42nd, 43rd or 52nd).
[28:2:2] - The Council of Ministers does **not include the Cabinet Secretary** – he is a civil servant, not a minister. Ministers without portfolio and Ministers of State are ministers.
[28:2:3] - The Constitution does not classify ministers into ranks – that is parliamentary practice.
[28:2:4] - **Article 75(2)** – **individual responsibility**: a Union Minister holds office **during the pleasure of the President** (not the PM, the party president or the Leader of the House). In practice the **PM** can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him.
[28:2:5] - A minister who resigns may explain it in the House by a **personal statement** with the **Speaker's consent**.
[28:2:6] TABLE head: Article | Responsibility | To
  [28:2:6.0] 75(2) | Individual | President's pleasure
  [28:2:6.1] 75(3) | Collective | Lok Sabha
  [28:2:6.2] 164(2) | Collective (State) | Legislative Assembly
[28:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.20-21 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Rocket Polity Part 2 p.2 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.25; Constitution of India Arts. 75, 352(3)
## SUB 3 | Cabinet Secretariat, Cabinet Secretary and Chief Secretary
[28:3:0] - **Cabinet Secretariat** works **directly under the PM**; administers the Business Rules. Functions: **preparation of the agenda for Cabinet meetings**, recording and circulating decisions, **secretarial assistance to Cabinet Committees**, inter-ministerial coordination – **not allocation of financial resources to Ministries** (UPSC 2014 → **1 and 2 only**).
[28:3:1] - **Cabinet Secretary**: the **senior-most / highest civil servant (bureaucrat)** of the Union – not the Home Secretary, the PM's Secretary, the Lok Sabha Secretary-General, a Chief Secretary or the Attorney General (a law officer, not a civil servant). "First among equals" among Secretaries; **11th** in the Table of Precedence; chairs the **Civil Services Board**.
[28:3:2] - He heads the **National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC)** for disaster management – not the Home Secretary, Defence Secretary or Central Relief Commissioner.
[28:3:3] - Appointed by the **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet** for **2 years**, extendable up to a total of **4 years**.
[28:3:4] - **6 Aug 2026**: Cabinet Secretary **T.V. Somanathan** given a one-year extension beyond 30 Aug 2026; Home Secretary **Govind Mohan** extended up to 22.8.2027.
[28:3:5] - **State**: the **Chief Secretary** is the State equivalent – in the State Secretariat **every file goes to the Cabinet through the Chief Secretary** (not a Departmental, Deputy or Under Secretary). **G. Sai Prasad** took charge as **AP Chief Secretary** (Feb 2026).
[28:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.24-25 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Cabinet Committees and appendix on Cabinet Secretariat; NDMA – National Crisis Management Committee (ndma.gov.in); old app notes row 28 (sub 6)
## SUB 4 | Cabinet Committees, Business Rules and Reports on the Machinery of Government
[28:4:0] - **Cabinet Committees**: **extra-constitutional**; set up by the **PM** under the **Transaction of Business Rules, 1961** (framed under **Art. 77(3)**); standing or ad hoc; usually chaired by the PM or a senior minister; decisions reviewable by the Cabinet.
[28:4:1] TABLE head: Committee | Chair | Concern
  [28:4:1.0] Appointments (ACC) | PM | Senior appointments – Cabinet Secretary, Solicitor General
  [28:4:1.1] Security (CCS) | PM | Defence, national security, nuclear doctrine
  [28:4:1.2] Political Affairs (CCPA) | PM | "Super cabinet"; Centre-State and political issues; decided caste enumeration in the Census (30 Apr 2025) – not the CCEA
  [28:4:1.3] Economic Affairs (CCEA) | PM | Economic and infrastructure projects – e.g. 3rd and 4th lines on Ballari–Guntakal (Rs 1,264 crore, Jul 2026)
  [28:4:1.4] Parliamentary Affairs | Rajnath Singh (2024) | Government business in Parliament
  [28:4:1.5] Accommodation | Amit Shah (2024) | Government accommodation
  [28:4:1.6] Investment and Growth | PM | Set up 2019
  [28:4:1.7] Employment and Skill Development | PM | Set up 2019
[28:4:2] - **Eight** Cabinet Committees (as of April 2025); not PM-chaired: **Parliamentary Affairs** and **Accommodation**.
[28:4:3] - **GoMs and Empowered GoMs** (ad hoc groups) – the existing ones were **abolished in 2014**.
[28:4:4] TABLE head: Report / Rule | Year | Point
  [28:4:4.0] N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report | 1949 | Reorganisation of the machinery of the Central Government – grouping of ministries; it did not call for a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform
  [28:4:4.1] Allocation and Transaction of Business Rules | 1961 | Under Art. 77(3); basis of Cabinet Committees
  [28:4:4.2] ARC | 1966 | Led to the Department of Personnel (1970), placed under the PM's charge
[28:4:5] - UPSC 2021: statement 1 (Ayyangar committee – minister and secretary solely for administrative reform) **wrong**; statement 2 (Dept of Personnel 1970, ARC 1966, under the PM) **right** → **2 only**.
[28:4:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.21, p.23-24 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Cabinet Committees and UPSC 2021 test paper key (Q3 = b) (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-03.txt); old app notes row 28 (subs 4-5)
## SUB 5 | Cabinet in Practice – Kitchen Cabinet, Shadow Cabinet, Coalitions
[28:5:0] - **Shadow cabinet**: a cabinet formed by the **main opposition party**, its members assigned to "shadow" (watch) particular ministries – a **British (UK)** institution; India has no formal counterpart. Not the PM's inner circle or ministers awaiting promotion.
[28:5:1] - **Kitchen cabinet**: the PM's **informal inner circle** of trusted colleagues and friends (ministers and non-ministers); criticised as an **extra-constitutional power centre** that may bypass the Cabinet.
[28:5:2] - **Single-party majority** eras → criticism of "**cabinet dictatorship**" over Parliament; **coalition era (1989–2014)** → coordination committees and allies' demands weakened Cabinet cohesion and collective responsibility.
[28:5:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Polity Notes Part 2 p.21 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Cabinet Committees / Parliamentary System; old app notes row 28 (sub 9)

=== NOTES 2:29 | Types of Legislatures – Unicameral and Bicameral; Arguments for A Second Chamber
## SUB 0 | Bicameral States and Legislative Councils – Articles 168, 169, 171
[29:0:0] - Part VI, **Articles 168–212** – State Legislature. Unicameral = Governor + Assembly; bicameral = **Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council**.
[29:0:1] - **Bicameral States now (2026): 6** – **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh**. Before the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019** there were **7** (J&K too – its Council of **36** members was abolished in 2019). So APPSC Group-II 2017 "how many bicameral States?" = **7** then, **6** now.
[29:0:2] - No Council: **West Bengal** (abolished 1969), **Tamil Nadu** (abolished 1986), Rajasthan, Goa, Mizoram, Sikkim and **Madhya Pradesh** – the **7th Amendment, 1956** provided a Council for MP but it was **never created**.
[29:0:3] - Largest Council: **UP (100)**.
[29:0:4] - **Art. 168(1)(a)** names the bicameral States (AP and Telangana included); **Art. 169** lets **Parliament create or abolish** a Council **by ordinary law** (not an Art. 368 amendment) after the Assembly passes a resolution by a **majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting**. The AP Council (abolished 1985) was **revived in 2007** under Art. 169; AP's 2020 resolution to abolish it again was **withdrawn in 2021**.
[29:0:5] - **Art. 171**: Council not more than **one-third** of the Assembly and **not less than 40**.
[29:0:6] - Composition: 1/3 by MLAs, 1/3 by local authorities, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated by the Governor.
[29:0:7] TABLE head: House | Dissolved? | Abolished?
  [29:0:7.0] Lok Sabha / State Assembly | Yes | No
  [29:0:7.1] Rajya Sabha | No | No
  [29:0:7.2] State Legislative Council | No (permanent) | Yes – Art. 169
[29:0:8] - **Art. 74 / 163** – Union / State Council of Ministers; **Art. 80** – Council of States.
[29:0:9] > Exam angle: "which State is NOT bicameral" (WB, TN, MP); Art. 169; minimum 40; "cannot be dissolved but can be abolished" = Legislative Council.
[29:0:10] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 2 p.2-3 (src/polity/rocket-polity-02.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.43-44 (2015 list of seven bicameral States), p.257 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. State Legislature; Constitution of India Arts. 168-171; J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 s.57
## SUB 1 | Unicameral and Bicameral Legislatures – India and the World
[29:1:0] - **Unicameral** = one House; **bicameral** = two Houses. India's Parliament is **bicameral** – **Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha** (not "federal" or "presidential" legislature).
[29:1:1] - **Article 79**: Parliament = **President + Council of States + House of the People**; the Vice-President (RS Chairman, a non-member) and State Councils are not part of it.
[29:1:2] - Bicameralism at the Centre first by the **GoI Act, 1919**; the **1935 Act** brought it to some provinces.
[29:1:3] TABLE head: Country | Legislature | Type / Houses
  [29:1:3.0] Japan | Diet (National Diet) | House of Councillors (upper), House of Representatives
  [29:1:3.1] Israel | Knesset | Unicameral
  [29:1:3.2] China | National People's Congress | Unicameral; 2,977 members – the biggest; rubber stamp of the Communist Party
  [29:1:3.3] Sweden | Riksdag | Unicameral
  [29:1:3.4] Spain | Cortes Generales | Bicameral
  [29:1:3.5] Poland | Sejm (with Senate) | Bicameral
  [29:1:3.6] UK | Parliament | House of Lords, House of Commons
  [29:1:3.7] USA | Congress | Senate, House of Representatives
  [29:1:3.8] Russia | Federal Assembly | Federation Council (upper), State Duma (lower)
[29:1:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.43-44 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); old app notes row 29 (subs 0-1); Britannica – Diet, Knesset, National People's Congress
## SUB 2 | Legislatures and Representation of Union Territories
[29:2:0] - UTs are represented in **both Houses**: Lok Sabha seats for UTs; in the Rajya Sabha only **Delhi (3), Puducherry (1) and Jammu and Kashmir (4)** elect members.
[29:2:1] TABLE head: UT | Basis | Assembly
  [29:2:1.0] Delhi | Art. 239AA (69th Amdt, 1991) | 70
  [29:2:1.1] Puducherry | Art. 239A | 30 elected + up to 3 nominated
  [29:2:1.2] Jammu and Kashmir | J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 | 90 elected; 24 seats kept vacant for Pakistan-occupied Kashmir
[29:2:2] - APPSC Group-I 2003: UTs with their own legislatures = **Pondicherry and Delhi** – not Chandigarh or Daman and Diu (J&K joined them in 2019).
[29:2:3] - **17 Apr 2026**: **UT Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026** extends women's reservation to the Delhi, Puducherry and J&K legislatures.
[29:2:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Union Territories; J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 s.14; old app notes row 29 (sub 5)
## SUB 3 | Second Chamber – Arguments For and Against; Rajya Sabha as Federal Chamber
[29:3:0] TABLE head: For | Against
  [29:3:0.0] Double check – every Bill discussed twice; hasty decisions reconsidered | Delay and duplication – does not speed law-making
  [29:3:0.1] Represents States and regions | Abbé Sieyès: "If it agrees it is superfluous, if it dissents it is mischievous"
  [29:3:0.2] Brings in experts through nomination | –

## SUB 1 | Lok Sabha – Composition and Strength (Articles 81, 330, 331)
[30:1:0] - **Art. 81**: not more than **530** members from **States** (direct election from territorial constituencies) + not more than **20** from **UTs** (as Parliament provides – UT (Direct Election to the House of the People) Act, 1965) → **maximum 550**.
[30:1:1] TABLE head: Figure | Meaning
  [30:1:1.0] 550 | Present maximum (530 + 20) – "full/maximum strength" today
  [30:1:1.1] 552 | Old maximum "fixed by the Constitution" = 530 + 20 + 2 Anglo-Indians (Art. 331), till 25 Jan 2020
  [30:1:1.2] 545 | Old actual strength = 543 elected + 2 nominated Anglo-Indians
  [30:1:1.3] 543 | Present strength = 524 from States + 19 from UTs
  [30:1:1.4] 20 | Maximum UT seats ("reserved for / represent UTs" in book keys); 19 actually filled now
[30:1:2] - Some keys ask the 104th-era question as "the maximum per the Constitution" → **552 before 2020, 550 now**.
[30:1:3] - **Art. 331**: the **President** (not the PM or the Minorities Commission) could nominate **2 Anglo-Indians** if the community was not adequately represented. **104th Amendment Act, 2019** did **not extend** it – nomination **done away with from 25 Jan 2020**; **no nominated members in the LS now**. (Governor: one Anglo-Indian per Assembly, Art. 333 – also ended.)
[30:1:4] - **104th Amendment** also **extended SC/ST reservation in the LS and State Assemblies by 10 years (to 2030)**. (10% EWS = 103rd; NCBC constitutional status = 102nd; Sixth Schedule councils' powers = 125th Amendment Bill.)
[30:1:5] - **Art. 330**: SC/ST seats in the LS (first for **10 years**, extended every 10 years); also in Assemblies (Art. 332) and Panchayats (Art. 243D) – **no reservation in the Rajya Sabha**.
[30:1:6] - Strength history: **7th Amendment, 1956** – LS **520** (uniform representation, Art. 81(2)); **31st Amendment, 1973** – **525 → 545** (States 500 → **525**, UTs 25 → 20) and the 530 + 20 limits. (The **1st Amendment, 1951** dealt with Art. 15(4) SC/ST special provisions, Art. 19(2) reasonable restrictions and the Ninth Schedule for zamindari abolition – **not** LS seats.)
[30:1:7] - **Art. 326**: elections to the LS and Assemblies on **universal adult suffrage** – voting age 21 → **18** by the **61st Amendment, 1988** (in force 1989).
[30:1:8] - LS = the **Popular Chamber / House of the People / First chamber** – members directly elected by the people (RS = indirect).
[30:1:9] - First LS: **489** elected seats.
[30:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.348-350 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.328-329 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 Sheet #12 p.33 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 2 | Parliament – Article 79 and the President's Place
[30:2:0] - **Article 79**: "There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the **President** and two Houses – the **Council of States (Rajya Sabha)** and the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)**." So Parliament = **President + RS + LS** – **not** the PM, the Council of Ministers, the Vice-President, the Speaker/Chairman or the Secretariat.
[30:2:1] - Parliament is the **Union Legislature** (legislative body), in **Part V**. Laxmikanth: **Articles 79–122** deal with Parliament (NextGen and keys: "**79 to 123**", counting the ordinance Article).
[30:2:2] - President is an **integral part** because **a Bill passed by both Houses cannot become law without his assent** (Art. 111) – the "**President-in-Parliament**" like the **Crown-in-Parliament** in Britain; the US President is not part of Congress. This "President is part of Parliament" is called the most distinctive feature.
[30:2:3] - **Article 59(1)**: the President is **not a member** of either House or a State Legislature; an MP/MLA elected President vacates his seat. He does **not sit or take part in discussions**.
[30:2:4] - President's legislative role: summons, prorogues, dissolves the LS; **Art. 86** – may address either or both Houses; **Art. 87** – **special address** to both Houses at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year; assent (absolute, suspensive, pocket veto); nominates **12** to RS; **ordinances (Art. 123)** when Parliament is not in session.
[30:2:5] - The **Lok Sabha** is a **constitutional** body (Arts. 79, 81) – the Planning Commission, NDC and the Deputy PM post are **extra-constitutional / not in the Constitution**.
[30:2:6] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [30:2:6.0] 80 / 81 | Composition of RS / LS
  [30:2:6.1] 83 | Duration of Houses
  [30:2:6.2] 84 | Qualifications
  [30:2:6.3] 85 | Sessions, prorogation, dissolution
  [30:2:6.4] 89(1) / 89(2) | Vice-President ex-officio Chairman of RS / Deputy Chairman (from RS members)
  [30:2:6.5] 93 | Speaker and Deputy Speaker
  [30:2:6.6] 100 | Voting and quorum
  [30:2:6.7] 108 | Joint sitting
  [30:2:6.8] 109 / 110 | Money Bill procedure / definition
  [30:2:6.9] 111 | Assent to Bills
  [30:2:6.10] 112 / 114 | Annual Financial Statement / Appropriation Bills
  [30:2:6.11] 330 / 331 | SC/ST reservation / Anglo-Indians
[30:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.348 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. p.327 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Constitution of India Arts. 59, 79
[30:2:8] - **Suspensive veto**: the President **returns a Bill once** for reconsideration (not a Money Bill); if re-passed he must assent.
## SUB 3 | Rajya Sabha – Composition, Election and Nominated Members (Article 80)
[30:3:0] - **Maximum 250** = not more than **238** representatives of **States and UTs** (indirectly elected) + **12 nominated** by the President. **Present 245** = 225 States + **8 UTs** + 12 nominated (233 elected).
[30:3:1] - Election (Art. 80(4)): by the **elected members of the State Legislative Assembly**, by **proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (STV)** – not non-transferable, cumulative or weighted vote. Nominated MLAs and MLCs do not vote.
[30:3:2] - **UTs**: only **Delhi (3), Puducherry (1), J&K (4)** – by an electoral college; **Lakshadweep, A&N, Chandigarh, Ladakh, DNH&DD have no RS seat**.
[30:3:3] - **Nominated (Art. 80(3))**: **12** by the **President** for special knowledge or practical experience in **literature, science, art and social service** – **not judicial matters, not sport** (sport is not listed).
[30:3:4] - Nominees take full part in debates; **vote in the VP's election, not the President's**; may join a party within **6 months**.
[30:3:5] TABLE head: Nominee | Fact
  [30:3:5.0] Rukmini Devi Arundale | First woman nominated (1952) – Rocket's "Nargis first nominated woman" is wrong
  [30:3:5.1] Nargis Dutt | First film actress nominated (3 Apr 1980 – 3 May 1981)
  [30:3:5.2] Vaijayanthimala Bali | Nominated 1993–99
  [30:3:5.3] Sachin Tendulkar, Rekha | Nominated April 2012; no category notified for Sachin – keys give Art (Centre told the Delhi HC the four fields are not exhaustive and cover sport)
  [30:3:5.4] Mary Kom | 2016, sportsperson
[30:3:6] - Jayalalitha – RS member from 1984 (elected, not nominated).

## SUB 4 | Terms of the Houses; Lok Sabhas and General Elections (Article 83)
[30:4:0] - **Rajya Sabha – Art. 83(1)**: a **permanent House**, **never dissolved** (not even by the President); **one-third of members retire every second year**; a member's **6-year** term is fixed by the **RPA, 1951**; casual vacancy filled for the rest of the term; first RS (1952) – retirees chosen by **lottery**.
[30:4:1] - **Lok Sabha – Art. 83(2)**: **5 years from its first meeting**; may be **dissolved earlier** by the President on the PM's advice. During a National Emergency it can be extended by law **one year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after the Emergency ends (5th LS, 1971–77).
[30:4:2] TABLE head: Lok Sabha | Duration | Fact
  [30:4:2.0] 1st | 1952–57 | Constituted 17 Apr 1952; first sitting 13 May 1952; dissolved 4 Apr 1957
  [30:4:2.1] 4th | 1967–70 | Dissolved 1 year 79 days early → first mid-term poll (1971)
  [30:4:2.2] 5th | 1971–77 | Extended twice during the Emergency (about 5 years 10 months)
  [30:4:2.3] 6th | 1977–79 | Dissolved after 2 years 4 months
  [30:4:2.4] 9th | 1989–91 | 1 year 2 months 25 days
  [30:4:2.5] 11th | 1996–97 | 1 year 6 months 13 days
  [30:4:2.6] 12th | 1998–99 | Shortest – 1 year 1 month 4 days (10 Mar 1998 – 26 Apr 1999)
  [30:4:2.7] 13th | 1999–2004 | Constituted Oct 1999 → 13 Lok Sabhas by the end of 2000; dissolved 253 days early
[30:4:3] - **First general elections**: **25 Oct 1951 – 21 Feb 1952** (mostly in early **1952**); **53 parties** contested; **489** seats; first Speaker G.V. Mavalankar.
[30:4:4] TABLE head: General election | Seats polled
  [30:4:4.0] 2nd (1957) | 494
  [30:4:4.1] 5th (1971) | 518
  [30:4:4.2] 8th (1984–85) | 542
  [30:4:4.3] 9th (1989) | 529 (Assam's 14 not polled) – not 520
[30:4:5] - **Normally three sessions a year** – **Budget, Monsoon, Winter** (Art. 85 only caps the gap at six months).

## SUB 6 | Rajya Sabha vs Lok Sabha – Equal Powers and Special Powers
[30:6:0] TABLE head: Equal | Lok Sabha superior
  [30:6:0.0] Ordinary and Constitutional Amendment Bills (no joint sitting for amendments – Bill fails) | Money Bill only in LS (Art. 109); RS cannot reject or amend it – only recommends within 14 days
  [30:6:0.1] Election and impeachment of President; election of VP | Speaker certifies Money Bill; presides over joint sitting (Art. 108)
  [30:6:0.2] Ordinances; all three emergencies | RS discusses Budget but cannot vote on demands for grants
  [30:6:0.3] Removal of judges, CEC, CAG | Only LS can discontinue a National Emergency
  [30:6:0.4] Considering CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission reports | No-confidence / censure only in LS – ministers are responsible to LS (Art. 75(3))
[30:6:1] - **No joint sitting for a Money Bill** because the **Lok Sabha has overriding powers** – the RS cannot block it, so no deadlock can arise.
[30:6:2] - **Financial Bill (I)**: introduced only in LS; equal powers in passage. **No tax without LS approval.**
[30:6:3] - A Bill becomes law only when the **President gives assent** (Art. 111) – not on Cabinet approval, passage alone or SC validation.
[30:6:4] TABLE head: Article | Special power of RS | Condition
  [30:6:4.0] 249 | Authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in national interest | Two-thirds present and voting; valid 1 year, renewable
  [30:6:4.1] 312 | Create new All-India Services (so RS does not share this "equally" with LS) | Same two-thirds resolution
  [30:6:4.2] 67(b) | Start removal of the VP | Only in RS
[30:6:5] - RS can **not** initiate censure of ministers, Money Bills or appointment of judges.
[30:6:6] - **LS dissolved**: an Emergency survives if **RS approves**; new LS must approve within **30 days** of its first sitting.
[30:6:7] - **Presiding officers**: RS is presided over by a **non-member** – the **Vice-President, ex-officio Chairman (Art. 89)**, elected by the **members of both Houses** (Art. 66); Deputy Chairman elected by RS from its members. (LS Speaker, Council Chairman, Assembly Speaker are members.)
[30:6:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Polity Part 1 Sheet #13 p.34-35 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.352 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Parliament (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt)
## SUB 7 | Qualifications and Minimum Ages (Article 84)
[30:7:0] - **Article 84**: citizen; oath before an **EC-authorised person** (Third Schedule form); **25 years (LS)**, **30 years (RS)**; other conditions by Parliament.
[30:7:1] - **RPA, 1951**: must be an **elector in a parliamentary constituency**; SC/ST to contest a reserved seat. **No educational qualification**.
[30:7:2] - RS **domicile** (voter in the same State) required only before **2003**; removal upheld in **Kuldip Nayar v. UoI (2006)** with **open ballot**.
[30:7:3] TABLE head: Age | Office | Article
  [30:7:3.0] 18 | Voter | 326 – 21 → 18 by 61st Amendment, 1988, in force 1989
  [30:7:3.1] 21 | Panchayat / Municipality member | 243F(1)(a) / 243V(1)(a)
  [30:7:3.2] 25 | LS, Assembly; PM/CM from lower House | 84(b), 173(b)
  [30:7:3.3] 30 | RS, Legislative Council | 84(b), 173(b)
  [30:7:3.4] 35 | President, VP, Governor (not 30) – highest entry age | 58, 66, 157
[30:7:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.353 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.102 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Parliament
## SUB 8 | Disqualification and Vacation of Seats
[30:8:0] - **Art. 102** grounds: **office of profit** (exempted posts apart – by a **law of Parliament**, Prevention of Disqualification Act 1959), **unsound mind declared by a competent court**, **undischarged insolvent**, loss of citizenship, a law of Parliament (RPA 1951) – **not lack of a degree**. "Office of profit" is **defined neither in the Constitution nor in the RPA**.
[30:8:1] - **Art. 103**: the **President** decides, on the **Election Commission's opinion**; **Art. 101(3)(a)**: seat vacant **immediately** – no House resolution needed.
[30:8:2] - **Tenth Schedule**: decided by the **Speaker / Chairman**, subject to judicial review – **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**; vote against whip unless **condoned within 15 days**; nominated member joining a party after 6 months.
[30:8:3] TABLE head: Situation | Result
  [30:8:3.0] Elected to both Houses | Choose within 10 days, else RS seat vacant
  [30:8:3.1] Two seats in the LS | Choose one, else both vacant
  [30:8:3.2] Parliament + State legislature | Resign State seat within 14 days, else Parliament seat vacant
  [30:8:3.3] Absence 60 days (Art. 101(4)) | House may declare seat vacant; prorogation and adjournments of more than 4 consecutive days excluded
[30:8:4] - Resignation in writing to the **Speaker / Chairman**; **33rd Amendment, 1974** – may be rejected if not voluntary or genuine.
[30:8:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.353-354 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Parliament
[30:8:6] - **Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959**: exempts listed posts from 'office of profit'; **amended five times** (UPSC 2019).
[30:8:7] - **Arts. 101-104** = 'Disqualifications of Members': 101 vacation of seats, 102 disqualifications, 103 decision (President on EC opinion), 104 penalty for sitting when not qualified.
[30:8:8] - **Absence rule used**: the first member to lose a seat for 60 days' absence was a **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States) member.
[30:8:9] - **Art. 106**: MPs' **salaries and allowances** are fixed **by Parliament by law**.
## SUB 9 | Sessions, Procedure and Privileges
[30:9:0] - **Art. 85**: President summons each House; **maximum six months** between sessions; **no minimum sitting days**. Usually **Budget, Monsoon, Winter**.
[30:9:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [30:9:1.0] Adjournment / adjournment sine die | Ends a sitting – Speaker/Chairman
  [30:9:1.1] Prorogation (85(2)) | President ends the session, not the House
  [30:9:1.2] Recess | Gap between prorogation and new session – ordinances possible (Art. 123)
  [30:9:1.3] Dissolution | Ends the House – Lok Sabha only
[30:9:2] - Sequence: adjournment sine die → prorogation → recess → new session. **Quorum (Art. 100(3))**: **one-tenth**. **Art. 118**: rules of procedure; **Art. 120**: business in **Hindi or English**. RS Secretariat under the **Chairman**.
[30:9:3] - **Privileges**: **Art. 105** – freedom of speech in the House; **Art. 105(3)** uncodified, historically those of the **British House of Commons**; also extend to ministers and the **Attorney-General**; **Art. 122** – courts cannot question proceedings for **irregularity of procedure**.
[30:9:4] TABLE head: Collective (House) | Individual (members)
  [30:9:4.0] Publish or prohibit publication of proceedings; exclude strangers | Freedom of speech
  [30:9:4.1] Be informed of a member's arrest, detention, release | No civil arrest during session and 40 days before and after
  [30:9:4.2] Punish breach and contempt | Exemption from jury service; freedom from attending as witness
[30:9:5] - **Sita Soren (2024)**, 7 judges: no immunity for a **bribe** to vote or speak – overruled **P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**.
[30:9:6] - **2026**: Monsoon Session 20 Jul – 13 Aug; **11 Mar 2026** resolution under **Art. 94(c)** to remove Speaker **Om Birla** rejected by voice vote.
[30:9:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.354-355 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Rocket Polity Part 1 p.102 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. ch. Parliament
[30:9:8] - **Quorum in numbers**: one-tenth = **55** in the LS, **25** in the RS (including the presiding officer).
[30:9:9] - **Art. 120(1) proviso**: the presiding officer may permit a member to speak in his **mother tongue**.

## SUB 11 | Functions of Parliament and Power Over States
[30:11:0] TABLE head: Function | Content
  [30:11:0.0] Legislative | Union and Concurrent Lists; only Parliament can change its existing law
  [30:11:0.1] Judicial | Impeaches the President (Art. 61, notice signed by one-fourth), removes VP, judges, CEC, CAG
  [30:11:0.2] Electoral | Elects VP, takes part in President's election, LS elects Speaker, RS elects only its Deputy Chairman – not appointing the CEC (President)
  [30:11:0.3] Financial | No tax without LS approval; Budget, grants
[30:11:1] - **14 days**: Money Bill in RS, removal of Speaker / RS Deputy Chairman (Art. 90(c)) – not 30.
[30:11:2] TABLE head: Article | Power over States
  [30:11:2.0] 3 | New States – Bill on the President's recommendation; Andhra State Act 1953, AP Reorganisation Act 2014
  [30:11:2.1] 249 / 250 | State List – RS resolution / during National Emergency
  [30:11:2.2] 252 | Law for two or more States on their legislatures' resolutions
  [30:11:2.3] 253 | Implement international treaties
[30:11:3] - The **Deputy Prime Minister** is not mentioned in the Constitution.

## SUB 12 | Expansion and Delimitation Debate (2026)
[30:12:0] - Raising the LS by ~50% (to **~815**) after the 1971 freeze: LS–RS ratio **2.2:1 → 3.3:1**; 15% ministerial cap **81 → 122**.
[30:12:1] - **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026**: LS maximum **550 → 850** – **defeated** in the LS, short of the Art. 368 special majority.
[30:12:2] - **Tamil Nadu Assembly** resolved to keep the LS at **543**. **Law Commission 170th Report (1999)**: 25% more seats by a **party list**.

3. Reassembly in a new session
4. Recess
  *2, 1, 4, 3 | 1, 2, 4, 3 | 2, 4, 1, 3 | 4, 2, 1, 3
  x: The Speaker or Chairman first adjourns the House sine die, the President then prorogues it, a recess follows and the House reassembles in a new session.

## SUB 1 | Powers of the Speaker – Money Bill, Casting Vote, Joint Sitting
[31:1:0] TABLE head: Power | Article / basis
  [31:1:0.0] Decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill – decision final | Art. 110(3)
  [31:1:0.1] Endorses his certificate on a Money Bill sent to the RS and to the President | Art. 110(4)
  [31:1:0.2] Casting vote only in a tie (no vote in the first instance) | Art. 100(1)
  [31:1:0.3] Presides over a joint sitting of both Houses (summoned by the President, Art. 108) | Art. 118(4)
  [31:1:0.4] Adjourns / suspends the House for want of quorum (one-tenth) | Art. 100(3)
  [31:1:0.5] Anti-defection decisions | Tenth Schedule – subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992)
  [31:1:0.6] Recognises the Leader of the Opposition (party with one-tenth of the House); LoP statutory since the 1977 Act | Speaker's direction
  [31:1:0.7] Decides admissibility of questions, motions and resolutions; adjourns the House sine die | Rules of Procedure
[31:1:1] - The Speaker's Money Bill decision cannot be questioned by the **President**, the **Rajya Sabha**, the **Finance Minister**, a JPC or the **Supreme Court**.
[31:1:2] - **Casting vote**: only "in case of a tie when votes are equally divided" – not to save the Government, not for Constitutional Amendments or emergencies; the President, PM and CJI have no vote in the Lok Sabha. The **RS Chairman** likewise has a vote **only in a tie**.
[31:1:3] - **Joint sitting**: presided by the **Speaker**; in his absence the **Deputy Speaker**; if he too is absent, the **Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**; then a person chosen by the members present. Never the RS Chairman / VP, the President, the PM or a minister.
[31:1:4] - A **minister who resigns** may make a personal explanation in the House only with the **Speaker's permission** (consent), not the PM's or President's.
[31:1:5] - Speaker is ex officio **President of the Indian Parliamentary Group** and chairman of the Conference of Presiding Officers; appoints chairmen of LS committees; chairs the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees.
[31:1:6] - Powers list (Raj PCS 2024): presides over joint sitting ✔, Money Bill certificate ✔, does not vote except in a tie ✔; "neither presides nor takes part during his own removal" ✘ (he may take part) → **(i), (ii), (iv)**.
[31:1:7] - **Panel of Chairpersons**: nominated by the **Speaker** (up to **ten**); a member presides when **both** Speaker and Deputy Speaker are **absent** (not when the Speaker's office is vacant). If none is present, the House determines who presides (Art. 95(2)).
[31:1:8] - **Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG)**: an **autonomous body** (1949); all MPs may be members, **former MPs** may become **associate members**; **Speaker** = ex officio President; **Deputy Speaker** and **Deputy Chairman** = ex officio Vice-Presidents; Secretary-General of the LS = its Secretary-General.
[31:1:9] > Exam angle: "Whose decision is final on a Money Bill?" (asked ×9) → Speaker, Art. 110(3); "presides over joint sitting" (×12) → Speaker; casting vote Art. 100.
[31:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.350-351 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliament and ch. 25 Indian Parliamentary Group (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 §24.8 IPG (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Constitution Arts. 95, 100, 108, 110, 118
## SUB 2 | Speaker of the Lok Sabha – Election, Oath, Resignation, Removal (Articles 93-97)
[31:2:0] - **Article 93**: the Lok Sabha **chooses (elects)** two of **its own members** as Speaker and Deputy Speaker – the Speaker is **not nominated or appointed by the President**, not elected by the public or by both Houses, but by **all members of the Lok Sabha**. Speaker's provisions: **Arts. 93-96**, 97 (salary), **100** (casting vote), **110** (Money Bill), **118** (joint sitting).
[31:2:1] - Must already be a **member of the House** when elected – the "six months to become a member" grace belongs to **Ministers** (Art. 75(5)), not to the Speaker.
[31:2:2] - Date of the Speaker's election is fixed by the **President** (Rule 7); the Deputy Speaker's by the **Speaker** (Rule 8).
[31:2:3] - **No separate oath of office** – the Speaker (and Deputy Speaker) take only the **oath as an MP**; the President (Art. 60), VP (Art. 69), PM / ministers (Art. 75(4)) and judges take oaths of office.
[31:2:4] - **Tenure**: not at the pleasure of the President – he holds office **so long as he is a member**; vacates on ceasing to be a member (**Art. 94(a)**).
[31:2:5] - **Resignation (Art. 94(b))**: Speaker → **Deputy Speaker**; Deputy Speaker → **Speaker** (not the President, PM, CJI or RS Chairman). In a State: Speaker → **Deputy Speaker of the Assembly** (Art. 179).
[31:2:6] - **Removal (Art. 94(c))** – of the Speaker **or the Deputy Speaker**: resolution of the **Lok Sabha** passed by a **majority of all the then members** (effective majority) after **at least 14 days' notice** – not two-thirds, not by the President, not by both Houses.
[31:2:7] - **Dissolution**: the Speaker **does not vacate** office – continues **until immediately before the first meeting** of the new Lok Sabha (second proviso to Art. 94); the Deputy Speaker and members go at once. Same for a State Speaker (**Art. 179**); State Speaker and Deputy Speaker are provided by **Art. 178**.
[31:2:8] - No constitutional duty to **resign from his party** on becoming Speaker (UPSC 2025: only I and III correct) – that is a British convention, not Indian law.
[31:2:9] - **Article 96** – while a resolution for **his own removal** is under consideration:
[31:2:10] TABLE head: Situation | Presides | Speaks / takes part | Votes in first instance | Casting vote
  [31:2:10.0] Normal sitting | Yes | Yes | No | Yes (Art. 100(1))
  [31:2:10.1] Own removal resolution | No, even if present | Yes | Yes | No
[31:2:11] - **Chairman (RS)** during his own removal resolution: cannot preside and **cannot vote** (not a member), but may speak.
[31:2:12] - **Art. 97**: salaries of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** (not voted).
[31:2:13] - **14 days' notice** is needed to remove the **President, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Deputy Chairman**; a **Governor** is removed by the President at will without notice.
[31:2:14] - **Warrant of Precedence**: 1 President, 2 VP, 3 PM, **4 Governor within his State**, 5 former Presidents (5A Deputy PM), **6 CJI and Speaker of the Lok Sabha**, 7 Cabinet Ministers – so a Governor (in his State) ranks above the Speaker, and the Speaker ranks above all Cabinet Ministers except the PM.
[31:2:15] - The Speaker is **not appointed by the President** – the CJI and the service chiefs are.
[31:2:16] > Exam angle: "chosen/elected by the Lok Sabha", "resigns to the Deputy Speaker", "majority of all the then members + 14 days", "continues after dissolution", "no oath of office".

## SUB 3 | Sessions, Adjournment, Prorogation, Dissolution; President's Address
[31:3:0] - **Art. 85(1)**: the **President summons** each House (separately or together) at such time and place as he thinks fit, but **six months shall not intervene** between the **last sitting of one session** and the **first sitting of the next** → Parliament must meet **at least twice a year**.
[31:3:1] - **Three sessions** – **Budget** (Feb-May, **longest**), **Monsoon** (Jul-Sep), **Winter** (Nov-Dec, **shortest**) – a **convention**, not in the Constitution; no fixed number of sessions or minimum sitting days is laid down. States: **Art. 174** (same six-month rule); State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings in 2025**.
[31:3:2] - **Session**: first sitting → prorogation/dissolution. **Recess**: the period between **prorogation** and the reassembly in a new session.
[31:3:3] - **Quorum**: **one-tenth** of the total members of the House, **including the presiding officer** – **Art. 100(3)**.
[31:3:4] TABLE head: Device | By whom | Ends | Effect on pending business
  [31:3:4.0] Adjournment | Presiding officer | A sitting, for hours/days/weeks | Session continues
  [31:3:4.1] Adjournment sine die | Presiding officer (Speaker / Chairman) | A sitting for an indefinite period (no date fixed) | Bills continue
  [31:3:4.2] Prorogation – Art. 85(2)(a) | President on the Council of Ministers' advice (Governor in States) | The session | Bills do not lapse; notices lapse (except to introduce bills)
  [31:3:4.3] Dissolution – Art. 85(2)(b) | President – Lok Sabha only | The life of the House | Pending business lapses (subject to Art. 107); the RS is permanent
[31:3:5] - Sequence: adjournment **sine die** → President's notification of **prorogation** → recess → new session. After prorogation, **only the President** can summon the House.
[31:3:6] - **Automatic dissolution**: the LS term is **five years from the date appointed for its first meeting** (Art. 83(2)); at its end it dissolves by efflux of time even without a formal order (UPSC 2004: a, b and c all correct).
[31:3:7] - APPSC G1 2018: "adjournment sine die = terminating a sitting for an indefinite period" (key); prorogation ends the session; dissolution applies only to the LS; adjournment **never** ends a session.
[31:3:8] - **Art. 86**: President may **address** either or both Houses, **require attendance** of members and send **messages** on pending Bills. **Art. 87**: **special address** at the start of the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
[31:3:9] - The address is **prepared by the Union Cabinet** (it states the Government's policy) and is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**; defeat of the Motion of Thanks = defeat of the **Government**, which must **resign**.
[31:3:10] - **Gap between two sessions** – "shall not exceed **six months**" (flashcard).
[31:3:11] > Exam angle: "minimum meetings a year" → twice; "how is six months counted" → last sitting to first sitting; prorogation by the President; recess.
[31:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.362-363 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliament – Sessions of Parliament (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); PMF Polity Notes Part 2 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt); Constitution Arts. 83, 85-87, 100, 107, 174
## SUB 4 | Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
[31:4:0] - The **Vice-President** is the **ex officio Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha (**Arts. 64, 89(1)**) – not the President, Speaker or Deputy Speaker.
[31:4:1] - The Chairman is **not a member** of the Rajya Sabha – so the **Rajya Sabha** is the House presided over by a **non-member** (the Speaker of the LS / Vidhan Sabha and the Chairman of a Vidhan Parishad are members of their Houses).
[31:4:2] - Vote: a **casting vote only in a tie** – not "like other members", not for Amendment Bills.
[31:4:3] - Functions: presides and conducts business, protects members' privileges, is the House's spokesperson; he **cannot dissolve the Rajya Sabha** – it is a **permanent House**, never dissolved.
[31:4:4] - Removal: only by **removal as Vice-President** (Art. 67(b)); during that resolution he cannot preside or vote but may speak.
[31:4:5] - **Art. 91**: when the VP **acts as President** (or the Chairman's office is vacant), the **Deputy Chairman** performs the Chairman's duties; the VP then draws the **President's** salary. **Jan 2026 (Justice Varma case)**: SC upheld the Deputy Chairman's Art. 91 power to decide a judge-removal motion while the Chairman's office was vacant.
[31:4:6] - **Deputy Chairman**: elected by the RS from its members (Art. 89(2)); resigns to the **Chairman**; removed by an RS effective majority after 14 days' notice (**Art. 90(c)**). **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the Chairman.
[31:4:7] TABLE head: Person | Fact
  [31:4:7.0] S. Radhakrishnan | First Chairman (1952-62), two terms
  [31:4:7.1] Mohammad Hamid Ansari | Chairman 2007-17 (two terms) – "present Chairman" in 2016-17 papers
  [31:4:7.2] M. Venkaiah Naidu | Chairman 2017-22
  [31:4:7.3] Jagdeep Dhankhar | Chairman Aug 2022 – resigned 21 Jul 2025
  [31:4:7.4] C.P. Radhakrishnan | Present Chairman – VP since 12 Sep 2025 (as of 2026)
  [31:4:7.5] P.J. Kurien | Deputy Chairman 2012-18
  [31:4:7.6] Harivansh (Narayan Singh) | Deputy Chairman since Aug 2018; re-elected 2020; second RS term ended 9 Apr 2026, nominated to the RS and re-elected Deputy Chairman a third time (Apr 2026) – first nominated member to hold the post
[31:4:8] > Exam angle: "presiding officer of the RS" (×6) → Vice-President; "House presided over by a non-member" → Rajya Sabha; "present Chairman / Deputy Chairman" – date-sensitive.
[31:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.350-352 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliament – Chairman of Rajya Sabha; Praveen CA360 April 2026 magazine "Harivansh Re-elected as Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman" (src/current-affairs/praveen-ca360-2026-04-magazine.txt); Constitution Arts. 64, 67, 89-91
## SUB 5 | Parliament Secretariat – Article 98
[31:5:0] - **Art. 98(1)**: **each House** has a **separate secretarial staff**, but **posts common to both Houses** may be created.
[31:5:1] - **Art. 98(2)**: **Parliament** may by law regulate recruitment and service conditions of the staff of either House.
[31:5:2] - **Art. 98(3)**: until such a law, the **President**, **after consultation with the Speaker** (or the Chairman for the RS), makes the rules; individual appointment orders are issued by the Speaker / Secretary-General.
[31:5:3] - **Independent of the Government (executive)**: the **Lok Sabha Secretariat** works under the **direct control and supervision of the Speaker** (the RS Secretariat under the Chairman) – not the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, Home Ministry, PM or President. It is a permanent body, not a five-year one.
[31:5:4] - Head: **Secretary-General** of each House – appointed by the **presiding officer**; rank of the **Cabinet Secretary**. The idea of a separate legislative secretariat was raised in **1926** by **Vithalbhai Patel**.
[31:5:5] - **Presidential election returning officer**: the **Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha or of the Rajya Sabha, by rotation** (appointed by the ECI).
[31:5:6] > Exam angle: "LS Secretariat under whom?" (×4) → Speaker; "separate secretariat but common posts" (Art. 98).
[31:5:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliament (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.350-351 (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Constitution Art. 98; Lok Sabha Secretariat (loksabha.nic.in)
## SUB 6 | Deputy Speaker and Pro-Tem Speaker
[31:6:0] - **Deputy Speaker**: elected by the LS from its members (Art. 93) on a date fixed by the **Speaker** (Rule 8), communicated to members by the **Secretary-General**.
[31:6:1] - That the Deputy Speaker comes **from the Opposition** is only a **convention** – no constitutional or mandatory provision (UPSC 2017, 2022). Likewise no rule that the Speaker comes from the majority party. (The winner of an LS/Assembly election needs only a **plurality**, not 50% of votes.)
[31:6:2] - **Art. 95**: performs the Speaker's duties when the office is **vacant** and presides when the Speaker is **absent**; when presiding he has the **same powers as the Speaker** and **no appeal lies to the Speaker** against his rulings – he is **not subordinate** to the Speaker.
[31:6:3] - Out of the Chair he is an ordinary member – may debate, move motions, **vote in the first instance**. On being appointed to a committee he becomes its **chairman automatically**.
[31:6:4] - Own removal resolution: cannot preside; may speak and vote in the first instance; no casting vote.
[31:6:5] - UPSC 2022: date fixed by the Speaker ✔; Deputy Speaker has the Speaker's powers in the Chair, no appeal ✔; "mandatory opposition/ruling party" ✘; "moved by Speaker, seconded by PM" ✘ → **A and C only**.
[31:6:6] - **Vacancy**: the LS Deputy Speaker's post has been **vacant since June 2019** – through the whole 17th and the 18th Lok Sabha (as of 2026); in the States, **Jharkhand**'s post was vacant for **21 years** (June 2026). Last LS Deputy Speaker: **M. Thambidurai** (2014-19).
[31:6:7] - **Pro-Tem Speaker (Art. 95(1))**: **appointed and sworn in by the President**; usually **one of the senior-most members** of the newly elected House (list prepared by the Legislative section, sent to the **Minister of Parliamentary Affairs**, who seeks the President's approval).
[31:6:8]   - Functions: **administers the oath** to new members and presides over the **election of the Speaker**; tenure ends when the regular Speaker is elected. Not elected by the House; not the outgoing Speaker, Deputy Speaker or LoP.
[31:6:9] > Exam angle: "Deputy Speaker from the Opposition – Constitution?" → only convention; "function of the Pro-Tem Speaker" → oath to members.
[31:6:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams p.350-351 (Deputy Speaker, Pro Tem) (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt); Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. Parliament – Deputy Speaker, Speaker Pro Tem (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt); Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure Rules 7-9; PRS India "Electing a Speaker & Deputy Speaker"; news reports Feb-Mar 2026 on the vacancy

=== NOTES 2:33 | Legislative Procedure – Ordinary, Money, Financial and Constitutional Amendment Bills; Joint Sitting
## SUB 0 | Joint Sitting of the Two Houses – Article 108
[33:0:0] # When it is held
[33:0:1] - **Article 108** = joint sitting; **Art. 109** = Money Bill procedure; **Art. 110** = definition of a Money Bill; **Art. 118(4)** = Speaker presides. "Art. 109 provides for the joint sitting" is **false**.
[33:0:2] - **Deadlock grounds** (after one House passes a Bill and sends it to the other): (1) the other House **rejects** it; (2) the Houses **finally disagree on amendments**; (3) more than **six months** pass without the other House passing it (periods of prorogation or adjournment for more than **4 consecutive days** are not counted).
[33:0:3] - "Both Houses agree to a joint sitting for speedy legislation" is **not** a ground – a joint sitting is only a deadlock-breaking device.
[33:0:4] - **Applies to:** **ordinary Bills** and **Financial Bills (I and II)**. **Not to:** **Money Bills** (the Lok Sabha has **overriding powers**, so no deadlock can arise) and **Constitution Amendment Bills** (each House must pass them separately by special majority).
[33:0:5] - A joint sitting is **not** used to elect the President or Vice-President.
[33:0:6] # Procedure
[33:0:7] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [33:0:7.0] Who summons | President – he "notifies his intention" to summon the Houses (Art. 108(1)); not the Speaker, PM or Chairman
  [33:0:7.1] Who presides | Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Art. 118(4)) → Deputy Speaker → Deputy Chairman of RS → person chosen by members present
  [33:0:7.2] Chairman of RS (Vice-President) | Never presides – he is not a member of either House
  [33:0:7.3] Quorum | One-tenth of total members of both Houses
  [33:0:7.4] Majority | Simple majority of members of both Houses present and voting (Art. 108(4))
  [33:0:7.5] Rules followed | Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha
  [33:0:7.6] New amendments | Only those causing final disagreement or made necessary by delay
[33:0:8] - After the President notifies his intention, **neither House can proceed further** with the Bill.
[33:0:9] - If the President **does not summon** the joint sitting, the **Bill comes to an end** (APPSC G2).
[33:0:10] - Bill already **lapsed** on dissolution → no joint sitting. But if the **Lok Sabha is dissolved after** the President has notified the joint sitting, the Bill does not lapse and the **joint sitting is still held**.
[33:0:11] - The Lok Sabha, with greater numbers, normally wins at a joint sitting.
[33:0:12] # Joint sittings held – only three
[33:0:13] TABLE head: Year | Bill
  [33:0:13.0] 1961 (first) | Dowry Prohibition Bill, 1959/60
  [33:0:13.1] 1978 | Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill, 1977
  [33:0:13.2] 2002 (last) | Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA)
[33:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.50-56, p.355; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.362-363; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.51
## SUB 1 | Money Bill – Articles 109 and 110
[33:1:0] # Definition – Art. 110(1)
[33:1:1] - A Bill is a Money Bill if it contains **only** provisions on: (a) imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any **tax**; (b) regulation of **borrowing** or the **giving of any guarantee** by the Government of India; (c) **custody** of the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund, payments into or withdrawals from them; (d) **appropriation** out of the CFI; (e) declaring expenditure **charged** on the CFI; (f) receipt, custody or issue of money of the CFI or Public Account, or the **audit of accounts of the Union or of a State**; (g) incidental matters.
[33:1:2] - **Not** Money Bills merely because they provide for (Art. 110(2)): **fines/penalties**, **fees for licences or services**, **taxes by local bodies** for local purposes.
[33:1:3] - **Speaker** decides finally whether a Bill is a Money Bill and **certifies** it (Art. 110(3)); the decision cannot be questioned in any court, in either House or by the President.
[33:1:4] # Procedure – Art. 109
[33:1:5] - Introduced **only in the Lok Sabha**, **only by a minister**, **only on the President's recommendation** (not the PM's). Never in the Rajya Sabha or a joint sitting.
[33:1:6] - **Rajya Sabha**: **cannot amend or reject** it; can only make **recommendations** and must return it within **14 days** (two weeks) – the maximum it can delay it.
[33:1:7] - **Lok Sabha may accept or reject** all or any of the RS recommendations – it is **not bound** to accept them, and no 14-day limit applies to the LS.
[33:1:8] - RS amends it substantially → the LS **may still proceed**, accepting or not accepting the recommendations. Not returned within 14 days → **deemed passed by both Houses** in the form passed by the LS, and sent to the President.
[33:1:9] - So **RS approval is not necessary** to pass a Money Bill; RS "has no power" over it beyond delay of 14 days.
[33:1:10] - **President**: may **give or withhold assent** but **cannot return** a Money Bill for reconsideration (normally assents, as it came on his recommendation).
[33:1:11] - **No joint sitting** for a Money Bill.
[33:1:12] - **Aadhaar Bill, 2016** was introduced and passed as a **Money Bill**; upheld in **K.S. Puttaswamy (2018)**; the Money Bill question went to a 7-judge bench in **Rojer Mathew (2019)**.
[33:1:13] - **Appropriation Bill** is a Money Bill (Art. 114).
[33:1:14] # Rajya Sabha in financial matters
[33:1:15] TABLE head: Rajya Sabha can | Rajya Sabha cannot
  [33:1:15.0] Discuss the Annual Financial Statement (budget) | Vote on the Demands for Grants (only LS votes, Art. 113)
  [33:1:15.1] Recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days | Amend or reject a Money Bill
  [33:1:15.2] Amend or reject Financial Bills I and II | Have a Money Bill or the Annual Financial Statement introduced first in it
[33:1:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.52-54, p.355, p.358, p.360; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.358-360; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.51
## SUB 2 | Financial Bills and the President's Prior Recommendation
[33:2:0] # Three kinds of financial bills (Art. 117)
[33:2:1] TABLE head: Feature | Money Bill (Art. 110) | Financial Bill I (Art. 117(1)) | Financial Bill II (Art. 117(3))
  [33:2:1.0] Content | Only Art. 110 matters | Art. 110 matters + general legislation | Expenditure from CFI, no Art. 110 matter
  [33:2:1.1] Where introduced | LS only | LS only | Either House
  [33:2:1.2] President's recommendation | At introduction | At introduction | Only before consideration
  [33:2:1.3] Rajya Sabha | Recommends in 14 days | Can amend/reject | Can amend/reject
  [33:2:1.4] Joint sitting | No | Yes | Yes
  [33:2:1.5] President can return | No | Yes | Yes
[33:2:2] - **Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.**
[33:2:3] - **Article 117** = "special provisions as to Financial Bills"; Art. 117(1): no Bill **imposing a tax** can be introduced except on the **President's recommendation**, and not in the RS. An amendment **reducing or abolishing** a tax needs no recommendation.
[33:2:4] - A Bill that merely **involves expenditure** (no Art. 110 matter) can be **initiated in either House**.
[33:2:5] - **Finance Bill** = gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals, i.e. how the government collects revenue for the year; usually certified as a Money Bill – so exam keys treat "Finance Bill" as a Money Bill (14 days; President must sign, cannot return).
[33:2:6] # Bills needing the President's prior recommendation/sanction
[33:2:7] TABLE head: Bill | Article
  [33:2:7.0] Money Bill; Financial Bill I | Arts. 109, 117(1)
  [33:2:7.1] New State, alteration of areas, boundaries, names | Art. 3 (either House; simple majority; not an Art. 368 amendment)
  [33:2:7.2] Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested | Art. 274
  [33:2:7.3] State Bill restricting inter-State trade | Art. 304(b)
[33:2:8] - **Ordinary Bills** need **no** prior recommendation (except the listed cases); nor do Constitution Amendment Bills.
[33:2:9] - A Bill for a **new State** can be introduced in **either House** – "must be first introduced in the Rajya Sabha" is false.
[33:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.53-55, p.358; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.360-362; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.50-51
[33:2:11] - A **Financial Bill I** needs **no Speaker's certificate** (only Money Bills are certified), though, like a Money Bill, it starts only in the LS, by a minister, on the President's recommendation.
## SUB 3 | Ordinary Bills – Kinds, Stages and the President's Assent
[33:3:0] # Public vs Private Bills
[33:3:1] - All legislative proposals come before Parliament as **Bills**; a Bill becomes an **Act** only after the **President's assent** (Art. 111).
[33:3:2] TABLE head: Public (Government) Bill | Private Member's Bill
  [33:3:2.0] Introduced by a minister (of either House) | By any MP who is not a minister (not necessarily nominated)
  [33:3:2.1] Reflects government policy | Does not reflect government policy
  [33:3:2.2] 7 days' notice | 1 month's notice
  [33:3:2.3] Drafted by the department with the Law Department | Drafted by the member
  [33:3:2.4] Rejection = loss of confidence in government | Rejection has no such implication
[33:3:3] - Both are governed by the **same general procedure** and pass through the **same stages**.
[33:3:4] - Only **14** Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in **1970** – none "recently for the first time".
[33:3:5] - **9 Dec 2022:** CPI(M) MP **Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharyya** introduced the private member's **National Judicial Commission Bill, 2022** in the Rajya Sabha.
[33:3:6] # Stages – three readings in each House
[33:3:7] TABLE head: Stage | What happens
  [33:3:7.0] First reading | Leave to introduce; Bill introduced and published in the Gazette
  [33:3:7.1] Second reading | General discussion, committee stage, clause-by-clause consideration with amendments
  [33:3:7.2] Third reading | Bill accepted or rejected as a whole – the formal vote/division
  [33:3:7.3] Second House | Same three readings; may pass, amend, reject, or keep pending (6 months → deadlock)
  [33:3:7.4] Assent | President: assent, withhold, or return once for reconsideration (suspensive veto)
[33:3:8] - An ordinary ("legislative") Bill can be introduced in **either House**.
[33:3:9] - **Defamation Bill, 1988**: passed by the Lok Sabha but **withdrawn** before the Rajya Sabha took it up, after press protests.
[33:3:10] # President's options on Bills (Art. 111)
[33:3:11] TABLE head: Bill | Assent | Withhold | Return
  [33:3:11.0] Ordinary / Financial I and II | Yes | Yes | Yes (once)
  [33:3:11.1] Money Bill | Yes | Yes | No
  [33:3:11.2] Constitution Amendment Bill | Must assent (24th Amendment, 1971) | No | No
[33:3:12] - President's powers also include summoning a joint sitting and **proroguing** the Houses and **dissolving the Lok Sabha** – he **cannot dissolve "Parliament"** (the Rajya Sabha is permanent).
[33:3:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.50-52, p.356-358, p.360; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.355-358; Deccan Chronicle / LiveLaw 9 Dec 2022 (NJC Bill); ThePrint (Defamation Bill 1988)
[33:3:14] - **Art. 312**: a new All-India Service is created only after a **Rajya Sabha** resolution (two-thirds present and voting) – a special power of the RS, not a Bill.
[33:3:15] - The LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** also classifies such Bills and examines private members' **Constitution Amendment Bills** before introduction.
[33:3:16] - **Pocket veto** is possible because the Constitution fixes **no time limit** for the President's decision on a Bill (e.g. Zail Singh, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986); India has no qualified veto.
[33:3:17] - **Time for Private Members' Bills**: in the **Lok Sabha** the **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** allots it; the **Rajya Sabha** has no such committee – its **Business Advisory Committee** does.
## SUB 4 | Lapsing of Bills – Dissolution, Prorogation, Adjournment
[33:4:0] TABLE head: On dissolution of the Lok Sabha – lapses | Does not lapse
  [33:4:0.0] Bill pending in the LS (originating there or sent by the RS) | Bill pending in the RS, not passed by the LS
  [33:4:0.1] Bill passed by the LS, pending in the RS | Bill for which a joint sitting was notified before dissolution
  [33:4:0.2] – | Bill passed by both Houses, pending assent
  [33:4:0.3] – | Bill returned by the President for reconsideration (even if the LS is dissolved)
[33:4:1] - **Prorogation** and **adjournment sine die** do **not** make Bills lapse – they remain alive and are taken up in the next session (only pending notices, motions, resolutions lapse on prorogation).
[33:4:2] - The **Rajya Sabha is never dissolved**.
[33:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.356, p.363-364; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.345; NextGen Rocket Polity Part 1 (src/polity/rocket-polity-01.txt) p.51
## SUB 5 | Constitution Amendment Bills and Overriding a Court Ruling
[33:5:0] TABLE head: Feature | Ordinary Bill | Constitution Amendment Bill (Art. 368)
  [33:5:0.0] House | Either | Either
  [33:5:0.1] President's prior recommendation | Not needed | Not needed
  [33:5:0.2] Majority | Simple | Special – majority of total membership + 2/3 present and voting, each House separately
  [33:5:0.3] States | – | Ratification by half the States for federal provisions
  [33:5:0.4] Deadlock | Joint sitting | No joint sitting – Bill ends if one House rejects it
  [33:5:0.5] President | Assent / withhold / return | Must assent
[33:5:1] - Apart from the special majority, an amendment Bill goes through the **same stages as an ordinary Bill**.
[33:5:2] - When Government and Parliament dislike a Supreme Court decision they may **amend the Constitution or pass a law** that removes the basis of the judgment (both options) – not ignore it or change the judges.
[33:5:3] - **Latest:** Constitution (**129th Amendment**) Bill, 2024 (One Nation One Election, new **Art. 82A**) – with the JPC (as of 2026).
[33:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.358-359; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity 8th ed. (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) ch. Amendment of the Constitution; app's old notes row 33 (old-notes.txt) sub 8
## SUB 6 | Assent to State Bills and Latest Developments
[33:6:0] - **Article 200**: the Governor may assent, withhold, **return a non-Money Bill**, or **reserve** a Bill for the **President** (Art. 201). He **cannot return a Money Bill**.
[33:6:1] - **AP Legislative Council** can only **recommend** on a Money Bill within **14 days**.
[33:6:2] - **April 2025** Tamil Nadu Governor judgment: fixed timelines and "deemed assent". **November 2025** advisory opinion (5-judge Bench, Presidential Reference): courts **cannot fix timelines** or declare **deemed assent**.
[33:6:3] - **Monsoon Session 2026**: **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** referred to a JPC; **Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026** ("Keralam", under **Art. 3**).
[33:6:4] - **Andhra State Bill**: introduced **10 Aug 1953**, assent **14 Sep 1953**.
[33:6:5] ~~ Sources: app's old notes row 33 (old-notes.txt) sub 3, 10; NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) State Legislature

  x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
